title: Prisoners of process
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IN Pakistan, the assumption of guilt overrides protecting innocence too often. The process becomes the punishment. A Peshawar High Court bench ordered the provincial government and the officials involved to pay Rs10m in compensation to a man who spent a decade in Karachi Central Prison after completing his sentence in a narcotics case without trial. Administrative oversight was the culprit: officials did not move him to KP on a murder charge. The ruling exposes the sad truth of our legal system — already flawed probation and parole processes continue to worsen. The Annual Prisons Data Report 2026, compiled by the National Commission for Human Rights and Justice Project Pakistan, reveals that consideration of protracted incarceration, delays in trials, and the obstacles to procuring bail is past due. It also highlights that, built to hold 68,832 inmates, jails presently function at over 160pc of their capacity. A staggering 110,513 are crammed in foetid conditions; three of every four prisoners, captive to legal limbo, wait for trial.
Courts need to mend fractures that paralyse lives. For starters, time limits should be set for both investigations and trial duration. Long-undecided undertrial cases can be heard within prisons, particularly those involving women, children, and people with disabilities. Each adjournment adds more time to a verdict that is yet to come. Bail reforms, assessment of remand decisions, and early legal aid are the need of the hour. The NCHR should be empowered to conduct spot checks and introduce separate prisoner complaint systems. Meanwhile, prison management, in order to ensure proper rehabilitation, must include vocational training and education. Rehabilitation programmes are imperative for those charged with minor offences while people with psychosocial disabilities require treatment, not confinement. The 2022 amendment to the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, which slashed parole and probation for drug offenders, has only led to a rise in imprisonments. The answer to this crisis is political will. Key reforms that centralise the right to liberty, beginning with the enforcement of Draft Prison Rules, 2022, which promise inmate wellbeing, cannot be postponed, together with community service and alternative sentencing. No compensation can return time.
Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

title: Love at scale
author: none@none.com (Madeeha Ansari)
content:
RECENTLY, the second Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children was held in Manila. Ministers and government officials from all over the world came together to assert their commitment to protecting children, and to make concrete pledges to work towards in the next two years.
Among the plenary speakers was Dr Nadine Burke Harris, a paediatrician and former surgeon general of the state of California. Her work has been dedicated to making the link between adverse childhood experiences (ACES) — including neglect, violence, poverty and abuse — and long-term impact on adults.
    
Prolonged exposure to toxic stress has a biological response, with negative impacts on health and life potential. These can range from heart disease to obesity and substance misuse, to impact on brain development, with difficulties in learning or self-regulating.
On the other hand, the experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of their difficult realities. Especially if support is offered early, it can transform a future. That’s why, she argued before global delegations, when it comes to child protection, “infrastructure is love at scale.”
The experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of difficult realities.
What this means is that if done right, child protection systems would represent a continuum of care. Right from prevention to recognising the signs for when an intervention is needed, to appropriate case management, response and essential follow-up. Allocating enough resources to have effective referral pathways, trained personnel and data management — that would be an act of love by those with power over budgets.
In Pakistan, the scale of challenges is both vast and daunting. Where do we even start? From children visibly exposed to insecurity on the streets, to those in distant villages quietly experiencing the impacts of climate change on their households, it seems impossible to address all the structural factors behind violence.
Chronic economic stress increases the risk of violence within households, as well as of child labour that sends children out without guardrails. Then there is the plethora of departments that need stitching together — health, education, social welfare, law enforcement. Each one has a role that needs to be clearly understood, so that the doctor or teacher seeing a child in suffering knows how to recognise physical and psychological injury, and who should be handling it next.
The minister for human rights, speaking before the world, shared the launch of a National Action Plan and strategy for child protection. It is apt that the oversight of this strategy falls under human rights, which must be guaranteed to every child regardless of geography, ethnic or religious identity.
However, what is crucial at this point is to acknowledge the need for inter-ministerial and inter-departmental cooperation, for which the MoHR can act as a conduit. The ministry of education and professional training, for instance, has a key role in ensuring that schools are both safe and enabling, and an important point of connection with children and families.
It also has a key role in creating a culture of care for children, with educators beginning to disrupt the normalisation of corporal punishment and violence as a tool for discipline. In that sense, the conference was a unique opportunity to really learn from global experiences of navigating bureaucracy and politics, to get to what matters.
    
All this being said, there are limitations to scale. Social services even in the most “developed” contexts can get it wrong, when mechanically applying standards to children or families under stress.
Love at scale cannot mean that children are not seen for their individual circumstances, or are separated from families without working through challenges. If anything, love will be made up of the countless tiny acts and steps taken by the frontline workers who come into contact with vulnerable children, the conversations they are able to have, the kindness they show in response.
Again, teachers can represent essential allies in a protective ecosystem. Not only do they know individuals, communities and their challenges, but can be reliable sources of support that children see every day. Within a compassionate classroom, they can create trust, joy, and hope for a positive future.
The theme for World Children’s Day this year was “My day, my rights, my future.” This is not the first time we have heard words like this; perhaps that is why it is a time of great reckoning in the sphere of human rights and development, with a tragic deficit of resources and trust in the sector. However, what finally needs to be understood is that civil society alone cannot stop all the gaps, even while being able to offer the state both technical support and insights from community work.
Manila was an illustration of how it is possible to make space for high-level official dialogue as well as learning from academic research, and ground-level implementation experience incorporating children’s voices. If this time we truly want love at scale, it will take all of us, working to cover the crevices that children can fall through.
The writer is CEO of Cities for Children, an organisation that works to protect childhood.
Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

summary: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) like neglect, violence, poverty, and abuse have profound, long-term biological and developmental impacts on adults, ranging from chronic diseases to learning difficulties.

Loving and nurturing support acts as a buffering mechanism against the negative effects of ACEs, with early intervention having the potential to transform a child's future, demonstrating that 'infrastructure is love at scale.'

Effective child protection systems require a continuum of care, encompassing prevention, early recognition, appropriate intervention, case management, response, and follow-up, necessitating adequate resources, trained personnel, and inter-ministerial cooperation.

While systemic 'love at scale' is crucial, it must not overlook individual circumstances; true love also manifests through countless tiny acts of kindness, trust-building, and personalized support from frontline workers and educators, especially within compassionate classrooms.

title: Referendum — a non-starter?
author: none@none.com (Shahab Usto)
content:
THE idea of holding a referendum to ascertain public opinion with regard to the creation of more provinces has been floated by some ministers. The prime minister, on the other hand, remains mum on this highly divisive and potentially destabilising subject.
No wonder Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari — who heads a major coalition party that also has a major stake in the current system — is vociferously decrying the government for keeping him in the dark and not taking him into confidence about the ‘reset’ or the referendum.
But the visible discord among the coalition partners should not be surprising. It is in the dichotomous nature of the hybrid system. The key policies are made outside the political sphere. But the onerous task of implementation is thrown on the shoulders of politicians, often at the cost of their careers and even constituencies.
    
The tradition of setting critical agendas — whether they are related to constitutional experiments, economic shifts, social policies, institutional restructuring, public accountability, internal security, strategic alliances, or war and peace — in secrecy and away from the public glare, is by now quite old. In many instances, even parliament has come into the picture only when the fig leaf of the law or the Constitution is needed to ‘legitimise’ a dubious plan. The ‘decision’ to hold the referendum is also par for the course.
The architecture of the reset has never been elucidated.
Its proponents are fully aware that a referendum can never substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment to alter the boundaries of provinces. They also know the tainted history of referendums, which were called to validate the capture of power by dictators. And they may also not deny the fact, as rightly pointed out by BBZ, that the prevailing sociopolitical and security environment in the country is unsuitable for holding a controversial referendum, that too on such a socio-politically explosive issue.
Yet, the advocates of referendum seem adamant to carry it through. Why? No one can conjecture the answer with surety because to this day the architecture of the reset has never been elucidated. All that we know is that ‘reset’ is ‘desirable’ for good governance and devolution of power to the lowest strata. But this ‘truism’ is flawed, conceptually and functionally.
Conceptually, good governance and devolution being the offshoots of a broader constitutional democratic framework are antithetical to the hybrid system that is extraconstitutional. And functionally, restructuring the entire state fabric requires not only public mandate but an array of democratic tools — an elected parliament, representative governments, independent judiciary, and an apolitical (military and civilian) bureaucracy.
Moreover, the increasingly arbitrary, if not authoritarian, mode of governance also makes the conversation on the imperatives of good governance and devolution rather absurd.
    
This raises a pertinent question: are the proponents of ‘reset’ willing to do away with the hybrid system to make way for a legitimate and functional democracy, fulfilling the ‘intended’ objects of reforming governance and empowering local communities? If the hybridity is to stay, then it would be disastrous to ‘reset’ in the name of good governance or devolution, which are the attributes of a functional democracy.
Even the reset on the logic of size or demographics is grossly misleading. Size and demography are only two of the many dimensions of an efficient democratic system. There are many countries where large and populated provinces are known for their excellent governance. In fact, the standards of measuring the success or failure of a political system lie in the degree of its constitutional legitimacy, electoral transparency, institutional capacity, and public administration. Therefore, the key questions probing the performance of our political system should be: is the electoral system credible? Is the public mandate respected? Are wealth and resources distributed fairly? Are public functionaries accountable? Is the justice system cheap, fair, and speedy? Is public safety and order a priority? Is the republic peaceable? And, are the citizens’ fundamental rights protected?
I would advise the proponents of the ‘reset’ to consider these questions before calling for a controversial referendum that is bound to pit individuals, groups, communities, and even provinces against one another, adding more fault lines to the already much-riven ethno-cultural landscape.
The people have seen enough of the ‘yes-no’ binary questions which were framed in referendums to seek personal legitimacy and institutional empowerment for military dictators, rather than reforming governance or empowering the people. Moreover, none of the referendums has earned a mark of credibility or fairness because they were rigged or state-managed. Therefore, they completely lost their utility or worth in the eyes of the people.
BBZ is not too off the mark when he warns that holding the referendum is ‘near impossible’ because of the insecure environment in the country. But also, the people, particularly in Sindh, would not accept the results of a referendum, even if it is somehow carried out.
Which brings us to the most critical question: what if one or the other of the provinces or a sizeable ethnic community rejected the results of the referendum? This question is crucial because there is hardly any ‘credible’ or ‘neutral’ forum — political, administrative or judicial — to resolve political disputes. Leave aside the grudges of the battered opposition, even BBZ has now cast doubts on the legitimacy of the 27th Amendment that led to the creation of the Federal Constitutional Court. And the FCC is the court of last resort in matters involving politico-constitutional disputes.
    
Given the thick air of mistrust in public institutions, how would a ‘controversial’ referendum act as a stepping stone towards the constitutional ‘reset’? And more so when, among others, the PPP is resolutely opposing the ‘division’ of Sindh.
How would the powers that be garner the requisite numbers to amend the Constitution? It would be tragic to pull off a wholesale restructuring of the state employing the carrot-and-stick method. The multiethnic state of 250 million people is too complex, conflict-ridden and even fragile to sustain yet another forced experiment. It requires meaningful dialogue, consensus-making, and democratic reforms to overhaul its political system, not a non-starter referendum or an arbitrary reset.
The writer is a lawyer.

title: Building tragedy
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
FOLLOWING Wednesday’s building collapse in Karachi’s Baloch Colony, the removal or suspension of over a dozen officials has been ordered. Speaking to journalists, Sindh CM Murad Ali Shah said categorically that such disasters cannot occur without the involvement of government officials. Investigations and accountability are as necessary as pinning responsibility and punishing the errant. But it is clearly not enough. While other officials easily replace those removed, very little is done to address the lack of oversight. As a result, unauthorised buildings are proliferating in Karachi. Much of the material used to raise them is substandard. Technical planning is flawed while owners recklessly add extra floors without assessing the strength of the foundations. Those responsible for monitoring construction are indifferent, induced to look the other way as regulations are flouted, or restricted by stay orders that bar action. In the most recent incident — where such a stay order had been acquired — workers added four floors to the reportedly ground-plus-one mandated structure. The CM has promised a “reset” at the Sindh Building Control Authority. There is reason to be sceptical: such vows have followed construction disasters in the past too — but have remained mere words. For instance, more than one building collapse was witnessed after the announcement of comprehensive SBCA reform in February this year. This shows official apathy and the lack of political will to take action.
Governance is interconnected, and the rot in one department is invariably linked to the overall failure of public administration. The Sindh government will have to look within to find answers to why laws are flouted with impunity, why corruption prevails, and why there is reluctance to ensure accountability for those who play with people’s lives. As the search for survivors and dead bodies continues, the administration should remember that a system built on broken promises usually proves to be the cause of its own undoing.

title: Public health reform
author: none@none.com (Zafar Mirza)
content:
TWO weeks ago, I participated in the Georgetown Pakistan Forum in Washington, DC, organised by Pakistani students at the university.
The forum brings together policymakers, business leaders, technologists, academics, students and diaspora representatives to discuss Pakistan’s future and promote evidence-based policies, public-private partnerships and solutions for Pakistan and its 1.2 million-strong Pakistani-American diaspora.
I acknowledge the two student leaders who, with their passionate team, organised the event: Rai Hasen Masoud of the School of Foreign Service, president of the Georgetown South Asian Society, and Shahaan Shafi of the School of Health, president of its Academic Council.
Seven policy working groups covered com-munity health, maternal health, defence and strategic stability, democracy and gover-nance, critical minerals and energy, technology for finance and ed­­­­ucation, and health financing and infrastructure.
Pakistan’s public health crisis is the consequence of political choices and misplaced priorities.
Public health was a recurring theme during the forum. I participated in two working groups, a panel discussion and the concluding plenary, where I spoke about reforming public health in Pakistan. Here is my argument.
The WHO defines public health as the art and science of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society.
Pakistan’s public health situation is a crisis. Consider a few indicators. Our population is growing at 2.4 per cent annually, while the total fertility rate is 3.6. We add a population more than that of New Zealand every year. Meanwhile, economic growth in 2025-26 is projected at 3.65pc, barely exceeding population growth. This leaves little room for per capita prosperity to improve.
Maternal and child health indicators are troubling. Pakistan has the world’s second-highest neo­­natal mortality rate, while approximately half of women of reproductive age suffer from anaemia.
A quarter of our children remain unvaccinated against vaccine-preventable diseases. Pakistan remains one of only two countries where polio cases persist, obstructing global eradication efforts. We also have the world’s largest hepatitis C burden, Asia’s fastest-growing HIV epidemic, increasingly spreading beyond high-risk groups, and the fifth-largest tuberculosis burden globally.
The situation is no better regarding non-communicable diseases. Every third adult above 18 suffers from type-2 diabetes, while every fourth adult above 40 has hypertension. Both increase risks of cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney complications. Lifestyle medicine needs to be integrated at all levels of the healthcare system. Mental health remains the most neglected area, with limited access to appropriate care.
What went wrong, particularly when so many of these conditions are preventable?
The answer lies in decades of government neglect, chronic underinvestment, an overwhelming emphasis on curative healthcare, growing social inequity and poverty, and failure to develop a strong primary healthcare system.
Can we reverse this situation? Certainly. Other countries have demonstrated that progress is possible. This requires political commitment and 10 reforms.
First, government spending on health should progressively move towards the WHO-re­­com­mended benchmark of 5pc of GDP. Health must become a fiscal priority. Essential public hea­­lth programmes, including immunisation, HIV and TB control, should be sustainably financed through domestic resources rather than continued dependence on development partners. Emergency preparedness also requires adequate investment.
Second, generalist bureaucracy has increasingly become a constraint on health sector development. Pakistan’s Central Superior Services comprises 12 occupational groups, but health is not among them. Ministries of health should be led predominantly by technically qualified professionals, supported by competent administrators.
Third, the 18th Constitutional Amendment devolved health responsibilities to provinces, but national coordination has weakened. Health challenges do not respect administrative boundaries. Common standards, surveillance, disease-control strategies, global health commitments and emergency preparedness require effective intergovernmental coordination.
Fourth, Pakistan needs a National Health Service (NHS) framework to ensure integrated healthcare delivery, bringing public and private providers together. Drawing lessons from the UK’s NHS, we should institutionalise public-private partnerships to expand access, improve quality and make better use of existing resources.
Fifth, primary healthcare must be strengthened. Prevention, early diagnosis and health promotion should form the foundation of our healthcare system. These services belong primarily at community and primary-care levels, not in tertiary hospitals. This requires empowered district health departments, functional facilities and a stronger focus on preventive and promotive services.
Sixth, we need to rationalise our health workforce through better planning of its size, distribution and skills. Medical education must respond to national healthcare needs, with appropriate proportions of doctors, nurses, allied health professionals and community health workers.
Seventh, responsible use of digital technologies and AI can improve health information systems, strengthen governance, expand access through telemedicine and standardise care. These investments must be guided by equity, accountability and data protection.
Eighth, patient safety and quality must become priorities, supported by stronger regulatory standards and enforcement. Healthcare should heal, not harm. Effective infection prevention and control, safe injections and blood transfusions are essential. The transmission of hepatitis C and HIV through unsafe medical practices demonstrates the consequences of neglecting patient safety.
Ninth, we must engage the Pakistani medical diaspora through a coherent government policy that institutionalises mechanisms to mobilise the expertise, experience, technology and investment of health professionals abroad.
Tenth, we must strengthen intersectoral action. Health is shaped well beyond hospitals and health facilities. Environmental pollution, climate change, food systems, urban planning, education and lifestyle behaviours all influence health outcomes. The health sector must lead collaboration to address these wider determinants.
Pakistan’s public health crisis is not inevitable. It is the consequence of political choices, misplaced priorities and institutional weaknesses. What is required is a shift from treating illness to protecting and promoting health. The challenge is not simply to spend more on healthcare, but to govern better, invest wisely and build a system that puts people and prevention first.
The writer is a former health minister, adjunct professor of health systems and president of Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine.

title: More credit, fewer women
author: none@none.com (Samia Salik)
content:
IMAGINE Sakina, up at the crack of dawn to go see her precious Billo, a fine cow her father had given her. This would be Sakina’s 30th day selling Billo’s milk to a nearby farm owner who wanted good milk for his young children. She was excited to get paid. She got ready to head out, feeling like a businesswoman.
Three years later, Sakina has four animals. She feeds them, looks after them and gets the milk ready for collection. She knows when a cow is giving less milk, when feed becomes heavier on the pocket and when it makes sense to buy another animal.
    
Her 40-plus customers know how rich the milk is. But ask them where it comes from and they’ll tell you it’s from Kareem bhai, the doodh wala. Kareem is Sakina’s husband. He delivers the milk and his name is also the one on the ledger that she has maintained all these years.
Sakina is sure she could manage 10 animals. She decides to start with two more cows and goes to a bank for a loan. That’s when the name in the ledger becomes a problem. She has years of milk sales to show the bank. She’s kept the records herself but they are in Kareem’s name. The bank decides against giving her a loan.
Pakistan’s agricultural lending ambitions must look beyond the size of the portfolio.
The State Bank of Pakistan’s Banking on Equality figures show that agricultural financing to women rose from Rs44 billion in 2021 to Rs105bn in 2025 in nominal terms. In those same years, the number of women agricultural borrowers fell from 436,000 to 377,000, a decline of about 14 per cent. The data doesn’t show why fewer women borrowed or who received the additional financing. Yet the amounts lent more than doubled while the number of women borrowers fell.
That matters for Banking on Equality 2026. The policy asks banks and development finance institutions to aim to double their financing portfolios for women and qualifying women-owned or women-led businesses across priority sectors by the end of 2028. A bank can grow its loan book by lending more to people it already knows. Reaching a woman like Sakina takes a closer look at who’s been running the business all these years.
Agriculture accounts for roughly 23pc of Pakistan’s GDP, and livestock makes up nearly two-thirds of the sector’s value added. The Labour Force Survey 2024-25 tells us that about six in 10 employed women work in agriculture, forestry or fishing. What’s harder to see is who gets paid for that work and who decides how the money is spent.
Take three women who look after cattle. One is paid a wage. Another tends the family’s animals and earns no income of her own. The third runs a dairy business like Sakina’s. To decide if a loan makes sense, a bank needs to understand how each woman earns her living and how much of that income she can use to repay it.
Sakina’s milk delivery records could give the bank a place to start. Then come the questions she already asks herself. How much does feed cost? What happens to her income when a cow stops producing milk? What does she already owe? Banking on Equality encourages banks to consider evidence like this when assessing women-owned and women-led businesses.
There’s one question the loan officer needs to ask a woman like Sakina directly. When the buyer pays for the milk, who can use that money? A buyer could put the supplier account in her name tomorrow and still hand the cash to Kareem. If the loan is in her name, the bank will expect her to pay it back. Can she decide where to sell the milk and set aside enough for the next instalment?
In Kenya, CGAP documented how Agrilife and New Kenya Cooperative Creameries used digital delivery records to help dairy suppliers get advances against milk they’d already delivered. A separate study of two Kenyan dairy cooperatives found that farmers short of cash or facing uninsured health expenses shifted sales towards buyers who paid on the spot.
Financing a cow means working out what it might produce in the future. And records kept in a farmer group’s name may tell a bank very little about what one woman sold. Could we use the records buyers already keep to show what women like Sakina actually sell and earn?
A provincial livestock department could bring milk buyers and banks together to work with women who already run dairy businesses and want to expand. Ask buyers to record what each woman delivers and what she’s paid. If she wants to be paid into an account, let her choose one she can operate herself. If the money is paid in cash or through several buyers, the department maintains a record. With her consent, the bank can use those records alongside its usual checks and see whether they change its decision.
    
After a year, we should know whether banks approved applications they would previously have declined and whether more women received payments directly. We can follow the loan cycles for longer too. Could the women keep up with repayments? After feed, veterinary bills and instalments, did they have more income left? Could they decide what to do with it?
SBP can do something now. Put the amount lent and the number of individual women who borrowed on the same page. Show how many took out a formal loan for the first time and where borrower numbers are falling.
Sakina knows the business and what it will take to grow it. She went to the bank to get support but came back without a loan or a clear way forward.
When the banks report back in 2028, we should look at how many women like Sakina got far enough to have someone sit down with them and assess their potential for growth. Sakina may still look at the instalment and decide to wait. But that should be her decision to make.
The writer leads the women’s economic and digital inclusion portfolio at Karandaaz Pakistan.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Karandaaz Pakistan.

title: Fatal journeys
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THESE tragedies are recurrent: another migrant boat that set sail towards European shores capsized near Libya on Saturday. While details are still sketchy, at least 25 people from Bajaur district may have perished or are missing. Endless economic pain, conflict, climate and political crises have long forced people to flee their land. Yet an apathetic government has only made patchy efforts to get tough on the country’s human smuggling problem. As a result, the desperate continue to be exploited, and hurled into perilous journeys. The toll of such accidents is among the gravest misfortunes of our times. It is, therefore, crucial that Western nations, especially Fortress Europe, also take responsibility for the devastation they continue to cause in many countries, and in so doing exacerbate the factors that fuel illegal migration.
The truth is that the government has allowed the social contract to fray.  Citizens remain without their right to quality education and economic security. A fresh approach is the need of the hour. Sustained action directed at the kingpins of this menace, not their minions, irrespective of their influence, must be enforced. But without alleviating the root causes — lack of opportunity and abject poverty — a long-lasting solution will be tough to achieve. Uprooting transnational human smuggling and trafficking webs is a battle that is as challenging as weeding out corrupt officials who facilitate this abominable business. Every offender and enabler must be held to account, alongside airtight collaboration with external LEAs. Lastly, the state, through job-creation drives, should make a convincing effort for the youth in areas with high rates of illegal migration to choose home over dreams of better prospects abroad. These traps of deceit expand when poverty and disorder rise: as per the 2025 IOM report, some 2,722 migrants from the Asia-Pacific region died or were untraceable; Pakistan’s total was 109. The trade, and not its victims, must be criminalised.

title: Constitutional liability
author: none@none.com (Aamir Latif Siddiqui)
content:
EVERY out-of-school child is a living reminder to the state of its constitutional commitment, and these reminders have been increasing since the inception of Pakistan. Now these living reminders have crossed 25 million.
Seventy-nine years after independence, Pakistan is still struggling to fulfil one of the most fundamental responsibilities of a modern state, ensuring that every child receives an education. A nuclear state has produced generations without an education system capable of accommodating them.
Pakistan’s failure to educate its children is not a recent phenomenon, nor did the constitutional responsibility of the state begin with Article 25-A in 2010. The commitment dates back to the country’s early constitutional history. The 1956 Constitution explicitly recognised the state’s responsibility to eliminate illiteracy and provide free and compulsory primary education. The 1962 Constitution retained this commitment. The 1973 Constitution went further through Article 37(b), requiring the state to remove illiteracy and provide free and compulsory secondary education within the minimum possible period.
    
The insertion of Article 25-A through the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010 was therefore not the beginning of the state’s educational responsibility. It was an attempt to transform a longstanding constitutional aspiration into an enforceable fundamental right. Yet, decades of constitutional commitments have failed to produce universal educational access.
From the promise of compulsory primary education in 1956 to the guarantee of education for every child aged 5-16 in 2010, the state has repeatedly renewed its commitment without ensuring its fulfilment.
Every child denied education represents lost human capital.
The question is why, despite repeated constitutional commitments, successive governments have failed to ensure that every child has access to a school. It seems every government has also failed to realise that every child denied education represents lost human capital and another potential victim of intergenerational poverty.
A country cannot build a knowledge economy, strengthen democratic institutions, or achieve sustainable development while leaving millions of its children disconnected from education and the opportunities that accompany it. The children are not the liability. The liability is created by a system that allows millions of children to grow up without education, skills, opportunities, or meaningful participation in society.
Unesco data indicates that Pakistan has a substantially higher proportion of primary-school-age children out of school compared with India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, and Sri Lanka. While these countries have made considerable progress in expanding educational access, Pakistan continues to struggle with millions of children excluded from the education system.
This regional disparity suggests that the crisis is not merely a consequence of poverty or population growth, but also reflects persistent failures of educational planning, governance, investment and political commitment.
    
Bringing over 25m out-of-school children into the education system is not merely a matter of an enrolment campaign. It requires an enormous expansion of educational infrastructure, human resources and recurring public expenditure.
Assuming 40 students per classroom, Pakistan would need approximately 628,750 classrooms to accommodate these children. At an illustrative staffing ratio of 1.2 teachers per classroom, the country would require approximately 754,500 additional teachers. If these teachers were recruited at the initial BPS-14 pay of Rs27,060 per mon­th, the annual salary bill alone would be roughly Rs245 billion. This estim­ate covers basic salaries only, excludes allowances, pensi­o­­ns, and teacher tr­­a­ining. The capital cost of constructing schools with basic amenities, as well as recurring administrative expenditure, would certainly be a substantially higher fiscal commitment.
The scale of the challenge is enormous, so is the cost of inaction. Pakistan’s reported education expenditure of Rs962bn in FY2024-25 was already insufficient to meet the needs of its existing education system. The question is therefore not simply how much it would cost to educate the excluded children, but why a country that has constitutionally guaranteed education to every child has failed to develop a sustainable financing mechanism to fulfil that guarantee.
A constitutional right cannot remain confined to the pages of a constitution, nor can the state continue to measure its educational achievements through policies announced, schools inaugurated, or budgets allocated. The real measure of its commitment must be the child sitting in a classroom, learning to read, write, think, and participate in society.
The writer is a social development practitioner.

title: Revamping audits
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE government’s decision to overhaul the audit system is long overdue. Weak audit oversight has undermined confidence in corporate financial reporting, discouraged investment and weakened accountability across the economy. The concerns raised by the Prime Minister’s FBR Task Force deserve serious attention. Investors, lenders and regulators depend on audited financial statements to assess the financial health of companies. When those statements cannot be trusted, the entire investment environment suffers. The country’s failure to meet international standards for independent audit oversight is particularly damaging. The International Organisation of Securities Commissions has declared Pakistan non-compliant with these requirements. The EU has also withdrawn its equivalence status for independent audit oversight. These setbacks should have prompted corrective action much earlier.
The proposed amendments to the SECP law and the Audit Oversight Board framework are therefore welcome. Greater independence for the oversight board, restrictions on members having links with audit firms and regular risk-based inspections could improve accountability. Giving the board powers to investigate complaints and pursue suspected falsification should also strengthen enforcement. However, changing laws and creating regulatory powers will not automatically produce credible audits. The question is whether the new arrangements can withstand pressure from influential companies, audit firms and other vested interests. Replacing one professional group’s dominance with greater state influence would hardly constitute reform. There is also a wider problem that cannot be ignored. Pakistan’s public-sector audit system suffers from similar weaknesses. An IMF governance assessment last year highlighted the Auditor General’s limited independence, staff shortages and poor parliamentary follow-up. Thousands of pages of audit reports have produced little corrective action. This illustrates a fundamental weakness in the country’s approach to accountability. Audit findings frequently expose irregularities, but those responsible rarely face timely consequences. The government must ensure that corporate audit reform does not become just another exercise in legislative compliance.

Proposed amendments to the SECP law and the Audit Oversight Board (AOB) framework aim to enhance independence, restrict conflicts of interest, and strengthen enforcement, but their effectiveness against powerful vested interests is questioned.

Beyond corporate audits, Pakistan's public-sector audit system also exhibits significant weaknesses, such as limited independence, staff shortages, and poor parliamentary follow-up, highlighting a broader national accountability deficit.

title: Beyond our means
author: none@none.com (Khurram Zia Khan)
content:
IT is unfortunate that most people in Pakistan spend more than they earn. It is a fact that inflation is seriously diminishing the public’s buying power and adversely impacting whatever savings they have. In this scenario, people should think about changing their lifestyle and focusing on saving more. This argument is supported by the fact that Pakistan has one of the highest rates of consumer borrowing for non-productive purposes in South Asia. People are not borrowing to start a business; they are borrowing to maintain certain lifestyles.
Pakistan’s domestic savings ratio is one of the lowest in the world. It dropped from 17.4 per cent of GDP in 1992 to just 6.4pc in 2024, the weakest in a generation and far lower than countries in the region. Pakistan’s 30-year average savings is 10.9pc of GDP. Bangladesh’s average is approximately 21pc, India’s is around 28pc, and Vietnam’s is around 30pc.
People should realise that whatever they earn is their own property, but rash spending habits are damaging for themselves and also for the country. The nation’s overall poor savings habits are also a critical reason for the state’s reliance on loans from global donors.
Pakistan’s savings ratio has fallen massively in the last 30 years because domestic lifestyles have changed. Parents of past generations knew how to say no. Yet many parents of today proudly fulfil their child’s every wish, come what may. This type of thinking has played a part in making people live beyond their means. If parents really love their children, they should focus on fulfilling their actual needs, which are food, clothes, education and health. All things other than these basics are actually demands.
Pakistan’s domestic savings ratio is one of the lowest in the world.
Good parenting involves fulfilling children’s needs and managing their demands in a rational manner. A good parent believes that he or she earns for their children, and it is his or her responsibility to secure their future by making sacrifices in the present.
We as a nation make wrong spending choices in our daily routines while during weddings and funerals, spending tends to go haywire because of social pressures. For weddings, many families spend beyond their means to keep up with the Joneses. Pakistan’s average monthly income is Rs40,000-80,000, but an average marriage easily costs Rs1.5 million to Rs2.5m, which is equivalent to three to five years’ total salary for a middle-class parent or guardian.
Dowry is another burden for a bride’s family. It is unfortunate that 13.5m women in Pakistan are unmarried because their families cannot afford dowry-related expenses. It is unfortunate that even after giving dowry, the greed of some remains unfulfilled, and they do not shy away from harming the bride whose dowry is not as per their expectations. According to the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, more than 2,000 women die each year in dowry-related disputes.
More than 1.6m marriages take place in Pakistan annually, and more than Rs110 billion is spent on these weddings every year.
Marriages are happy occasions, but even during moments of grief, such as a death in the family, unnecessary expenditures are made, because of various rituals.
As these examples illustrate, living beyond one’s means appears to be the daily economic behaviour of the nation. Moreover, a middle-class family pays 30pc-40pc of its income to private schools and private hospitals because the government is unable to provide the basic rights of health and education to the people. The majority of the population is relying on private setups for health and education, and this segment is eating up a large chunk of income.
The world is be­­coming unstable, and wars are now becoming the new norm. These conflicts are not only impacting the countries involved but are also having an adverse effect on the availability and pricing of global resources, such as oil and gas. In this changing scenario, it is highly critical that awareness campaigns be launched at all levels to highlight the benefits of savings. The public should be convinced to bring simplicity into their lives. Chapters about the benefits of savings and living with simplicity should be included in the curriculum and be propagated through social media platforms. It is also incumbent on the state to improve health and education facilities, particularly for the lower-income bracket.
Saving is a good habit. Even religion has preached moderation. Those who prepare for the worst in good times reap the benefit in the long run. It is high time that the nation should learn from its past errors and reset its spending habits to bring stability in the present and to secure its future.
The writer is a publicist.

title: Opposition disarray
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE PTI on Wednesday distanced itself from Mahmood Khan Achakzai’s proposal for a national government and his demand for political and constitutional reforms. The party has not issued a formal reaction, but its leaders have made its stance clear in background conversations with the media.
This shows the alliance chief did not consult other parties before making the proposal public.
A similar disconnect between the PTI and other member parties of the TTAP surfaced a couple of months ago, when the PTI gave a call for a protest march on Islamabad.
Speaking at a conference in Lahore, Mr Achakzai also stressed constitutional supremacy, parliamentary sovereignty and the restoration of democracy. His concerns about worsening insecurity in KP, Balochistan and AJK deserve serious attention. These problems will not be solved by unilateral decisions or political expediency.
    
However, the demand for a national government appears premature and offers no clear way out of political uncertainty. Replacing the present setup with an arrangement whose mandate and duration remain undefined could deepen existing divisions.
More concerning is the opposition alliance’s lack of coordination, which has again exposed its differences. Opposition parties need to settle whether their leaders speak for the alliance or only for their own parties. Contradicting one another in public weakens their credibility.
    
A coalition that cannot agree on a public position will struggle to offer a credible alternative programme. The opposition would be better off using the rest of the parliamentary term to press the government on issues that bear directly on democratic governance. These issues include protection of civil liberties, curbs on freedom of expression and the matter of political prisoners. The restoration of normal democratic administration in KP also requires attention.
Moreover, both sides of the aisle need to begin working out arrangements to ensure free, fair and credible elections when the present government’s term ends. That requires agreement on electoral safeguards, the neutrality of state institutions and an environment in which parties can compete without intimidation.
Calls for constitutional supremacy will carry little weight unless political parties show their own commitment to parliamentary democracy. Sustained engagement in parliament would help the opposition build public confidence, and it should not squander that chance on premature demands for another political arrangement.
The government would do well to reckon with the cost of poor governance, heavy-handed treatment of the opposition and other sections of society, and a weak economic record. Left unaddressed, these issues will hand its critics ample ammunition for more agitation.

title: New search trends
author: none@none.com (Usman Tauqir)
content:
PAKISTAN’S IT and software export story is told in remittance figures, freelancer rankings and new export targets. One question gets far less attention. When a buyer in Austin, Manchester or Dubai goes looking for a software vendor, where do they look now, and are Pakistani firms anywhere in the answer?
For 20 years the answer was Google’s 10 blue links. Our software houses, Software as a Service (SaaS) start-ups and agencies learned that game: rank for the right phr­ases, get the click, win the call. Many still treat a page-one ranking as the finish line.
The finish line has moved. My firm recently ran 1,500 real software-buying questions through four AI systems that buyers now use: ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Google’s AI Mode and the AI Overviews that sit at the top of ordinary Google results. We asked each question three times, from fresh sessions in the United States, and collected 18,000 answers across 20 software categories, from CRM and accounting to recruitment and e-signature tools.
Three findings should worry anyone who sells Pakistani software or services abroad.
Our IT exporters are optimising for a search page buyers no longer read.
First, the AI answer is now the first thing a buyer sees. Google showed an AI Ove­rview on 98 per cent of the software-buying searches we tested. The summary sits above the links, names a handful of products and often settles the question before anyone scrolls. A buyer can form a shortlist without visiting a single vendor website.
Second, ranking on Google no longer guarantees a place in that summary. We looked at 27,307 websites cited inside AI Overviews. Only 28.1pc also ranked in the top three organic results on the same page. More striking, 36.5pc of the cited websites did not appear in the organic results shown at all. The AI is reading, and trusting, sources well beyond the page-one list our marketing teams obsess over.
Third, the AI leans on what other people say about a product, not only on what the product says about itself. Review platforms such as G2, Capterra and TrustRadius were cited in 25.6pc of ChatGPT’s answers. Google’s AI Overviews cited YouTube in 80.5pc of answers and Reddit in 52.8pc. In plain terms, the machines are listening to reviews, videos and forum threads.
Put those together and the problem for Pakistani exporters becomes clear. A firm can do everything right by the old rulebook, rank well and still be invisible when a foreign buyer asks an AI assistant for options. If that firm has no reviews on the platforms AI reads, no independent coverage and no presence in the conversations where buyers compare tools, the assistant simply has nothing to say about it.
This matters more for us than for an American or European competitor. A Paki­stani vendor already starts with a trust gap: unfamiliar brand, distant time zone, questions about payments and support. Third-party proof is how that gap gets closed. AI systems now automate the hunt for that proof. A buyer who would once have found us on page one may never hear our name.
There is a fix, and none of it is exotic.
Exporters should treat reviews as infrastructure, not vanity. Every satisfied foreign client is a potential review on a platform the AI reads. Many firms have satisfied foreign clients and few or no public reviews to show for them. That gap now costs visibility as well as credibility.
They should earn mentions outside their own websites. Comparison articles, industry publications, podcasts, credible forum answers and exp­ert commentary are now inputs to the AI shortlist. A website alone is not enough.
They should measure the right thing. Ask the questions a real buyer would ask, in ChatGPT and Google, every month, and record whether your firm is named and how it is described. If you are not tracking that, you are not tracking whe­re your next client is making up their mind.
There is also a role for the industry bodies. P@SHA and the Pakistan Software Export Board already run trade delegations and export promotion. A modest programme to help member firms build verified review profiles, publish credible case studies and track their visibility in AI answers would do more for the “Brand Pakistan” tech story than another glossy brochure. The country’s export targets depend on buyers who have never met us. The first impression they get is increasingly written by a machine.
None of this replaces good work. AI systems are not easily fooled for long, and what they repeat is mostly what credible people already say. But the rules of discovery have changed, and they have changed for everyone at once. That is rare, and it is an opening. Firms that adapt early can be named alongside global brands. Firms that wait will keep winning page-one rankings that fewer and fewer buyers ever see.
The writer is founder and CEO of a search and AI visibility firm.

title: Choking the provinces
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
LET’S be very clear about one thing: this business of cutting the provinces up into “administrative units” has nothing to do with good or bad governance. It is mainly about recentralising control over the state’s resources.
A paper written by three eminent Pakistani academics in 2005 made a related point that is worth revisiting in the present debate. The authors were Ali Cheema, Asim Ijaz Khwaja and Adnan Qadir and the document was published in 2005 as a working paper for Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government. They took a longer view of all attempts to bring in local governments in the country’s history, and came to the following conclusion: “local government empowerment has always been combined with centralisation of political power in the hands of the non-representative centre. The centralisation of political power has undermined representative institutions not only at the level of the centre but also at the level of the provinces.”
    
Their analysis is especially relevant all over again, as the same gambit to centralise power is being rolled out for the fourth time in our history. They noted that in all such experiments in the past, “[o]ur interpretation is that these reforms have been used as a means for a non-representative centre to gain legitimacy by by-passing the political agents at the provincial and national levels”.
Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow.
The seventh NFC award agreed to in 2009 and made effective in July 2010 reversed the centralisation of powers and resources that the federal authorities had grown accustomed to over the decades. It was the first time in Pakistan’s history that powers and, more importantly, resources, flowed down from the federal government towards lower tiers of government in such large quantities. And almost immediately, from its very first year of operation, a thrust emerged from the federal authorities to try and undo this.
It began slowly at first. Then in the middle of the decade it achieved its first written form. Here is a brief timeline of how small, subtle changes in how fiscal resources are measured and counted turned into a full-blown programme for reversing the flow of these resources to the provincial governments.
    
In FY2011, the first year after the seventh NFC award, the federal government “successfully pressed” the provincial governments to run a surplus and not spend all the money being devolved down to them. Then the next year they asked for these surpluses again, but with no Fund programme in force, the provincial governments did not comply.
This changed in 2013 when the IMF made it a prior action for provinces to post a surplus, and provincial deposits with the State Bank leapt from Rs42 billion in June 2013 to Rs257bn by March 2014. This was ratified in the Council of Common Interests, and provincial finance secretaries agreed to continue the practice into 2015. By June 2015 the IMF programme called for written agreement from the provinces to raise their surpluses, as a prior action and a few months later, in September, provincial spending was capped at 6.5 per cent of GDP.
By June 2016, as the programme was winding up with only a few months left in it, the government set up the Fiscal Coordination Committee to ensure that centre and provinces coordinate their spending and surpluses. The very next year, as the Fund programme ran out, provincial governments ramped up their spending, running a deficit of Rs163bn in FY17.
In July 2019 another IMF programme was signed, after replacing finance ministers. This one again made it a prior action to get provinces to run surpluses, and raised the surplus targets from one to 2.7pc of GDP. That agreement was renewed in the two years that followed, and provincial surpluses leapt from Rs77bn in FY20 to Rs314bn in FY21 and Rs351bn in FY22. That was the most troubled programme of Pakistan’s history, with more false starts than any other programme Pakistan had ever signed.
The blowout came in 2024. As part of the bailout in July 2023, the provinces now had to agree not only to post a surplus, but also submit spending plans. Provincial deposits were already netted against government borrowing in the IMF’s targets for the budget deficit and SBP’s net domestic assets, thereby helping the federal government meet its targets under the Fund programme. Most importantly, the targets for provincial surpluses agreed to in that programme rose to Rs1.2 trillion in the first year, rising to Rs1.9tn by FY27.
So in 2011 the provinces left unspent 13.5pc of what they received as a transfer under the NFC award. This figure fell as soon as the Fund programme lapsed, then rose again every time Pakistan entered a Fund programme. Today it stands at 19pc, skyrocketing in the last three years.
Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow.
In May 2025, for example, provinces were required to put surplus cash into T-bills. Their holdings of federal government debt rose from Rs19bn in June 2025 to Rs1.8tn as of October 2026, though this figure fluctuates a lot with maturities every few months. And then in June 2026, under Article 164 grants, the provinces were made to hand over Rs1.0tn to the federal authorities, or about 12.66pc of each province’s NFC share.
What began as a plea to restrain spending in 2011 slowly grew into a codified demand to run a surplus. Then the targets for these surpluses were raised. Then came requirements to buy government debt paper followed by a reverse flow from province to centre as a “grant” under Article 164. And now they want to dismantle the whole set-up altogether, in the name of governance. The irony here is that it is the governance failures of the federal authorities themselves that have fuelled their hunger for resources from the provincial authorities.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Red lines
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi is right to say that freedom of expression cannot be a licence to promote terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence or child sexual exploitation.
No responsible media outlet or citizen would argue otherwise. And few would object to curbing such content on social media. Those who spread such material should expect to answer for it under the law. But drawing red lines is only half the job. The state must also show that it respects them. This is where its record raises questions.
There are visible red lines against hate and violence. But there are also invisible ones that journalists and citizens encounter every day when they question powerful quarters or report matters considered inconvenient. Journalists have been picked up, threatened and intimidated for publishing stories that upset those in power.
Media organisations have faced pressure over their editorial choices. Reporters often find themselves working out what they can safely publish and which subjects are best avoided. This has created a vacuum that social media is rapidly filling. So when Mr Naqvi tells journalists they are free to report, and that citizens are free to ask questions, it rings hollow.
Terms such as “anti-state activity”, “misinformation” and “hate speech” are elastic. And when officials interpret them without checks, they become tools for silencing critics. Having a law or a regulator does not make its use legitimate. Enforcement agencies should operate within defined legal limits, give valid and legitimate reasons for their decisions, act in proportion to the harm and be answerable to the courts. The rules should apply equally to everyone, whatever their politics or standing. Otherwise a measure meant to protect citizens ends up policing public debate. The minister’s assurance that dissent, including criticism of the state, will be heard is welcome. But assurances count for little while media organisations and journalists are still being intimidated.
The state must guarantee complete press freedom, subject only to clearly defined constitutional and legal restrictions. A sensible first step would be to bring journalists and their representative bodies, media owners, civil society and relevant state institutions together to agree on what responsible expression means in practice. Such consultations should produce a clear commitment to protect journalists, safeguard editorial independence and prevent the misuse of regulatory powers.
Freedom of expression carries responsibilities. But those responsibilities cannot be imposed on the media alone. The state must also accept its own obligations and allow uncomfortable questions to be asked. Rules against violence and hatred are fair enough. Unwritten and invisible ones against independent journalism are not.

title: Curtains on COP31
author: none@none.com (Aisha Khan)
content:
THE 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) took place in the backdrop of geopolitical fragmentation, a rising cost-of-living crisis, tightening of national and international budgets and the imminent threat of a 1.5ºC overshoot.
Despite high stakes, the talks — instead of propelling the agenda forward — highlighted significant gaps in international cooperation and revealed critical areas where progress was stalled, resulting in an underwhelming outcome.
At its core, COP31 faced a leadership vacuum, leaving parties to navigate the negotiations with limited political direction. Turkiye’s presidency for hosting and Australia’s presidency of negotiations were unable to shepherd political compromises for the highest possible ambition. The result was a watered-down draft cover decision with the lowest common denominator that failed to secure consensus and was therefore not adopted.
    
The lack of ambition was visible across all critical workstreams. The negotiations failed to get a tangible commitment from major emitting countries to ratchet up their 2030 greenhouse gas emission reduction targets in line with the Paris Agreement.
COP31 reaffirmed that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action.
Many nations maintained vague promises without concrete policies or mechanisms to accelerate carbon cuts. This failure underscores the persistent divide between developed and developing countries over responsibility and capacity. Financial pledges for climate adaptation and loss and damage remained grossly insufficient, especially for vulnerable countries grappling with the worst climate impacts.
    
COP31 did not substantially increase the promised climate finance commitment, nor did it establish clearer mechanisms for operationalising this support. This shortfall deepened the trust deficit between richer and poorer nations and hampered purposeful progress. COP31 made little headway in solidifying a comprehensive loss and damage framework that would provide timely financial assistance to countries suffering from climate-induced disasters.
Despite long-standing calls for compensatory mechanisms, negotiations were bogged down in political disagreements, reflecting the complexities and sensitivities surrounding liability and responsibility.
Although adaptation is a critical pillar of climate action, COP31 showcased a yawning gap between rhetoric and reality. Concrete and enforceable commitments for adaptation planning, funding, and technology transfers failed to materialise.
Perhaps the most glaring omission at COP31 was the absence of decisive action on phasing out fossil fuels. Despite growing scientific consensus on the need to rapidly transition to renewable energy, the conference sidestepped a clear, actionable roadmap away from fossil fuel dependency, highlighting the influence of entrenched economic interests.
While these shortcomings are disappointing, they offer a valuable opportunity for reflection and reform. The failure at COP31 should not be viewed as the collapse of the global climate effort but as an urgent signal that the status quo in multilateral climate negotiations is insufficient to meet the scale and immediacy of the crisis.
This moment calls for re-energising international cooperation, urging countries to bridge their divergent interests and work with renewed transparency and solidarity. It also brings to light that the current voluntary pledging model needs firmer accountability mechanisms for enforcing compliance and incentivising larger, more actionable and ambitious commitments.
The inability to get an overarching political consensus also demonstrates that countries are no longer willing to go along without assurance of financial, technical and policy support needed to adapt and recover. The setbacks also highlight the need to examine new approaches that include civil society, indigenous voices and private-sector leadership for fresh perspectives and urgency into a traditionally slow-moving process.
The weak outcome at COP31 should not cause despair but create a renewed sense of purpose. Sometimes a failure in negotiations is less damaging than weak agreements (like previous COPs) that create a false sense of security. COP31 has forced a reset and serves as a crucial pivot point for rejecting unfair agreements and harnessing the moment to strengthen the spirit of the Paris Agreement, keeping its promise alive and escalating its ambition. The failure of COP31 is in fact a triumph of COP21.
COP31 may have faltered but it reaffirmed the essential truth that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action. The diplomatic disagreements at COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 resulted in the milestone triumph of COP21 in 2015 in Paris. The failure of COP31 can serve the same turning-point purpose for future COPs and multilateralism.
The writer is a climate policy analyst.

title: Unchanged features
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
“IF Cleopatra’s nose had been shorter,” the French philosopher Blaise Pascal once mused, “the whole face of the world would have been changed.” One wonders whether Indo-Pak relations might have been different, had Mrs Indira Gandhi’s nose been shorter.
She was always self-conscious about it. In a letter to her American friend Dorothy Norman, Mrs Gandhi admitted: “Ever sin­ce plastic surgery was heard of, I have been wanting to get something done to my nose.” In 1967, she had the chance when, during an election rally, a projectile struck her directly in the face. Her son Rajiv recounted her concern later that “her already long nose would now be crooked too”.
Perhaps the most memorable reference to her nose came from Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw, who, after the 1971 war, answered her fear that he might topple her in a military coup: “You see, you have a long nose, even I have a long nose, but that doesn’t mean I poke my nose in your business of running the country and you poke your long nose in my Army.”
Mrs Gandhi never warmed to Pakistan. She never forgot Yahya Khan belittling her as “that woman”, nor forgave Z.A. Bhutto’s dismissal of her as “a mediocre woman with a mediocre intelligence [,] a diligent drudge of a schoolgirl [,] devoid of initiative and imagination”.
Sonia Gandhi’s attitude towards Pakistan has hardened.
She did not share her father Pandit Nehru’s sentiment about northwestern India. In his day, before 1947, he had travelled and canvassed there extensively. For example, writing to her from Lahore in August 1945, he described a tour from Nathiagali to Abbottabad, Haripur and Taxila, with a stop at the Mughal garden in Wah where he wanted to bathe in “the pool of wonderfully clear water”.
In an earlier letter, written from Bareilly Central Prison, he reminisced: “I like going to Lahore [.] It is like a growing child, very immature in many ways, yet with an air of sophistication [.] However, there is an atm­osphere of a fake and superficial gaiety”.
If Pandit Nehru had been partly responsible for the first partition of India in Aug­ust 1947 and his daughter Indira for the subsequent partition of Pakistan in Dece­m­ber 1971, their successor Rajiv made a dete­rmined effort to bring his country and Pak­istan closer. In her memoir Belonging (2026), Sonia Gandhi describes Rajiv’s conciliatory mission in 1989, the first visit by an Indian PM since his grandfather’s in 1960.
Then, Nehru’s host had been a general, Ayub Khan. In 1989, Sonia recalls the freer atmosphere: “The air was full of excitement and expectation [.] Thirty-five-year-old Benazir Bhutto had recently been elected prime minister in Pakistan’s first democratic election since 1977, the first woman of the country to hold the post [.] Both Rajiv and Benazir had lost a cherished parent to political violence.” In time, both would be assassinated.
Rajiv and Sonia, accompanied by their children Rahul and Priyanka, arrived in Islamabad on July 16, to be welcomed by Benazir and her husband Asif Zardari. The same evening, they had a private dinner with the couple. She recalled: “The atmosphere was informal, as we were young and found much in common”. However, “whenever the discussion veered towards political matters, our host [Benazir] would increase the volume of the music playing in the background, thereby warning us that people were listening in to our conversation”.
Sonia was struck “by how much is recognisable between our ways and theirs: food, apparel, language, customs [.] We came away feeling that if only our two countries could sink their differences, how much both could benefit! Instead of armaments and wars, how much could be done for our people on both sides”.
Gradually, Son­ia’s attitude tow­a­rds Pakistan hardened, as dom­estic imperatives made her relapse into an Indian stereotype. While she admired Nelson Man­d­ela’s spirit of forgiveness, she found it imp­o­ssible to follow his advice to convert “negative feelings” into “positivity and courage.” She allowed her PM Dr Man­m­o­han Singh to improve Indo-Pak contacts, to promote a Lambah/Aziz backchannel, but fell short of allowing them to reach fruition.
Today, PM Modi’s government has ens­ured that Pakistanis and Indians still need to go abroad to meet each other. (In 1989, Rajiv Gandhi regretted that as an alternative.) They know each other now only thr­ough ricocheted news and pirated editions.
Will this current freeze ever defrost? It seems unlikely.
Recently, Rahul Gandhi (now his mother’s successor as opposition leader), acknowledged that improved ties are possible, provided Pakistan eschews “cross-border terrorism”. Pakistan’s well-thumbed retort is first a resolution of the 78-year-old Jammu and Kashmir issue.
The stance of each country, like Mrs Gandhi’s nose, remains an unchanged feature in the subcontinent’s politics.
The writer is an author.

summary: Personal attitudes and historical grievances of leaders, such as Indira Gandhi's resentment towards Pakistani leaders, significantly shaped Indo-Pak relations.
Despite diplomatic efforts like Rajiv Gandhi's 1989 visit and cultural commonalities, underlying political imperatives and unresolved issues continue to harden stances.

title: Cashless divide
author: none@none.com (Salma Khan)
content:
IMAGINE a woman in Islamabad arriving at a government office to pay a fee. She has the money, but no bank account and no smartphone of her own. The counter no longer accepts cash. The official points her towards a QR code. She asks someone nearby to make the payment for her. The payment goes through, but she has had to depend on a stranger to make it.
This is a hypothetical situation, but it captures a problem beneath the government’s plan to make Islamabad cashless by the end of December. Do people have the means to participate? And what happens to those who do not?
There are good reasons to encourage digital payments. They can make transactions easier to trace, reduce delays and help bring economic activity into the formal system. Raast and other payment infrastructure can make this possible at a scale that cash cannot. But encouraging digital payments is different from withdrawing cash before people have a workable alternative. That distinction matters.
The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics’ Household Integrated Economic Survey 2024-25 puts the gap in perspective. Internet use among individuals stands at 57 per cent, falling to 49pc in rural areas, compared with 69pc in urban areas. Only half the population owns a mobile phone. Ownership is 69pc among men and 39pc among women. These figures do not tell us how many people can use a banking application, but they do show how uneven access to the basic tools of a cashless economy remains.
People should not be turned away from a government office because they cannot make a digital payment.
The gap is even wider when we look at access to financial services. According to the World Bank’s Global Findex 2025, based on 2024 data, only 12pc of women in Pakistan have an account, compared with 42pc of men. Digital payment use stands at 13pc for women and 40pc for men. Among the poo­r­­est 40pc of adults, only 9pc made digital paym­e­nts, compared with 33pc among the wealthiest 60pc.
    
For someone with a bank account, a smartphone and reliable internet, cashless payments may simply be more convenient. Someone paying in cash, living on an irregular income, sharing a phone or unfamiliar with digital interfaces may experience the same change as an additional expense. They may have to travel to an agent, pay a fee or ask someone else to make the transaction. They may also be unable to pay when a system is unavailable. The fact that everyone is being asked to use the same system does not mean everyone is equally able to use it.
This becomes a more serious concern when the state makes digital payment the only option. From Dec 1, Islamabad’s ICT administration and CDA departments are expected to stop accepting cash. What will happen to someone who has no bank account or cannot use a digital application? Will there be assisted payment facilities? What happens during a network outage, a failed transfer or a disputed transaction? People should not be turned away from a government office because they cannot make a digital payment.
Access is only part of the issue. A cashless economy also changes the information generated by ordinary transactions. A digital payment can create a record of who paid whom, how much and when. Depending on the system, it may also be linked to a location or other identifying information. Over time, these records can reveal patterns of work, movement, consumption and association.
Of course, this does not mean government departments can simply access everyone’s financial records. That depends on the legal powers they have and the arrangements governing access to the information. But as more everyday activity moves onto digital payment systems, these questions become harder to ignore.
Pakistan’s wider digital transformation makes this concern more immediate. Government departments are developing systems to exchange data, while digital identity and AI-assisted services are becoming part of policy discussions. Much of the promise of these systems lies in bringing information from different sources together. But that also creates the possibility of using information beyond the reason it was originally collected. Data generated to complete a payment should not become available for unrelated profiling or decision-making simply because it is technically possible to combine datasets.
This raises some basic questions. Who can access transaction data, and for what purpose? How long is it kept? What safeguards apply when banks, payment providers and public bodies are involved? Can individuals find out if their information has been misused and seek a remedy? Pakistan has sectoral financial regulations and legal protections, but it still lacks an enacted, comprehensive personal data protection law. As the amount of financial information being generated grows, the absence of clear and enforceable rules becomes harder to justify.
The government should measure Cashless Islamabad by more than the number of merchants displaying QR codes. It needs to establish who is being left out and provide assisted, low-cost ways to pay. Cash or another accessible alternative should remain available where digital access cannot reasonably be assumed, particularly for essential public services. A policy deadline cannot substitute for evidence that these arrangements actually work. There should also be clear procedures for failed transactions, refunds and complaints. Access to payment data must be limited by law and purpose, with proper audit trails and independent oversight.
Moving towards digital payments may help document economic activity and make transactions easier. But before making cash unavailable, the government needs to ask a more basic question: can people actually use the alternatives being offered to them?
The state is changing more than the way citizens pay. It is changing the conditions on which they participate in public and economic life. That change should make participation easier, not leave people behind because of their income, gender, location or access to technology.
The writer is a technology lawyer specialising in data protection.
