title: Raising our sons
author: none@none.com (Van Nguyen)
content:
IN June, a seven-year-old girl in Sargodha went to a grocery store and never returned. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi lost her life after being sexually assaulted by a teenage relative. Two weeks later, Hina Javed, a 45-year-old professional, was found raped and murdered in her own home in Rawalpindi. Days later, a five-year-old girl in Haripur who had gone out to play was found dead in a well.
These cases broke through in a single summer; many more never did. Each time, Pakistan said “never again,” then turned the page.
    
On paper, Pakistan has made progress. The Anti-Rape Act of 2021 and the rules that followed strengthened how rape is investigated and tried, and how survivors are protected. Yet law ministry figures, reported by Dawn, record 47,452 cases across five categories of rape-related offences in the four provinces between 2021 and mid-2026. And that is only the reported picture: the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights noted that an estimated 70 per cent of gender-based violence incidents go unreported.
In Pakistan, rape is treated as a woman’s problem.
After every case, we ask the same questions. Where were her parents? Why was she alone? Why did she let him in? The questions are always about her.
But we rarely ask the questions that matter. Who are these men and boys? Where did they learn this? And who around them noticed something and said nothing?
In Pakistan, rape is treated as a woman’s problem even though it is something men do, most often men she knows. In cases of reported child sexual abuse, child protection group Sahil found that acquaintances remained the most common category of abusers in 2025. We have spent decades teaching our daughters to be careful but barely begun teaching our sons.
    
Nothing excuses these crimes. But we must look honestly at how boys grow up. Many learn early that anger is the only feeling a man shows, and that a sister’s freedom is his to police. Few ever learn about consent, at home or in school. When they struggle, there is rarely anyone to talk to, because mental health is still a whisper in most homes.
By official count, nearly 12 million boys are out of school. Many grow up without the guidance, support and opportunities that help shape their understanding of relationships and respect. Poverty does not make a rapist, and rape happens in wealthy homes too. But do we want to leave a generation to learn about women from the street and the screen?
So where do we start?
In the classroom. Every child should learn what safe and unsafe touch is, what consent means, and that respect for women is not optional. This belongs in the school curriculum, not in a one-day workshop.
Through UNDP’s work, from strengthening gender-responsive justice and the security sector to supporting Pakistan’s first national strategy on technology-facilitated gender-based violence and expanding women’s economic opportunities, I have seen why institutional reform matters. But I also believe that institutions are too often asked to correct attitudes that have hardened long before a man enters a police station, courtroom or workplace.
    
Which is why men must own this work. For fathers, it starts with how they speak to women at home and with the first time they teach a son that consent is not negotiable. Men who run governments, police stations, courtrooms, mosques and newsrooms can stop interrogating what she was wearing and start asking what he did. Every man who laughs at the joke, forwards the video or keeps the secret is making a choice. Young men, online and in the street, can challenge their peers in ways no elder can.
Most of all, we need to talk about this far more consistently and loudly. Advocacy campaigns come in short bursts: around int­ernational days or after a case trends, before falling silent until another assault dominates the airwaves. When I was growing up in Vietnam, the government ran a family planning campaign with one simple message: “boy or girl, two children are enough.”
It was on billboards, on television and on the radio, year after year, until it became common sense. The context was different, but the lesson stayed with me. A message repeated often enough, for long enough, can reshape what a society considers normal.
    
Pakistan can do the same. Government, media and advertisers could carry one national message, every day, not once a year: rape is a man’s choice and a man’s shame, and every man has a responsibility to speak up.
Every man and boy in this summer’s headlines was shaped in Pakistani homes, schools, and communities, by what the men around them said, did, and allowed. That is where this begins, and where it must end. Pakistan does not only need to protect its daughters. It must raise its sons better.
The writer is deputy resident representative, UNDP Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 25th, 2026

title: Justice or just this?
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
THE wheels of international justice tend to grind slowly. The Gambia launched its complaint against Myanmar at The Hague in November 2019. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its verdict last Thursday, seven years later.
Following the unprecedented finding that the state was indeed guilty of genocide against the Rohingya minority, the biggest question now is whether it will make much difference to the survivors, most of whom found refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Hundreds of thousands more are scattered across various other countries including India and Pakistan, but mostly concentrated in Thailand and Malaysia. The latter, which last month welcomed U Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s president and former military chief, regularly threatens deportation.
The visiting leader offered to take back all citizens; however, a 1982 law stripped most Rohingya of citizenship. The community’s roots in northern Rakhine state go back centuries, yet politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have long tended to pejoratively (and inaccurately) refer to them as ‘Bengalis’. In the early stages of the ICJ case, Suu Kyi even turned up in The Hague to defend Myanmar’s hybrid regime against the charge of genocide.
Suu Kyi had defended Myanmar’s regime against the genocide charge.
At the time she served as the popularly elected ‘state counsellor’ in a political set-up dominated by the Tatmadaw. Within little more than a year, she was deposed in a military coup and thrown behind bars. By then she had lost much of the international respect she had built up over decades as a defender of democracy and human rights.
Suu Kyi remains under detention (albeit not in jail), while red carpets are regularly rolled out for Min Aung Hlaing by his neighbours. The switch from military fatigues to civilian garb ahead of last April’s elections instantly rendered him more palatable to purported democracies in the region. Others, however, were less apprehensive from the start. Beijing, for instance, is reported to have courted the junta set up in Naypyidaw after the 2021 coup while also backing some of the insurgencies ranged against it, but pulled back its support from the latter once it became apparent that the rebels might actually thrash the Tatmadaw.
Partly as a consequence, state forces have been gaining ground, although large parts of the country remain under rebel control and the civil war is far from over. Some of its components, notably the Karen state insurgents, have been at war with the state since soon after Burma, as it was then known, won independence in 1948. Even before that, some Muslim-majority areas evidently sought to become part of East Pakistan. But Mohammad Ali Jinnah demurred, and the Burmese leadership said no.
Across much of Asia and Africa, history and geography are often at odds in the national boundaries bequeathed by retreating empires. However, multiethnic entities are not necessarily destined to be failed states, provided prejudice can be cast aside. As former Human Rights Watch chief Kenneth Roth puts it, “Myanmar has 135 recognised ethnic groups but refuses to accept the Rohingya as the 136th.” The state has also been in combat for decades with other ethnic groups, but ‘clearance operations’ with a view to some manner of extermination were reserved for Rakhine.
After seven years of litigation, the ICJ has given Myanmar another two years to respond to its rulings on restitution, reunification and/or compensation. What can anyone expect in the meanwhile from the UN Security Council, or the individual states that have lately re-embraced Myanmar despite its continuing excesses against its own population?
The ICJ verdict has been greeted as an indication of its eventual ruling in South Africa’s case against Israel. It’s true that the criteria invoked in acce­pting the charges against Myanmar — making clear that ‘counter-insurgency’, ‘counterterrorism’ or ethnic cleansing efforts are not incompatible with genocidal intent — suggest that the case against Israel is a slam dunk. There is no dearth of official statements dehumanising Palestin­ians and vowing extermination. Horrendous as they are, the number of child deaths cited in the verdict on Myanmar is but a fraction of the toll that Israel has notched up. And I hope South Africa will add the documentary NAZA to its brief.
Six of the ICJ’s 15 judges dissented from the majority verdict. The pattern of voting might be different in the case of Israel. But no decision is expected before 2030-31 at the earliest. By then, even if Israel is convicted for a genocide it continues to commit, will it make any difference? Or will it be just another feather in the cap of a postwar legal order that has always struggled to stay relevant in the face of superpower-sized odds? Now, and possibly in the future, one could ask the ICJ: thank you for your verdict, but where’s the justice?

title: Oman oil deal
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S new oil supply agreement with Oman comes at a difficult time for its energy sector. Under the agreement, Oman will supply petroleum products and extend a $200m credit facility. The credit line is important because Pakistan’s fuel imports place considerable pressure on its forex reserves. Deferred payments can ease immediate dollar requirements and provide greater flexibility in financing its purchases. Similar arrangements with other suppliers have helped manage import obligations. But credit facilities are borrowing arrangements at the end of the day. The agreement’s significance, however, extends beyond the deferred payment facility. The arrangement would offer some relief amid uncertainty over regional oil supplies. The continuing disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has exposed Pakistan’s vulnerability to regional conflicts. The country imports nearly 80-85pc of its petroleum requirements, with much of its supplies traditionally passing through this critical maritime passage. Oman offers an important alternative because its ports provide access to the Arabian Sea outside Hormuz. This geographical advantage could help Pakistan reduce its exposure to disruptions affecting traditional Gulf supply routes.
The state must ensure that the agreement translates into reliable supplies at competitive prices. More importantly, the arrangement should prompt a wider rethink of the nation’s energy security. The country has repeatedly faced difficulties whenever international conflicts disrupt oil and gas supplies. Its over-dependence on imported petroleum leaves the economy exposed to external shocks, drains foreign exchange and adds to domestic inflation. Building strategic petroleum reserves, improving storage capacity and developing alternative supply routes must receive greater attention. At the same time, Islamabad also needs to reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels through faster adoption of indigenous renewable energy. Solar and wind power can lower the country’s exposure to international fuel markets over time. The agreement with Oman is welcome. But a new supplier and a credit line cannot, by themselves, resolve Pakistan’s energy vulnerabilities. Energy security requires a sustained reduction in import dependence.
Published in Dawn, November 25th, 2026

title: A referendum leading where?
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
IT seems the regime has decided to push ahead with a referendum on the creation of new provinces, setting aside the intense controversy over the matter. The minister for parliamentary affairs had earlier declared that a referendum on the issue “will happen”; the defence minister now says the process is likely to move forward early next year.
Meanwhile, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, the chairman of the PPP, warned that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces — particularly Sindh — could lead to bloodshed. His statement reflects an extremely volatile situation in the country’s second-largest province. It marks the widening political divide over the proposed referendum, a complex, constitutionally and politically sensitive matter involving a reset of the system, and contradicts the defence minister’s assertion that all stakeholders were close to reaching a consensus on the issue. The differences seem too wide to bridge.
The PPP is a critical stakeholder in the power structure that emerged from the controversial 2024 elections. Yet for all the compromises its leadership has made — compromises that have undermined the democratic process — the party cannot afford to concede, given the strength of the political reaction the issue has provoked in its bastion of power.
Seemingly under pressure, Bilawal is now even calling for “restoring the supremacy of parliament, trust in the judiciary and the electoral system”.
    
It is an interesting development, given that his party played a critical role in getting the 26th and 27th Amendments passed — amendments that have drastically curtailed the independence of the judiciary and further diminished public trust in it. The party has also been a beneficiary of the political system created through manipulated elections. Public trust in state institutions cannot be restored until those anti-democratic amendments are reversed.
The entire debate on this critical issue is taking place outside of parliament.
Notwithstanding the young PPP chairman’s newfound rhetoric, parliament has long since lost its supremacy under the shadow of creeping authoritarianism. The idea of resetting the system through a referendum cannot be seen in isolation; it seems part of a move to consolidate autocracy further.
Interestingly, the entire idea of a “system reset” and a referendum has been triggered by Mohsin Naqvi, the interior minister whose close association with the powers that be is well known. And the entire debate on this critical issue is taking place outside of parliament.
Interestingly, the controversy triggered by Naqvi’s repeated remarks about the collapse of the system and the urgency of resetting it has also prompted some cabinet ministers to question the motive behind the whole campaign. It has brought the divisions within the ruling party into the open.
While the minister for parliamentary affairs and the defence minister have endorsed the reset and referendum plan, the prime minister and the PML-N leadership are conspicuous by their silence on this important constitutional matter.
At the same time, there are signs that the uneasy ruling coalition is unravelling, with public polemics breaking out among the allies. Federal Minister Salik Hussain of the PML-Q is engaged in a legal battle with the Punjab chief minister over alleged corruption charges. It is getting uglier, with other members of the group joining the fracas.
The public exchange of allegations between the two federal ministers — Rana Sanaullah and Mohsin Naqvi — exposes the disarray within the cabinet.
The government looks more like a rudderless ship with no one in charge. It seems the prime minister is more interested in foreign visits than in attending to domestic affairs. For him, it seems, these trips abroad earn his government the legitimacy it lacks at home.
While the debate on the system reset and the referendum rages on in various public forums and in individual statements by federal ministers, the government has yet to come out with any concrete plan for an “administrative reset”, or with the question that would be framed for the vote in the referendum. No plan has been presented before the cabinet either, nor deliberated within the ruling coalition. It leaves us wondering where this plan is being prepared.
Still, the defence minister insists that a joint document would be prepared with input from all stakeholders to ensure that the proposal is acceptable to everyone.
“It will be a joint document in which all the stakeholders will have their input,” he said in an interview with a private TV channel. He also appears hopeful that an agreement on a joint document could be reached by the end of the year.
Notwithstanding his optimism, the latest statement from Bilawal rejecting any proposal for the creation of a new administrative unit in Sindh or the holding of a referendum indicates that no discussion is taking place among the stakeholders.
    
A major question is whether the same question will be framed for the entire country, or separate questions for each province. How can a vote in favour of creating new provinces be applied to Sindh, where an elected assembly has already rejected any such proposal? A referendum could create a political crisis that could bring down the entire edifice.
It is certainly a bad idea for the unity of the country. There is a real need for decentralisation and for empowering elected local governments, and there are constitutional provisions that need to be implemented through a mandate from parliament. But the idea of creating new provinces outside the constitutional process — and that too through a referendum — could be disastrous.
Intriguingly, the referendum issue has been raised at a time when the country is in the midst of political and economic instability and serious internal and external challenges. The two strategically located provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, are facing violent militancy that presents an existential threat to the country.
Now the reset and referendum plan has dangerously polarised Sindh. Can the country afford further political instability in the face of internal and external security challenges? There seems to be no realisation where the proposed referendum on a critical constitutional question would lead to. We also know how the referendum is manipulated to get positive results.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Global Order - the verdict
author: Inam Ul Haque
content:
For the last two weeks, we are discussing the biennial 'Margalla Dialogue' conducted by IPRI (Islamabad Policy Research Institute) on November 10-11, 2026, on the theme 'Global Order in Transition'. After a round-up of the theme's validity and relevant deliberations, this piece would sum up the iterations of other eminent speakers during the Dialogue.

Prof Sayyed Vali Raza Nasr, the Irani-American academic with John Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, agreed with the notion of an Emerging Global Order (EGO), wherein the old Middel East is redefined, under Israeli ambition and America's imperial overreach, that failed to subdue Iran; America's notion of security (especially for the KSA) is severely damaged; drones, missiles and electronics command the new warfare; regional nuclear arms race is in the offing; China has got more space; and Iran has demonstrated surprising societal mobilisation. Iran employed a strategy to fight an empire that is upending the 'developmental strategies' of contemporary militaries, the professor opined.

Ambassador Robin Lynn Raphel, also a former CIA analyst, lamented the US inadvertently accelerating the Global chaos. In her formulation, and echoing other analysts, the 'global concert of cooperative powers' was a more stable framework. She mentioned the changing perception of Israel within the US, as an evolving dynamic. Dr Timofey Bordachev (Russia) spoke about multipolarity, the Sino-US rivalry, Russian foreign policy and the Eurasian integration under his construct of 'three IR factors' and 'four paradoxes'. He was of the view that Russia cannot use its entire military might against Ukraine. Germany's Prof Carl Masala sounded Eurocentric when he, differing with John Meresheimer, asserted that the war in Ukraine will dictate the EGO. Terming multipolarity as wishful thinking and (correctly) disagreeing with imminent demise of the US, as touted, he was confident that a democratic-led Congress would reverse Trumpism, injecting new life into Euro-Atlantic Alliance, because EU was alive and well. According to the worthy professor, Europe needs to learn the language of power and re-arm.

Sherry Rehman spoke online, emphasising geography and economics with regional connectivity as the glue. Geography, she said, is permanent, rivalries need not be. And while history cannot be changed, future can be better navigated. She characterised the EGO by quoting from Chairman Mao: "There is great chaos under heaven. The situation is excellent." She reiterated deterrence and diplomacy not being mutually exclusive. Conventional rivalries are not permanent, and capacity to prevent conflict is important. She criticised New Delhi and IEA respectively for Indus Water Treaty's unilateral abrogation and TTP-sponsored terrorism. IEA, in particular, shares the blame for torpedoing regional connectivity, by providing shelter and tolerance for TTP and terrorism.

Former Foreign Secretary Aizaz Choudhry characterised India as USA's partner of choice, while Pakistan as a random friend. To him energy policies, geography and geopolitics affect regional connectivity. He agreed to the subservience of geoeconomics to geopolitics. Pravin Sawhney, founder and editor of the Force magazine and a former Indian Army officer, participating in person for the second time in Margalla Dialogue, spoke about the 'Global Geopolitics', a term he coined. He characterised the EGO by five big changes, namely the multipolarity, major power rivalry, Russia and China envisioning the EGO, competition in AI and critical technologies, and Chinese-led Global geopolitics affecting our region.

Mr Sawhney was of the view that Russia is more focused on security and stability and Eurasian partnership; whereas the Chinese prism is BRI/CPEC, ECO and President Xi's Global Governance Initiative. Russian, to him wanted a multipolar, but not a polycentric world, being unstable. Opposed to multipolarity, in polycentricity, poles influence their areas/countries of interest. Russia considered China and India as poles in the EGO.

He said China's PLA was as powerful as the US military, and emphasised that Beijing should be part of SAARC to reinvigorate this important regional forum. India and Pakistan, he lamented, were stumbling blocks to realising SAARC's full potential. He agreed that India would not want China in SAARC. In a departure from Prof Mearsheimer's iterations, Pravin opined that the US does not make institutions. He was appreciative of Pakistan being part of major institutions-making, and conflict prevention. He emphasised continued engagement between New Delhi and Islamabad. Replying to a question, Mr Sawhney interestingly observed that Iran will not acquire nuclear weapons, as it makes her a hegemon, and that goes against Tehran's regional framework.

Having discussed IPRI deliberation of interest on Day 1, one must reiterate what was written about International Programme for Development and Stability (IPDS-26), at NDU, as mentioned here previously. Three days of IPDS deliberations and two days of Margalla Dialogue covered a lot of ground, including EGO and its implications for the world, the region and especially for Pakistan. In such deliberations, encapsulating all aspects of such an expansive debate in the allotted time is next to impossible. However, as suggested to NDU, one would like to see a sequel to the Margalla Dialogue, whenever, to dilate certain other important aspects, that are affecting global governance and populations.

Sociologically, the emerging discontent among global youth and a youth-led culture of AI, energy, protest and changed value systems is already overtaking the archaic societal and sociological models. Technology especially AI is rapidly shaping this sociological transformation across national frontiers, warranting serious debate and dialogue.

Geopolitically, lawless unilateralism by the US-Israel nexus in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria and its possible wider emulations by rising powers like India and others sound the alarm bells, asking for 'return to rules' in the EGO, to protect national interests, sovereignty and geographic boundaries. Politically, ethics, religion and nationalism are the newly energised factors that shape EGO. These also need serious and engaging debate. From an academic standpoint, the General-Politician debate needs to be highlighted and possibly settled – whether Generals mislead the Politicians to score career highs or Politicians brow-beat Generals to have their way on globe-altering junkets, like the US war on Iran.

Militarily, the AI proliferation and its effects on human intelligence and cognitive capacity need further exploration and regulation, before it is too late. Recent AI-enabled military technologies have hastened the worrying trend about acceptance of greater civilian losses in warfare, as the non-contact warfare is no more subservient to the logic of conscience. (Concluded)

title: Absenteeism woes
author: none@none.com (Parvez Rahim)
content:
EMPLOYERS face multiple challenges while managing their businesses. Besides setting up the necessary infrastructure, the quality of manpower plays a key role in the success of an enterprise. The top operating companies in Pakistan, the numbers of which have shrunk substantially over the last 30 to 40 years, employed the best technicians and operators, who were much wanted by petroleum giants, such as Safco and Aramco.
Such workers are mostly committed to their company’s interests in complying with safety policies and fulfilling job responsibilities. Regular attendance plays a crucial role in judging an employee’s commitment to his job and organisation.  In progressive companies, there is a provision of two weekly rest days, and between 20 to 25 days of annual leave against the statutory requirement of 14 days per annum. The quantum of other leaves in the law comprises 10 days of casual leave, 16 days of sick leave, and around 15 days of festival-related holidays per year. The total number of leaves and holidays is approximately 165 days, leaving just 200 days of work in a year. Despite this time off, if an employee is absent from work without approval, they should be disciplined.
Excessive absenteeism exists in industrial and commercial undertakings across the world. The most common reason that is given is sickness. Illness can be feigned; no doctor can ascertain whether the absence was in any way related to a disease. Employees also miss work because of social, cultural and economic reasons. Many are absent because the work is either unrewarding and hazardous or stressful. An employee’s grave personal issues, too, can have a negative impact on their attendance.
Other key causes of absenteeism include a heavy workload, long hours, and high-pressure tasks coupled with the expense of commuting. Chronic illness, injury, and anxiety make sick leave necessary, as does lack of childcare or eldercare. Workers who feel unappreciated or disconnected from company goals are too discouraged to show up, while bullying and lack of support from supervisors make the workplace unsafe.
Employers should identify the causes of absenteeism.
Chronic absenteeism is the consistent absence of an employee from the workplace. This prevents them from carrying out their duties in a timely and productive fashion, which violates a company’s personal or sick leave policy. The hidden costs of absenteeism include overtime for those who cover for absent employees, temporary hiring costs, and the low morale or reduced productivity of those who have to work harder for someone chronically absent. Meanwhile, when such absentees return to the office, they spend the first few days in either catching up, or attending to pending work.
According to Standing Order 15 of the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance, 1968, “habitual absence without leave or absence without leave for more than ten days” constitutes misconduct. An employee guilty of misconduct may be dismissed from employment if the charge against him is proven in the domestic inquiry held to investigate the allegation.
However, employers are often advised to proceed against errant employees gradually. The former should first explore the causes of an employee’s absenteeism and, if possible, try to correct inconvenient factors within their organisations. If such an exercise alleviates the absenteeism of an employee, counselling sessions can then be instituted to address stress and anxiety for all. The result will not only be improved overall attendance but also a content and productive workforce. Introducing incentive schemes for employees who maintain an exemplary attendance record also goes a long way in encou­raging people to be present in the office.
In the case of an employee becoming entangled in a criminal case and imprisoned for an unspecified period, the superior courts maintain that it is unfair to expect an employer to keep a post vacant indefinitely.
In all such cases, the employers had invoked the provisions of Standing Order 12 (3) of the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordi-nance, 1968.
It provides that the services of a workman may be terminated by an order in writing, which shall explicitly state the reason for the action taken and is paid one month’s wages in lieu of notice.
In its judgement on April 26, 2021, the Supreme Court of Pakistan agreed with all the judgments of the lower courts, in which the employers had resorted to the aforementioned Standing Order to terminate the services of employees absent for an indefinite period. The SC also held that the services of an employee may be terminated if he is unable to return to work for a period of two months.
The writer is a human resources consultant at the Aga Khan University Hospital.
Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026
topic: Causes, Impact, and Management of Absenteeism in the Workplace with Legal Implications in Pakistan

Chronic absenteeism imposes significant hidden costs on employers, such as overtime expenses, temporary hiring, decreased employee morale, and reduced overall productivity.
Pakistani law, specifically Standing Order 15 of the 1968 Ordinance, identifies habitual absence exceeding ten days as misconduct, potentially leading to dismissal after a domestic inquiry.

Employers are encouraged to proactively address root causes of absenteeism through counselling and incentive schemes before resorting to disciplinary action, although superior courts support termination for indefinite absence.

Standing Order 15 of the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance, 1968, defines "habitual absence without leave or absence without leave for more than ten days" as misconduct.
The Supreme Court of Pakistan, in a judgment on April 26, 2021, affirmed that an employee's services may be terminated if they are unable to return to work for a period of two months.

title: The missing link
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
RULERS who don’t bring power closer to people via strong local bodies want us to believe that they will now bring power closer to people via more provinces. So, the false idea of making many provinces as a cure for our many ills is back with a bang.
Months after it first emerged, the bang is still more noise than a clarion call of reason. I have seen three key reports against it, but none in its favour.
Support — strong on rhetoric but weak on evidence — comes mainly from ministers and friendly analysts. One minister cites Afghanistan’s 34 units. That’s odd as Afghanistan helps us avoid the blushes of being last in South Asia on key governance metrics. It’s a unitary state whose units lack legislative powers and elected bodies. We have 150-plus stronger units (districts) which have elected bodies, at least as per the law.
Some cite unitary France’s 18 units. They too lack legislative powers. Counting them is easier than proving they cause its progress. It has democracy and civilian sway, unlike us. These key parts of the causal chain are not cited in our French politics lessons.
    
Rulers also ignore the proven merits of local bodies. These offer no instant cure. But with higher democracy and civilian sway present, they bring power closer to people globally. And when the two aren’t in place, nothing usually does that. But they remain our missing link between power and the powerless.
Most of us don’t have elected local bodies, they being absent in Gilgit-Baltistan, Quetta, Punjab and Islamabad and now KP due to emergency rule. Even when and where they exist, they are too weak to fix problems.
Provinces often delay their elections for long but dissolve them early. Elections are often held on non-party basis; local officials often lack a public mandate, as in Punjab, and seats for weak groups are often hogged by elites. Citizens have little say in what they do, little recourse when they fail and little voice in how they spend money. Uneven council sizes and missing tiers weaken them further. Local tasks are split among local bodies and many higher-level agencies. Local heads often lack effective control as vague supervisory powers allow interference from above. Weak coordination and capacity gaps further hamper them. Such split and bureaucratic control is high in Islamabad, Sindh and Punjab.
The setups closest to the people have the least powers.
Provinces first make voters wait for local bodies. They later make local bodies wait for cash. They only spend about five per cent of our total state funds, much lower than in many similar states. They depend heavily on provincial funds and can’t legally and practically collect much cash locally. For example, over 95pc of their funds come from such transfers in Sindh. It is often hard to see how provinces divide money across districts, but easy to see that favoured districts get more cash per head.
So, the setups closest to the people have the least powers. Would rulers who have kept local bodies so weak for so long empower new provinces? Their new capitals may be closer, but still out of reach of the masses.
The aim behind dividing provinces may be to make them powerless like local bodies and actually move power away from the people. What provinces have done to local bodies, the centre may now do to the provinces. So, the masses will have one more government level between them and real power.
    
Deep divisions within a setup held together tightly by its strong fear of PTI and its weak mandate make the division of provinces dicey. Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s diatribes exposing its electoral misdeeds and warning against forcing matters via a referendum emitted shockwaves. Our new troi­­ka — the president, prime minister and interior minister — representing all key parts of the hybrid regime, soon agreed on talks. Perhaps those fond of force have shelved it, for now.
The PPP was largely mum when judges, the opposition and activists faced abuses. It has reacted strongly, now that it’s at the receiving end of the stick. Even though it opposes the idea for the wrong reason — the fear of losing the golden goose of Karachi — the right reasons do exist.
PML-N supports this latest demand of powerful quarters via ministers, but the Sharifs stay mum. Perhaps it wants strong promises of extended patronage before giving top-level support. But it, too, may be forced to speak up when it eventually faces problems.
While our hybrid rulers continue to play self-serving games, a nuclear-armed state of nearly 250 million inches closer to multifaceted crises given their misrule. Uninterrupted democracy and civilian sway are the only way to avoid doom.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

summary: The push for new provinces is a 'false idea' and a distraction from the proven merits of strengthening local bodies, which are the true 'missing link' for bringing power closer to the people.

Arguments supporting new provinces are weak, based on misinterpretations of other countries' governance models (e.g., Afghanistan, France) which lack legislative powers and elected bodies at sub-national levels.

Local bodies in Pakistan are systematically weakened by provincial governments through delayed elections, early dissolutions, limited financial autonomy (spending only ~5% of state funds), reliance on provincial transfers (e.g., >95% in Sindh), lack of public mandate, and administrative interference.

The author suggests that the real aim behind creating new provinces might be to make them as powerless as local bodies, effectively moving power *away* from the people and adding another layer between the masses and real authority.

The debate is mired in self-serving political games of a 'hybrid regime,' with deep divisions among ruling parties, risking multifaceted crises for the nuclear-armed state, emphasizing uninterrupted democracy and civilian sway as the only way to avoid doom.

title: COP collapse
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE collapse of climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya recently is a stark reminder of a world disinclined to cooperate for the common good. The first climate conference to end without a deal since the 2009 Copenhagen Summit, COP31 succumbed to entrenched divisions among the delegates.
The main sticking point was the phasing out of fossil fuels, which was not mentioned in the draft agreement because of pressure from the petro-states including Saudi Arabia and Russia. This omission was rejected by the EU, Britain, and some small, climate-vulnerable states, which rightly hold fossil fuels responsible for global warming. Another stumbling block was the lack of commitment to providing climate finance.
Ironically, many of the countries that opposed the deal for not including the transition away from fossil fuels, refused to move forward on earlier pledges to provide and mobilise funding for poor climate-vulnerable countries. It has been noted, in fact, that many of the latter prefer funds over curbs on fossil fuels at this stage, given their need to rehabilitate lives already impacted by climate change and build infrastructure strong enough to withstand future shocks. This may have been one reason why some vulnerable countries curtailed their objections to the draft deal.
    
Day by day, the climate question is assuming greater urgency. Indeed, nature has been unrelenting against the backdrop of COP31. While Pakistan was largely spared the onrush of swelling rivers this year, Nepal witnessed a tragedy when a massive glacier collapse led to the flooding of vast tracts of land, killing hundreds. Heatwaves in Europe reportedly killed over 50,000 people last summer, while wildfires in Spain and France forced thousands of families from their homes.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes […] along with devastating human impacts,” warns the UN’s main environmental agency in its latest Emissions Gap report. The need for cooperation and consensus on tackling climate change has never been greater.
Luckily, the failure of COP31 does not spell the end of climate diplomacy. International regimes built over years to combat a danger that knows no borders are too far advanced to come undone because an agreement was not reached in Antalya. But time is running out.
Given national interests and the nature of geopolitics, absolute consensus may be hard to forge. However, smaller regional initiatives, where countries — especially of the developing world — share green technology and other climate-friendly solutions can be pursued. These countries — which pollute the least but bear the brunt of global warming — have every right to ask for funds from the world’s chief polluters. The question is whether they have the will to safeguard their future through collective action.
Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

title: Terrorism and preparedness
author: Dr Syed Akhtar Ali Shah
content:
The November 11 armed attack on a police contingent at Darbukach in Kohat's Gumbat tehsil portrays a disturbing picture of the erosion of the writ of the state in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Reports emanating from different sources indicate that ten police personnel were martyred while returning from an operation against illegal placer-gold mining. Police also reported killing eighteen assailants. This loss follows attacks on the Speen Mela Police Post at Hassan Khel, Bannu's Gumbati checkpost, and a Karak ambush that claimed the lives of four policemen. Praising the valour and sense of duty of the fallen is necessary to keep motivating the force engaged against terrorism, yet it remains insufficient. Their sacrifice makes it all the more urgent to examine why such violence persists.

Gold deposits along the Indus, from Kund and Khairabad towards Shakardarra, should have been a gift of God for local communities and a boost to the provincial economy. Unfortunately, that belt has been swarmed by armed gangs busy in illegal extraction, reportedly with the support of militant networks. Areas rich in natural resources appear to have been turned into a proverbial "Wild West", where these groups impose their will at gunpoint. The police themselves allege a nexus between illicit miners and militants in Kohat. Given such lethal retaliation, enforcing mining laws now extends far beyond ordinary mineral regulation.

The incident also brings the issue of operational preparedness to the fore. Was adequate intelligence obtained about the adversaries and their capacity? Was the surrounding terrain, including possible vantage points, properly assessed? Were withdrawal routes, communications, reinforcements and casualty evacuation planned for a hostile environment? Was it anticipated that, in such an eventuality, the force might encounter a more sophisticated militant threat? Yet without an independent, professional inquiry, these possibilities cannot be treated as established facts. The objective of posing these questions is to improve training, equipment, command arrangements and officer safety - not to diminish the courage of those who died.

Another dangerous aspect is the shadowy economy it sustains. Violent non-state actors can gain access to mining, mint money, control transport, influence mineral markets and nurture relationships with people whose livelihoods have become dependent upon illegal activity. Some residents may view them as providers of income or dispute resolution; others may submit out of fear. Both circumstances weaken intelligence gathering, encourage recruitment and sustain militant finances. The government must, therefore, go after not just the gunmen, but also the financiers, buyers, suppliers, facilitators and anyone else who protects these illegal operations.

The reported task given to the Area Representative and Development Council to engage with militants raises another serious concern.

At a press conference on November 11, a spokesperson for the Council, quoting the Prime Minister, said that militancy could vanish from the twelve disturbed districts forever within three months if council members and residents persuaded militants to leave. But what does "leave" mean? Would militants lay down their weapons, renounce violence and live in accordance with the law? Or would they simply move to greener pastures, cross the border or regroup? Shifting them elsewhere cannot eliminate the threat, nor does it constitute a lasting restoration of state authority.

My own experience serving in conflict zones in senior police and administrative positions, reinforced by research for my PhD thesis, "Fault Lines of Governance: Challenges of Militancy and Extremism in Pakistan", suggests that comparable measures have not produced the desired results in the past. Tribal elders may be effective in mediating disputes of a local nature, but they cannot be expected to neutralise organised armed movements. Indeed, the South Asia Terrorism Portal recorded at least 194 tribal elders killed in 143 incidents between 2005 and early March 2024. Many were targeted for standing with the government. To expose their successors to similar risks without enforceable protection is to ignore this tragic history.

The 2022 negotiations - followed by the TTP ceasefire - which involved tribal elders, failed to yield the dividends of peace. Demands regarding the withdrawal of security forces and the reversal of FATA's merger became major obstacles. Dialogue and peace agreements are not inherently objectionable, but their terms and conditions must be unambiguous, and in no case should they appear to be a surrender of the writ of the state. The mandate, safeguards, verification mechanisms and consequences for non-compliance must be clearly defined.

Political scientist Francis Fukuyama's concept of "stateness first" is relevant here. Following 9/11, he emphasised that weak institutions result in disorder and the proliferation of transnational security threats. Yet stateness means the capacity to enforce legitimate laws and deliver basic public goods, not arbitrary coercion. Governance ultimately concerns citizens' security, justice, welfare and ability to live without fear. Ideological extremism, including the selective misuse of religious narratives to legitimise violence, must be challenged; however, security operations alone cannot fill the institutional vacuums in which armed groups thrive.

The response must combine intelligence-led policing, a capable Counter-Terrorism Department, sound investigations and credible prosecutions with decisive action against illicit mining and militant financing. Transparent licensing, environmental safeguards and legitimate employment can help detach communities from the underground economy. In the merged districts, meaningful administrative and judicial integration must be matched by adequate financial resources. The announced special funding for police capacity and anti-drone systems should translate into measurable protection on the ground. Furthermore, the government should publish verifiable data on attacks, extortion, kidnappings, illegal mining, prosecutions and civilian safety.

The true measure of the writ of the state lies not in temporary clearance operations, casualty counts or promises that militants will depart within three months. Its real test is whether citizens can travel, work, attend school and obtain justice without seeking permission from armed groups. In essence, the duty to ensure the security and freedom of citizens belongs solely to the state; it cannot be delegated to vulnerable elders.

title: The US & India
author: none@none.com (Touqir Hussain)
content:
A CRITICAL look at US-India relations is essential to understand US-Pakistan ties. It might help dispel a long-held public perception in Pakistan that US-India relations have somehow been a function of the ups and downs in US-Pakistan ties. And that in establishing the extraordinary relationship with India in the last couple of decades Washington has finally “chosen” India over Pakistan.
The foreign policy establishment acknowledges the cyclic nature of US-Pakistan relations. But uplifted by the recent fissures in US-India ties, charmed by President Trump’s compliments, infused by an enduring faith in the US-Pakistan alliance, and confident of Pakistan’s coveted geopolitical salience, it remains ever optimistic that Washington would come back, and relations would be rekindled to their “halcyon” days.
Both the public and official views need revision, based as they are on faulty assumptions that consider the two relationships as competitive and comparable. That is why one keeps hearing successive Pakistan leaders asking the US to treat the two countries equally, and arguing at home that Pakistan needs to keep a balance in relations with China and the US. This is an erroneous view.
Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas.
The problem is Pakistan cannot wean itself away from the pride of having been a preferred ally of the US once upon a time. But this notion refers to a world of the Cold War days in which the US had a single interest in South Asia, which Pakistan was capable and India was unwilling to advance. That South Asia is no more.
There is a new world out there. Its complexity and disorder present a multiplicity of security and strategic challenges, its globalised economy offers exceptional opportunities, and its uncertainty compels countries to hedge, expand, and diversify their partnerships. In this world, India and Pakistan would both have roles for the US, though relations with Pakistan would be transactional and of limited bandwidth, and with India strategic and broad-based. These are two different relations, and neither derives from the strength or weakness of the other, or is based on “choosing” one over the other.
    
Coming to US-India ties, beneath the trade dispute and H1-B visa frictions US-India strategic cooperation and economic relations continue to thrive. There is substantial collaboration on defence production, space, AI, and maritime security.
In a recent piece, Sameer Lalwani of the Carnegie Endowment pointed out that trade rose to its highest level of $240 billion last year. And the new 10-year framework for the US-India Major Defence Partnership calls for advanced exercises and closer defence-industrial ties. Major US tech companies pledged nearly $68bn towards AI infrastructure investments in India last year. Micron, a leading semiconductor firm, opened its first assembly and test facility in India early this year. And recently Applied Materials and Lam Research announced investments in India’s semiconductor industry.
Prime Minister Modi bruised President Trump’s ego by not acknowledging his role in the 2025 India-Pakistan ceasefire. But this has not impacted the substance of relations. Trump has not reversed ties; he has simply put a brake on them.
    
As for tariffs, these have indeed caused strains but they are not India-specific; they are being applied across the board as Trump’s economic instrument and geopolitical weapon. The reality is he would not allow countries to become economic competitors and geopolitical rivals with America’s help and at its expense. US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in his speech at the Rai­sina Dialogue ear­­ly this year that the US would not repeat mistakes made with China with India.
India was so pa­­­mpered by Pre­­sident Biden and Trump in his first term that it came to have a sense of entitlement. Now it is complaining about losing its extra-special status.
Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas. The US, for instance, has long supported Indian indigenous technology development. GE engines have been central to India’s domestic fighter jet industry. India’s first indigenous fighter aircraft Tejas relied on an F-16 testbed, and its development of a fifth-generation fighter relies on US wind tunnels.
From Pakistan’s standpoint, what is im­­p­ortant is that US-India differences have not impinged on India’s importance for Wash­in­­gton in the US-China strategic competition. And it will likely endure. Any occasi­o­nal adjustment in it will not bring dividends for US-Pakistan ties. We need to delink the two relationships in our analysis.
The bottom line: the US will continue to engage both India and Pakistan as there are no alternatives to each relationship. The alternative to India is India, and the alternative to Pakistan remains Pakistan.
The writer, a former ambassador, is adjunct professor at Georgetown University.
Published in Dawn, November 23rd, 2026

title: AMR awareness
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IT is an irony in the world of medicine that even as new treatments bring hope to millions of patients, some older therapies are rapidly losing their efficacy. This point merits serious reflection as we approach the end of World AMR Awareness Week 2026. Although primarily focused on the misuse of antibiotics, which kill bacteria, antimicrobial resistance also encompasses the immunity developed by fungi, viruses, and parasites in the body to standard drugs. The 2026 theme for AMR Awareness Week — ‘One health, one action: prevent AMR now’ — widens the scope of the campaign by underlining the importance of collective efforts and shared responsibility in fighting a scourge that kills millions every year. An interconnected world — where the health of people, animals, and the environment is inextricably linked — demands as much.
The numbers are concerning. WHO says that over 4.7m annual deaths worldwide are associated with antibiotic resistance. The number of such deaths is projected to rise to 39m by 2050, with developing countries bearing the brunt. Official figures for Pakistan indicate that AMR contributes to around 200,000 deaths every year. Given a fragile healthcare system, limited medical accountability, and few public health awareness drives, this number does not come as a surprise. Doctors routinely prescribe antibiotics even for viral ailments. There is also a tendency to self-medicate, and pharmacists often sell antibiotics that might not be needed at all. On the other hand, many of those who do need antibiotics may stop taking them midway through the course when their symptoms improve. In this way, germs learn to withstand the onslaught of the very drugs intended to destroy them. The high incidence of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and typhoid in the country bears alarming testimony to the fact. Sadly, official apathy reigns — public health authorities have not even focused on the prevention and control of infection, let alone regulating the use of medicine. Clean surroundings, uncongested accommodation, safe drinking water, and regular vaccination have a direct bearing on people’s health. To guard against a greater crisis and curb infection rates, Pakistan must ensure that appropriate drug usage goes hand in hand with preventive measures to reduce the need for medicines.

title: The ECO dream
author: none@none.com (Khurram Abbas)
content:
THE 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers was held in Islamabad on November 15-16. The event offered a timely reminder of a regional bloc that remains rich in potential, yet under-realised. Convened under Pakistan’s 2026-27 chairmanship with the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO,” the gathering brought together foreign ministers and senior diplomats from across the 10-nation bloc to adopt the Islamabad Communiqué and chart the road toward ECO Vision 2035.
While the diplomatic optics in the capital projected a renewed commitment to trade facilitation, transport connectivity, and energy security, the real test lies in whether member states can finally translate decades-old aspirations into tangible economic interdependence.
To understand the promise and pitfalls of this forum, one must look at its origins as the Regional Cooperation for Development (RCD), founded in July 1964 by Pakistan, Iran and Turkiye. The RCD sought to leverage historical and cultural affinities for socioeconomic and infrastructural collaboration. However, hampered by limited economic complementarities and geopolitical shifts, most notably the 1979 Iranian Revolution, the RCD eventually became dormant.
It was revived as the ECO in 1985 and underwent a transformative expansion in 1992 with the inclusion of Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, and the five newly independent Central Asian Republics. In contemporary international relations, this bloc spanning over eight million square kilometres and home to nearly 500m people matters immensely as a Eurasian bridge. At a time when global supply chains are fragmenting and great-power rivalries are hardening, the ECO represents a vital non-Western platform capable of linking resource-rich Central Asia with the warm waters of the Arabian Sea and European markets via Turkiye.
The real test lies in whether members can translate aspirations into economic interdependence.
Despite operating in one of the world’s most conflict-prone neighbourhoods, the ECO possesses compelling structural drivers for regional integration. First, the economic complementarity between its members creates a natural logic for cooperation. The hydrocarbon and mineral wealth of Central Asia and Iran pairs seamlessly with the industrial bases, agricultural output, and massive consumer markets of Pakistan and Turkiye. Furthermore, the landlocked geography of six of its 10 members makes regional connectivity not merely an economic preference, but an existential necessity for diversifying trade routes.
Second, regional integration within the ECO framework can serve as a stabilising buffer against geopolitical volatility. In a region marred by lingering sanctions on Iran, prolonged instability in Afghanistan, and shifting security dynamics in the South Caucasus, economic interdependence raises the cost of conflict and institutionalises dialogue. Projects such as the Istanbul-Tehran-Islamabad (ITI) cargo corridor, the Ashgabat Agreement, and emerging joint border trade zones demonstrate that technical and commercial frameworks can survive political friction. By focusing on low-politics areas such as customs harmonisation under the ECO Trade Agreement, climate resilience, and tourism, the bloc allows neighbours, despite having strained ties, to compartmentalise security disputes while gradually building the physical and institutional infrastructure of peace.
For Pakistan, the ECO occupies an increasingly central place in its geo-economic and strategic calculations. With the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation effectively paralysed by New Delhi’s political intransigence, Islamabad has deliberately pivoted westward and northward to avoid regional isolation. The ECO provides Pakistan with a natural diplomatic forum where it enjoys deep historical, cultural, and religious ties without the hegemonic friction that characterises South Asian politics. Being an active member of ECO, Islamabad is eager to position itself as the indispensable transit hub connecting landlocked Central Asia to global maritime trade through the ports of Karachi and Gwadar.
Beyond diplomatic utility, the ECO directly aligns with Pakistan’s domestic economic imperatives, particularly energy security and trade diversification. Islamabad views regional energy initiatives such as the TAPI gas pipeline and the CASA-1000 power project as critical lifelines that can only succeed within a cooperative ECO ecosystem. Also, Islamabad believes that expanding preferential trade agreements with Central Asian states and Turkiye offers Pakistani exporters access to untapped markets, reducing Islamabad’s over-reliance on traditional Western destinations.
Yet, any realistic assessment of the ECO’s future must confront its most critical geographical and political bottleneck: Afghanistan. Positioned squarely at the crossroads of South and Central Asia, Afghanistan is the indispensable land bridge required to turn ECO’s connectivity blueprints into reality. However, due to the presence of transnational terrorist groups like IS-K and TTP, chronic insecurity continues to deter international investors, inflates transit insurance costs, and stalls flagship projects such as the Trans-Afghan Railway and TAPI. Without verifiable counterterrorism guarantees and secure transit corridors across Afghan territory, the physical integration of Central Asia with Pakistani ports remains an aspiration rather than an actionable trade route.
Further, the absence of an inclusive governance structure that prevents Kabul from gaining formal international recognition creates operational, legal and technical impediments. Without recognising the Taliban’s legitimacy in Kabul, it is difficult to standardise customs, enforce binding trade treaties, or unlock international financing needed for cross-border megaprojects.
The ECO dream cannot be realised if member states do not confront several difficult questions in the 19th ECO summit, to be held in Islamabad in 2027. How will ECO devise resilient financial and trade mechanisms to bypass or overcome the crippling impact of US sanctions on Iran, which routinely paralyses banking channels and stalls joint energy ventures? What viable security framework can be established with Kabul to neutralise terror threats when the interim administration remains diplomatically unrecognised and politically exclusive?
More critically, can ECO members muster the collective political will to forge a unified regional security architecture specifically tasked with protecting transnational pipelines, railways, and pow­er grids traversing insecure Afghan territory?
The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.

title: Drilling for oil
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S renewed effort to explore oil and gas reserves in its offshore waters, this time in partnership with Turkiye, calls for cautious optimism.
We have been here before. Successive governments have pursued offshore exploration. But the efforts have produced little. Some 18 exploratory wells have been drilled in offshore waters since independence. None has resulted in a viable discovery.
The most prominent recent attempt was the Kekra-1 well in 2019, when an international consortium spent around $100m. The well was eventually abandoned without finding oil or gas.
That episode was particularly instructive because of the political hype surrounding it. The premier at the time publicly raised expectations of a potentially enormous discovery, suggesting that Pakistan might find enough gas to end its dependence on imports. The speculation generated excitement, only to fizzle out when drilling results proved disappointing.
    
Such premature claims do little to help a sector in which exploration is inherently uncertain and commercial discoveries require years of investment and technical work. The present initiative must not be burdened with similar expectations.
The Turkish vessel will collect data over approximately 670 square kilometres in the Eastern Offshore Indus-C Block. The surveys and their interpretation are expected to take several months, with the first exploratory drilling targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027. The block is estimated to hold 1.5 to 2tn cubic feet of gas, but this remains a geological estimate. Only drilling can establish whether commercially recoverable resources exist.
    
Still, there are good reasons to welcome the renewed push. The nation’s dependence on imported oil and gas leaves its economy exposed to international price volatility, supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions. The recent instability around vital shipping routes has once again demonstrated the economic costs of relying heavily on external supplies. Indigenous discoveries could reduce the import bill, ease pressure on forex reserves and strengthen long-term energy security.
Turkiye’s participation also offers an opportunity to bring in technical expertise, investment and experience. But the government must ensure that this partnership translates into sustained exploration rather than a one-off exercise. Regulatory consistency, security, competitive terms and a predictable investment environment will be essential to attract other foreign firms.
There is no guarantee of a major discovery, but the country cannot afford to leave its potential unexplored. This time, the hope should rest on science, investment and results.
That said, even a commercially viable offshore oil or gas discovery must not be allowed to distract attention from the adoption of renewables, which remain the long-term solution to the country’s energy problems.

title: Problems and prescriptions
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
THE upward trajectory of the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) reading, which clocked in at 110 in October 2026, is a frequent subject of debate among economic commentators. Some argue that it shows the currency is being ‘artificially managed’, as was the case in past such episodes which usually preceded painful adjustments. Others have pointed out that the REER is just one indicator among several to assess the position of an economy’s health.
An excellent piece by Dr Ishrat Husain on these pages lays out the latter’s position quite categorically: “REER has a legitimate but limited purpose. It measures changes in the nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price movements against trading partners. But an index reading of 100, based on a selected base year, doesn’t establish an optimal exchange rate. Nor does a deviation from 100 automatically signal overvaluation or undervaluation. REER says little about balance-of-payments sustainability, foreign exchange availability from non-trade sources or exporters’ ability to compete through quality, technology, productivity, and delivery.”
    
Knowledgeable experts will continue to weigh in on this issue, but it is worth looking at the exchange rate from the economy’s current vantage point. A minor current account surplus, a primary (fiscal) surplus, monthly central bank purchases, not sales, of dollars from the open market, increasing reserves, and a very narrow spread between the interbank and open market rate suggest there is nothing immediately scandalous about the current rate.
The PKR’s value is where it is because the inflow of dollars has been robust on account of some export growth plus significant remittance inflows, positive real interest rates, selective administrative checks on imports, and the dollar’s own position against other currencies.
FDI’s future looks uncertain under geopolitical fracturing and tariffs are loudly back on the menu.
Taking a slightly broader timeframe, what is also clear is that at its existing level of productivity the Pakistani economy’s current rate of sustainable growth — ie growth that doesn’t blow up the external sector and/or cause domestic inflation — is around 4pc. Of this, 2.5pc is attributable to natural population growth, and the remaining is what the economy contributes by way of actual productivity.
It is with this bleak baseline condition that many experts push for a gradual, enforced devaluation of the currency as a policy position. The argument here is that this downward flexibility is an important ingredient, among others, for export competitiveness. Given the government’s stated position of catalysing export-led growth, enforced depreciation along with import liberalisation appears to be the logical path to take.
This prescription can be found with near-universal frequency in government documents, multilateral donor/lender documents, and in expert/technocratic commentary at any point over the last two decades. The fact that it is never acted upon in full is a political economy question. The government, in practice, prioritises some societal segments over others (importers over exporters), picks some objectives over others at different times (stabilisation versus growth), and chooses to inflict pain on some rather than others (who gets rents versus whose subsidies get taken away).
But there is another cloud looming on the horizon of this prescription. What if the country has missed the boat of beneficial global trade integration altogether?
The strategy of economic development of much of the Third World/Global South since the mid-20th century has gone through three phases: protectionist import-substituting industrialisation from the 1950s to the 1970s; structural adjustment and market-led liberalisation (starting in the 1980s); and dreams of integrating into global value chains (GVCs) through export-led strategies (from the 1990s onwards).
Pakistan repeatedly pays homage to the third approach, but success remains limited at best. It has achieved reasonable integration in textiles and a few other sectors, but has little else to boast about. The wide range of conflicts that characterise its political economy have constrained baseline productivity to such a large extent that the country possesses or makes little of note that the world wants. Its natural advantage in cheap labour has been undone by poor human capital formation and other burdens, such as its energy sector and struggles with political violence. As a result, its industrial base remains shallow and growth remains anaemic.
    
In the current moment, the prospects for favourable integration look even dimmer. If AI and robotics development continues at pace, the marginal cost of labour across the world will fall further. Why then would integrating Pakistan’s cheap and mostly unskilled labour into any value chain, at any level of sophistication, make sense?
Bluntly put, where the world produces the things it consumes has already been decided to a very large extent. China is the factory of the world, and those economies functionally integrated with China’s factors (its South-East Asian partners) have a future in global trade. The rest of the developing world mostly does not.
Simultaneously, we’re witnessing increased insistence on new domestically oriented industrial policies, which prioritise re-industrialisation and on-shoring. FDI’s future looks uncertain under geopolitical fracturing and tariffs are loudly back on the menu of policy options to protect industrial employment. This means that an emerging multipolar world order might see economic delinking rather than greater integration.
All of this is to say that while the benefits of export-led growth are well known, the world in which export-led growth is possible for Pakistan may no longer exist. If this admittedly pessimistic reading is correct, does our current conversation have any space for a different type of economic strategy to shake off this anaemic 4pc per annum baseline? Do we, in effect, have a backup answer for how Pakistani labour and Pakistani capital can be productively combined to generate employment, reduce poverty, and improve human flourishing?
The writer teaches politics and sociology at LUMS.

title: COP failure
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
OVERSHOOT. That’s the word we’ll now hear to gloss over the global collective failure to tackle climate change. No more talk of the climate apocalypse, not even of the emergency or breakdown. Instead we get three simple syllables, which in an age of hyper-masculinity, techno-determinism and intergalactic ambitions may even have a positive ring.
This is the outcome of the UN climate change conference, COP31, which was wrapping up this weekend in Turkiye. Overshoot is the term being used to accept, for the first time at a COP, that humanity has failed to stick to the 1.5-degree warming goal agreed in Paris in 2015. The first step to recovery is admitting you have a problem, but sadly this COP, with its resignation to the overshoot reality, is more likely the beginning of the end.
This COP’s largest failure did not unfold in Antalya, but rather in Shenzhen, where the leaders of the world’s superpowers met and agreed to ramp up oil production. There could be no greater slap in the face of the climate movement.
China’s decision not to bid to host COP33 in 2028 was also a disappointment, denying the climate movement the strong leadership it needs. With its turbo-charged approach to electrification, China would have been the fillip needed. But Beijing has opted not to enter the fray of climate diplomacy, given that COP33 will be a stocktake moment following the publication of the latest climate reports from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. These reports will cover topics such as the causes of climate change, adaptation ideas and options to avoid worsening the situation, and hosting COP33 would be an implicit endorsement of the science, one Beijing is not willing to make.
The fight against climate change will be fought by the people.
The fact that COP31 ran over because countries were disagreeing over whether to explicitly mention fossil fuels in the conference agreement is a sign of how dire the climate debate has become. Fossil fuel producers, led by Saudi Arabia, were pushing to remove mentions of oil, gas and coal (and the related requirements to transition away from these) in favour of fantasies of carbon capture and storage. Panama’s environment minister hit a nerve when he decried fossil-fuel producing countries’ and companies’ efforts to hold the climate negotiations hostage, saying the world was in ‘love with [its] kidnappers.’ (This is an uncomfortable situation for Pakistan, as it juggles the reality of its climate vulnerability, its position as a leading voice among climate-affected developing countries, and its growing closeness and defence ties with the Kingdom.)
Talk of climate justice was also muted. The adaptation fund generated paltry pledges, and there was intense lobbying, led by a few countries including Saudi Arabia and the Vatican, against maintaining a gender lens for conference commitments. This is another setback given how hard-won the acknowledgement was that climate change affects different groups differently, with the impact being significantly higher on women and marginalised and vulnerable communities. The overshoot will intensify challenges.
This bleak outcome is particularly upsetting because the emphasis on electrification for this COP under Turkiye’s leadership was a positive step to tackling policy implementation challenges. A key priority was the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which commits to increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35pc by 2035. This felt like a realistic goal given this year is the first time that renewable sources (solar) outstripped oil and gas to contribute the largest share of global energy.
Pakistan was ce­­lebrated as a pos­ter child for this electrification ef­­f­ort, given we have boosted the share of electricity generated from solar from one to 28pc between 2018 and 2025. But the real lesson Pakistan can offer the world in the wake of COP31 is that the fight against climate change and its impacts will be fought by the people, irrespective of the failures of their leadership.
Pakistan’s renewables and electrification story is not one of the success of top-down climate policy. It’s what happened when a desperate public’s survival instinct kicked in. People installed solar panels as a response to expensive energy, endless blackouts, and extreme heat, against the backdrop of rapidly reducing Chinese solar panel costs.
Perhaps it’s time to give up the COPs and global commitments, and start from the bottom up. There is now no community (except perhaps Elon Musk’s fantastical colony on Mars) that is not worried in a tangible way about their homes being flooded, their crops failing, their businesses closing, their weak and old collapsing due to extreme heat. Let them organise to do the necessary if world leaders won’t.
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
