title: Legislative scrutiny
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
PAKISTAN’S parliament and the provincial assemblies have an elaborate infrastructure of parliamentary oversight and scrutiny of the executive. There are more than 200 parliamentary committees in the six houses, including 35 in the National Assembly, 45 in the Senate, 45 in the provincial assembly of Punjab, 34 in Sindh, 38 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 15 in Balochistan.
Each committee comprises 20 to 30 members varying from house to house. These members elect a committee chair in their first meeting; the chair is entitled to two personal staffers, a chauffeur-driven and fully maintained official car and an exclusive office. The committee members and the chair are entitled to travel and daily allowances for the days of the meeting and two days before and after the meeting. All this is paid for from the taxpayers’ pocket and is fully justified in view of the work assigned to these committees. Unlike the British parliamentary committees, which meet only during the plenary sessions of parliament and therefore do not incur any extra travel or daily allowance cost, parliamentary committees in Pakistan mostly meet when the legislature is in recess and hence, extra travel and daily allowances are to be paid separately.
The Indian parliament has adopted another measure and constituted joint committees of the Lok Sabha (equivalent to our National Assembly) and the Rajya Sabha (like Pakistan’s Senate), which not only speeds up scrutiny in the committees, but results in some savings as well. In Pakistan, we have independent and separate committees both for the National Assembly and the Senate. Although the Indian joint committees system is efficient, it deprives parliament of a double layer of scrutiny which is available in Pakistan.
The problem arises when important bills are summarily processed within days or even hours.
In all systems of governance, whether presidential like the US, parliamentary like the UK and Pakistan, the parliaments — whatever name these are known as — rely on the committees to do most of the substantive work, especially the oversight of the executive, which primarily includes scrutiny of legislation. In any work which requires detailed scrutiny like the annual budget, a constitutional amendment, ordinary legislation or, as in the case of the US, confirmation of senior appointees in the executive and judiciary, committees play a pivotal role. It is not practical to do such work in plenary.
Rules of almost all the legislatures in Pakistan provide that each legislation, after it is introduced in the plenary, will be referred to the relevant committee for detailed deliberations and scrutiny. In extraordinary circumstances, the plenary has the authority to suspend the rule and consider the legislation in the plenary without referring it to the committee concerned. One of the criteria by which the quality of democracy and effectiveness of legislative oversight in a country is assessed is the percentage of legislation which is not referred to the committees; the higher the percentage, the less democratic and effective the country and the legislature are considered. An associated criterion is the time taken and the number of meetings held to scrutinise the legislation in a committee. If legislation is referred to a committee to fulfil a formality and the committee returns it to the plenary in a day or two, it reflects very negatively on the democratic credentials of the parliament.
As far as the number of bills passed by the legislatures is concerned, Pakistan has a reasonably good record. In the National Assembly, an average of 50 bills have been passed per year during the past four assemblies. The problem arises when the bills, especially the most important ones like constitutional amendments, are summarily processed within a couple of days, and sometimes within hours. For example, a record 279 bills were passed during the previous 15th National Assembly (2018-2023), which is the highest compared to the previous three assemblies starting from 2002.
Although legislative activity had increased, the way these bills were passed without debate and scrutiny of the committees was widely criticised by legislators, media and political commentators. The coalition government passed 73 bills in the last session alone within 21 days. Almost half the bills (36) were not referred to the standing committees concerned and rushed through the plenary without a meaningful debate.
The current 16th National Assembly has so far passed 162 bills in its 32 months of existence. The National Assembly data shown on its official website does not indicate the statistics about the bills referred to the committees or otherwise. Transparency demands that this particular information should be available to citizens and media. In the absence of such data, time-consuming research needs to be undertaken bill by bill to know the extent to which the standing committees were involved in the legislative process.
According to analysis carried out by Pildat, 39 per cent of the bills passed by the current assembly so far were not referred to the committees and instead, the rules were suspended to pass the bill in the plenary directly. This translates to 48 (38pc) government bills and 15 (42pc) private members’ bills. This, by no means, is a good record.
The situation becomes even more disappointing when we see that such important legislation such as the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments — which have had far-reaching impact on state institutions like the judiciary and the armed forces — are passed within a couple of days. The 26th Amendment was introduced in the Senate on Oct 20, 2024 and was passed the same day. The National Assembly passed it the next day and the president gave his assent later in the day. It was notified in the Gazette later in the evening. Such important legislation was wrapped up in two days. The 27th Amendment was also passed with the same hurry.
Laws decide the fate of a nation for a long time. It is about time our legislative leadership gave more time to the committees and the plenary to improve the quality of legislation.
The writer is president of Pakistan-based think tank, Pildat.

title: 1971, again: a quick scan of who is still speaking
author: Dr Rakhshinda Perveen
content:
The backyard is where we look last. How many of us are genuinely concerned about human rights violations there, those lasting decades, involving people whose predicament complicates our national narratives?

I have long asked this about the abandoned Pakistanis of 1971, also called stranded, most of them Biharis, who still "live" in ghettos in Bangladesh.

Whataboutism is distasteful, yet every writer's freedom to choose subject, perspective and silences deserves respect. Nobody's scholarship or right to a platform is in question. But why does one part of this history command sustained attention while the fate of Bihari patriots, and of generations devastated after 1971, remains peripheral? Respecting a writer's choices should not require us to accept collective amnesia.

Why do we so rarely hear Pakistan's intellectual and literary circles speak about the human rights of Pakistanis abandoned in Bangladesh, many living in deeply inhumane conditions

Solidarity with the mazloomeen, the oppressed, of Bucha, Gaza or elsewhere is right, and selective morality must be challenged. This is not about competing tragedies, but universal rights must also reach those closer to home.

In the first week of November 2026, I conducted a rapid online archive scan of opinion articles published in The Express Tribune between 1 October 2025 and 31 October 2026. It was a quick scan, not a systematic audit. Using the keywords 1971, Bangladesh, East Pakistan, Fall of Dhaka, stranded Pakistanis, Biharis, Urdu-speaking and Geneva Camp, in headlines or article text, the search yielded 21 op-eds by eight contributors (six men and two women, including myself). They address Bangladesh's political transition, diplomacy, trade, historical grievances and the legacy of 1971.

The limits should be stated plainly. The scan covers a single newspaper, so it is indicative, not representative of Pakistan's wider discourse. My keywords include Bihari-specific terms, and eleven of the 21 pieces are mine, so the count is shaped by my own writing. A keyword search can also miss articles that take up the Bihari question in other words. Readers should weigh the findings accordingly.

The male contributors accounted for nine pieces: Air Vice Marshal (retd) Shahzad Chaudhry (1), Maj Gen(retd) Inam ul Haq(1), Brig (retd) Dr Raashid Wali Janjua (1), Imtiaz Gul (3), Syed Mohammad Ali (1) and Dr Moonis Ahmar (2).

Dr Ahmar has spoken and written about the Bihari question elsewhere, though his articles here during these 13 months focused on other aspects of Bangladesh.

I list these names as data, not as criticism of anyone's choices. Among these articles, I found no headline or central focus addressing the suffering, sacrifices and slaughter of the Biharis, nor their repatriation and right to redistributive justice, by which I mean the state-led reallocation of wealth, resources, property and opportunity to those long denied them. I apologise in advance if my scan missed an empathetic reference by any of them or another contributor.

The sole exception was the other woman writer, Shazia Tasneem Farooqi, whose column "Iqbal Rabbani's Blood-Stained Shirt" (16 December 2025) moved me deeply. By bringing her family's loss into the public narrative, she humanised a history too often reduced to abstractions. Over the same period, The Express Tribune graciously gave me space for eleven opinion pieces examining the Bihari question, the erasure of 1971, Bangladesh's political developments, and our broader obligations of historical and humanitarian empathy. Nine by the men, one by Farooqi and eleven by me make the 21. A twelfth piece of mine, "America at 250: Love, Doubt, and the Debts We Haven't Paid", explored unpaid historical debts in a wider context and also addressed 1971 and the stranded Biharis. I have kept it outside the count of 21.

Political transition, the military history of 1971 and diplomatic rapprochement between Islamabad and Dhaka are important subjects in their own right. But no discussion of Bangladesh is complete without 1971, and no account of 1971 is complete without the devastation it brought to my community. Where, within these conversations, are the people who remain stranded?

My separate independent research on television, "Do Pakistani Television Channels' Current Affairs Talk About the Abandoned Pakistanis of 1971? A Rapid Mapping of Broadcast Journalism (2020 to 16 December 2025)", is available on my websites. It found sustained, agenda-setting engagement difficult to identify across the channels examined. Where the issue did appear, it was a fleeting reference, charity appeal or incidental mention rather than structured inquiry. The periods and methods differ, but the question is the same: what place does this issue hold in our public discourse? Silence in the media matters because it leaves real lives unresolved.

Legal recognition has not ended the problem. Bangladesh's 2008 High Court ruling on citizenship did not reach everyone in the so-called camps, and even those recognised remain unequal in practice, many still living in what are, in reality, ghettos.

The Bihari question is about more than repatriation, citizenship or bilateral relations. It concerns historical responsibility, human dignity and generations left on the margins of political priorities. That responsibility belongs to writers and broadcasters, and also to the state. These people need recognition, rights, security and a durable political solution, not periodic reminders that they exist.

Do we defend human rights as a principle, or only for comfortable stories? Fifty-five years on, generations have been born in those ghettos, and Pakistan rarely says their names. If we can revisit 1971, we can ask what became of those left behind.

Please look again, human rights community, academics, historians, journalists, civil society, think tanks and strategic experts. Pakistan must also counter anti-state literature on 1971 built on unverified or disputed accusations, through dedicated desks and think tanks that respond with documented, evidence-based scholarship.

A stable state can afford introspection. Those who stood with Pakistan's unity deserve its care. Begin with a parliamentary hearing and a clear Foreign Office position.

Stability is measured by the dignity we give our own.

Pakistan, please, open your heart.

title: Future wars
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
THE four-day military confrontation between India and Pakistan last year and the US-Iran war this year have revealed how today’s wars have become far more complex than the conventional conflicts humanity has experienced over millennia. The days of massed soldiery, mechanised armour, and standardised formations are over. Today’s wars are hybrid and employ every instrument of power a state can muster.
These wars involve cyberattacks, economic coercion, psychological manipulation through electronic and social media, and cultural invasions. Critically, today’s wars employ lethal technologies, which have left traditional battlefield concepts behind. These autonomous weapons are guided by specialised semiconductors, microchips, and sensors.
The changing nature of war has coincided with the sharp descent of the world order into disarray. Wars and armed conflicts between and within states have broken out in various parts of the world. The pledge that all states had made to the UN Charter to respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is no longer being honoured.
Two distinguishing features of today’s warfare are advanced missiles and armed drones, which have transformed the nature of war by enabling high-precision, long-range, and rapid response capabilities. In last year’s India-Pakistan war, Pakistan used missiles to down several Indian aircraft flying well beyond visual range. In the US-Iran war this year, both sides relied mostly on missiles guided by infrared sensors and satellite communication rather than conventional confrontation.
Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context.
Advanced robotic systems are being employed for intelligence, surveillance, and even targeted strikes. Drones and robotic dogs can provide real-time data, improve combat efficiency, and operate for high-risk functions such as clearance of mines or locating captured personnel. Unarmed aerial vehicles provide real-time intelligence, and are equipped with AI-driven capabilities to analyse data. Targets can be independently tracked and even struck by loitering munitions or suicide drones. Transporting supplies and ammunition entails no life losses thanks to unarmed ground vehicles. Drone swarms can now be trained to carry out coordinated attacks. It’s only a matter of time before humanoid robots are deployed for military roles.
The spectrum of modern wars employs other technologies as well, such as quantum computing, which solves complex problems faster than classical computers. It ensures unhackable and secure data transmission during conflict situations. Next-generation structural battery composites can store energy for longer periods.
Future wars will move further away from face-to-face engagement or human-controlled systems. Intelligent autonomous systems will be central to making decisions, often without human intervention. However, this raises some serious ethical questions. Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context or apply compassion. There is greater likelihood of violating the laws of war and committing war crimes without assigning accountability. Further, the speed and agility of these technologies could cause conflicts to spiral out of control.
These technologies will also be used to break an adversary’s morale by targeting its economic assets or supply chains. During the Iran war, for instance, President Trump threatened to destroy Iran’s power grid and bridges, even its civilisation.
The kind of technologies a nation possesses will now determine the extent of damage that a future war would impose on an adversary’s policy options. The ability of a nation to acquire and em­­ploy modern technologies is thus cri-tical to both wag­-ing future wars and surviving them.
What makes future wars more frequent and unaccountable is the evolving global ecosystem, where use of force has emerged as the primary arbiter of international relations. Major powers have no qualms about using force illegally, unilaterally, and disproportionately to overpower adversaries. In such an uncertain environment, middle and small powers are looking for ways to fend for themselves and make alliances with like-minded countries. This has nudged countries to focus more on R&D for developing not only war-related technologies but also their own digital and satellite-based communication links. That requires a stronger economy, credible information instruments, and creative narrative-building to deter aggression.
Diplomatic tools must be geared up to avert such complex multidomain future wars. The world needs a new global compact of indivisible security, akin to the UN Charter, to bind states into mutual respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. This is the only way to avert the devastating wars of the future.
The writer is Chairman Sanober Institute and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

The increasing reliance on intelligent autonomous systems raises serious ethical concerns regarding accountability, understanding context, and the potential for violating laws of war.

The breakdown of the global order, marked by unilateral use of force, necessitates that nations invest in advanced R&D for deterrence, while the world urgently needs a new global compact for indivisible security.

title: Reforming Karachi’s governance
author: none@none.com (Dr Noman Ahmed)
content:
KARACHI’S governance appears to be in a serious paradox. On one hand, one finds political leaders of various ranks cutting ribbons and unveiling plaques around pedestrianised food streets and making promises for more such amenities. On the other hand, a major regional financial institution is expressing its frustration with the alleged inability of the government for slow progress on a major transportation project. The ordinary resident of Karachi is ever critical of the poor service levels in respect to water supply, sewerage, waste management, disruptions in transport corridors, rising road accidents, declining air quality and many other problems.
It is also disappointing to note that in many neighbourhoods, the local government entities have also fared poorly. While the news of ruckus in the municipal halls between rival political factions does reach the common man through media reports, the presence on the ground and engagement of municipal councillors and office-bearers of other ranks is conspicuous by its absence. There are several points that need to be reviewed to bring about real reform.
In the present form, there is fragmentation in roles, responsibilities and budgetary allocations for routine affairs. Take infrastructure development as an example. In the past, this task was largely performed by the Karachi Development Authority (KDA). Bridges, culverts, siphons, flyovers, arterial roads, parks, playgrounds, pedestrian bridges and a range of other components of infrastructure were planned, designed and developed either through departmental undertaking or through consultancy and contractual arrangement. As the authority was manned by capable technocrats and dedicated engineers and staff, the quality of works was satisfactory. Many of these facilities still continue to serve, with minor repairs and adjustments.
A Karachi-level steering committee should be formed comprising the heads of all civic bodies functioning under the Sindh government.
It was assumed that with the expansion of the city, increase in population and other complexities, new entities were needed to perform similar functions. Two new development authorities were created for Lyari and Malir. Similar functions were assigned to them. But the overall performance, quality of human resource, and capability to perform those functions stipulated in their respective laws leaves much to be desired. We now have multiple authorities, entities and corporations for overlapping tasks. We have separate authorities and entities for managing mass transit, waste management, katchi abadis, master planning, water supply and sewerage, and construction of bus rapid transit (BRT). An ordinary resident is directly or indirectly affected by the performance of these entities or lack thereof. Citizens are unsure whom to contact in respect of any specific grievance. Additionally, the three-tier municipal system with a metropolitan corporation, town municipal corporations and union committees adds further to this confusion. If an excavator comes and digs the lane in front of houses without notice, the residents run from pillar to post to find out the real culprit. In an ideal situation, if these entities were responding to their assigned tasks and delivering services according to mandates, the situation may have been acceptable. But this is not what one observes.
The political leadership at the provincial and city level generally speaks in quantitative terms. Number of development schemes announced, ongoing and completed; inauguration ceremonies held; billions of rupees budgeted, processed and spent; and the geographical locations covered are some of the figures of speech in performance claims highlighted by politicians. But none of these helps the ordinary citizen in addressing the chronic issues this metropolis continues to suffer from.
There is an exponential rise in the city’s population due to migration. Poor law and order conditions in many parts of the country and loss of livelihood in several underdeveloped locations push people towards Karachi for survival. The bulk of this population needs basic urban services and low-skill employment opportunities to access a decent living. Urban housing is a perennial issue, especially for those who wish to start a new life.
Due to ultra-high prices of developer-built housing, overcrowding in the existing housing stock results. The extremely low number of large public buses makes a decent commute an uphill task. While BRTs are being planned and developed, they will only account for a fraction of total passenger trips generated daily in the city. Drinking water comes with a cost. Where piped water is available, its quality remains questionable.
Even in katchi abadis, people buy water from shops with unverified brand names and tariffs. There is a serious parking crisis in the southern and eastern commercial zones of the city. Vendors and hawkers along transport corridors are routinely evicted, though they sell merchandise at prices generally conducive to low-income households. But there are no designated spaces for hawkers and vendors’ markets. The city also suffers from absence of animal shelters and asylums. A sizable animal population suffers from cruelty. This must be addressed.
So, what can be done? There are several steps that can be taken almost instantly. A Karachi-level steering committee can be constituted comprising the heads of all the civic bodies functioning under the auspices of the provincial government. This committee must review the individual performance of each authority according to its legal mandate and suggest reforms where required.
The operational and financial details of planned, ongoing and completed projects must be put on a central digital dashboard, accessible to citizens. A complaint redressal system for service delivery agencies must be put in place. Some agencies do have complaint-registration windows, but the general response is very slow. A broad-based consultation must be carried out with the citizens of Karachi whenever any major development initiative or urban planning work is undertaken. Without the people’s input, development has no relevance.
The writer is an academic and researcher based in Karachi.
Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

title: Unlocking history
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
LAHORE, a living archive of history, is having a moment in the sun. After the city’s selection as the Tourism and Cultural Capital for 2026 to 2027 by the SCO, it now assumes the title of the ECO Tourism Capital for 2027. Not only does this put Pakistan’s cultural and historical wealth on the world stage, it also showcases the country’s syncretic values. Undoubtedly, this is a tremendous chance to expand our heritage economy with regional support. While the Punjab government has made positive interventions to preserve many iconic remnants that dot Lahore, consequential inputs from historians and conservation experts are missing in the country. International recognition brings great responsibility. Economic salvation for Lahore’s inheritance requires investment in specialised training, clean air, security, and conservation efforts guided by international techniques so that the character of antiquity is not lost.
Cultural activities alone are never enough. Tourism will thrive once proper infrastructure is in place, and the tendency to treat preservation as an added expense for a fragile economy is abandoned. The large-scale project entails lenient visa policies and heightened security, an easy transport network, tour guides, site-related literature, small hotels and rest houses, amplified through local and international publicity. Meanwhile, seasonal festivals and traditions planned around heritage sites highlight Pakistan’s inclusivity for all visitors. Importantly, civilisational heirlooms extend beyond Punjab and so should such infrastructure. Every province promises a tourism boom, which is both a shot in the arm for the economy, and a driver of robust bonds with other countries. In short, there is little time for complacency. Every citizen has the right to benefit from national treasures, which comprise cuisine, languages, communities, and customs. Historical places in most parts are on the verge of caving in due to neglect. To rewrite the unflattering narratives about Pakistan it is crucial that life return to our priceless sites.

title: Muslim populations
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
BY 2035, Muslims will overtake Christians to become the largest religious group in the world, according to the Pew Research Centre’s report The Future of World Religions: Population Growth Projections, 2020-2070. The report also projects that, at the current rate of population growth, by 2070, there will be 3.6 billion Muslims and slightly less than 3bn Christians globally. And Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population.
Presently, the average fertility rate for Muslim women is 3.1 and 2.5 for Christians. At 24, Muslims also have a younger median age than Christians, whose median age is 31.
On the face of it, many would consider overtaking Christianity to become the largest religious group cause for celebration. But what might temper the sentiment is that power and sway in world affairs largely elude the Muslim world. The Muslim population in both South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa is growing. Likewise, the fertility rate for Christians in sub-Saharan Africa is much greater than it is in Europe.
Moreover, the Democratic Republic of Congo is expected to surpass the US as the country with the largest Christian population. At the same time, Pakistan will overtake Indonesia as the largest Muslim country. Both Pakistan and DRC are struggling nations, and the lives of their inhabitants will not be made any better as populations grow.
In Pakistan, high population growth is causing what demographers call the ‘youth bulge’, with millions of young people without jobs. Official data in Pakistan shows that last year alone more than 762,000 — mostly young — people left the country to work abroad. This situation is likely to become complicated in the coming years.
While the majority of migrants find work in Arab countries — that have their own labour restrictions — those going to Europe and the US must increasingly contend with social and cultural barriers.
Islamophobia is on the rise in large parts of Europe and the US, where Muslims are treated with suspicion. In a sense, the Pew study raises more questions than it answers. Islam may become the dominant faith, but will Muslims be equal to non-Muslims in terms of human dignity?
Power & sway in world affairs largely elude the Muslim world.
The situation in richer or more educated Muslim countries is quite different. For instance, fertility rates in Iran, Turkiye, Indonesia, Tunisia, and the UAE have dropped to below replacement levels.
    
But this will pose different problems — similar to those in the West, where ageing populations challenge the state through diminishing human labour and high healthcare and other costs for older people. So, while some countries like Pakistan must figure out what to do with their surplus of young people, others will have to figure out how to handle ageing generations.
Each situation also carries political risks. In Turkiye, falling fertility rates threaten the ethnic balance — with parts of the country having higher fertility rates than others. This is likely to create problems for a country where the Turkish identity tends to subsume other groups numerically, politically, and culturally.
Meanwhile, recent revolts led by the Gen Z cohort in South Asia reveal the peril that restless and frustrated young people pose to regional states. No matter what tactics repressive regimes in South Asia employ to quell the protests, the dissatisfaction felt by young people is real and cannot be ignored.
    
Pakistan may not have seen the kind of momentous Gen Z movements that led to the collapse of governments in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. But its youth bul­ge continues to grow, and in the coming years, un­­less the state ta­­k­es steps to satisfy the demands of young people, the threat of revolutionary moveme­nts will only increase — a situation that radical Islamist groups can exploit by tapping into the religious sentiments of angry youth. Keeping that threat in mind, South Asia must work not only to create more employment opportunities for its young but also to promote the tolerance associated with Sufi traditions.
A change in numbers does not always predict a change in global power dynamics. But in this case, the figures do provide justifiable grounds for pointing out the inequity that exists between Muslims and the adherents of other dominant faiths.
Pakistan will soon be the country with the most Muslims. The pitfalls are obvious as resources shrink for a growing population. The silver lining is that, if the state ensures better opportunities for its youth, it will have a greater chance of producing future leaders in world affairs.
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

In contrast, some wealthier Muslim nations face demographic challenges similar to the West, with declining fertility rates and aging populations, leading to different economic and social pressures.

Despite increasing numbers, Muslims globally often experience inequity, rising Islamophobia in the West, and a lack of human dignity, suggesting that demographic dominance alone does not guarantee equality or influence.

title: Before we design new provinces
author: none@none.com (Ashtar Ausaf Ali)
content:
THE interior minister’s call for a referendum on creating new provinces, followed by the information minister’s press conference, seemingly puts the cart before the horse.
Consider a citizen told that a new province will bring government closer to their home. What does that mean to them? Will their land dispute be heard more expeditiously or decided more justly? Who will collect their taxes, and how will those revenues be spent? What does this vision of new provinces look and feel like? What will the new administrative arrangements cost, and who will pay? So far, the answers to these questions seem to vary depending on each province.
    
Without defining what new provinces would actually mean for everyday citizens, a binary question posed nationally can’t provide meaningful insight into the change Pakistanis want. When developers market a new housing scheme, they show prospective buyers what they intend to build. Here, it seems, citizens may be asked to buy into something before knowing what they are buying.
Citizens may be asked to buy into something before knowing what they are buying.
The Constitution already prescribes how provincial boundaries may be altered. Under Articles 238 and 239, a constitutional amendment requires a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House of Parliament. Article 239(4) further requires any bill altering a province’s limits to secure a two-thirds majority of that provincial assembly’s total membership before presidential assent.
    
A national majority through referendum may favour a change whose costs fall chiefly on the people of one particular province. This safeguard gives the people most directly affected, through their elected representatives, a decisive voice. It is, in effect, a constitutional veto.
Article 48(6) permits a referendum on a matter of national importance, following approval by a joint sitting of parliament, while Article 48(7) provides for legislation governing its procedure. Yet neither parliamentary approval for a referendum nor its result can substitute for the legislative majorities mandated by Article 239. The question remains: can a referendum, by itself, effect the extensive constitutional changes that creating new provinces would entail?
The case for a new province should begin with the grievances arising from existing arrangements. If citizens travel hours to reach hospitals or government offices, publish the travel times and service gaps. If districts complain of unequal investment, disclose what was allocated and spent. If communities seek greater control over decisions affecting them, identify the powers they require.
Article 140A already obliges provinces to devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected local governments. Proponents must therefore demonstrate what a new province could achieve that meaningful devolution and stronger district administration cannot.
Every proposal should be accompanied by an administrative map and five- and 10-year financial projections. Which districts and divisions would be regrouped? Where would headquarters be located? How many officials would be required, and what would their offices cost? Who would collect provincial revenues, and within which jurisdictions? How would water resources and gas allocations be determined? Do we have answers ready for these vital questions?
The judicial implications deserve equal attention. What high court facilities, district courts and subordinate courts would need to be established or reorganised? What would buildings, judges, staff and operations cost? Where would litigants go, and what would become of pending cases? Surely, access to justice must be among the measures by which any promise of bringing government closer to citizens is judged.
Financial projections must establish what each administration could realistically raise, the federal transfers it would require, and the consequences for National and Provincial Finance Commission arrangements. Water entitlements, mineral and energy revenues, public assets, debts and pension liabilities cannot be left unresolved. Nor can the implications for employment, investment and public services, or the question of who bears the cost of transition, and keeps services running.
An independent commission could examine these matters, publish its evidence and assumptions, and conduct hearings across affected districts. A referendum confined to a proposed province would exclude others whose finances and institutions may be altered. Conversely, a province-wide tally could obscure substantial differences between districts. Hearings and forums would allow communities on both sides of any proposed boundary, including minorities and those distant from seats of government, to share what they want and why.
If the evidence supports creating a new province, a clearly defined proposal should then be placed before the legislatures whose consent the Constitution requires. Elected representatives must vote publicly and remain answerable to their constituents for the boundaries, costs and commitments they approve.
At this critical juncture in our nation’s history, we ought to think before we leap.
The writer is a former attorney general of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

title: Climate diplomacy in retreat
author: editorial
content:
Global climate negotiations have reached a point where even acknowledging the principal cause of global warming appears to be beyond the willingness of major economies. After more than three decades of international conferences, governments are still reluctant to commit themselves to reducing their dependence on fossil fuels, despite mounting scientific evidence and increasingly destructive climate disasters. COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, was expected to advance the transition agreed upon in Dubai in 2023. Instead, it has exposed how readily political and commercial interests can undermine climate commitments.

A revised draft agreement has removed all references to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, while placing considerable emphasis on carbon capture and storage technologies. Although these technologies may have a role in reducing emissions, they cannot substitute for a systematic reduction in fossil fuel consumption. Their adoption on the scale envisaged remains uncertain, and presenting them as a principal solution offers energy producers an opportunity to prolong existing practices.

While an agreement may emerge from the negotiations, its value will be severely diminished if it fails to address the fossil fuel transition. Britain's prime minister was the only G7 head of government to attend the summit, reflecting the weakening leadership of First World countries. Their reluctance to commit to the transition has wider consequences, particularly when developing countries are expected to pursue costly transitions. Worse still is the retreat on climate finance. The proposed annual adaptation funding target of $120 billion by 2035 has disappeared from the revised draft, leaving developing countries with another uncertain promise of future discussions.

COP31 has already proven to be a failure - that is the bottom line. Unless governments commit to a credible fossil fuel transition, climate summits like this will continue to produce declarations that grow progressively more detached from the realities confronting our world.

title: Reining it in
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WAS it damage control by the president, or a genuine effort to mend fences before a spiralling dispute caused lasting damage? With questions being raised on where the senior leaders of the PPP and PML-N stand in the debate over new provinces, the president, prime minister and interior minister met on Thursday.
Their huddle appears to have gone well. The Press Information Department soon released a picture of the three, all smiles. A brief readout from the Presidency stated that they had reviewed the political situation and agreed to resolve all outstanding issues through dialogue.
This more measured approach contrasted sharply with the escalating rhetoric from the pro- and anti-new-provinces camps within the ruling coalition. Consecutive, no-holds-barred speeches from PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had dominated headlines for most of the outgoing week, raising speculation about an impending showdown.
But it appears that there will be no showdown, at least for now. President Asif Ali Zardari will likely attempt to reason with the PM and the interior minister. The more restrained approach from the president should not be taken to mean that the PPP’s stance on administrative restructuring has shifted, however. His party’s unfiltered views have been elucidated quite clearly — perhaps too clearly — by his son.
    
The president will merely be hoping to convince the PM and others to look past the rhetoric and understand the substance of the PPP’s concerns. Mr Bhutto-Zardari’s media blitz has made the stakes clear; it remains to be seen whether the PML-N is willing to cooperate or part ways with its coalition partner. So far, the PML-N has kept its formal position under wraps. Whatever its view, it should state it openly rather than leave the field to its partner’s loudest voices.
While it is good that the issue is finally being discussed between the head of state and head of government instead of being litigated on TV screens, it would be better still if the debate over administrative restructuring were held in parliament. After all, there is no route to new provinces that bypasses the legislature: Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment backed by two-thirds of both houses, as well as the consent of two-thirds of the affected provincial assembly.
    
The ruling coalition has already enacted two major legislative packages, the 26th and 27th Amendments, without an adequate discussion of their merits and with their contents kept from public view until the eleventh hour. That mistake should not be repeated.
It is not enough for the president and PM to ‘sort’ this matter out in private discussions. Whatever understanding they reach, it must be brought before parliament — before, not after the fact — so that the people’s representatives can weigh in.

summary: A high-level meeting involving the President, Prime Minister, and Interior Minister aimed to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the debate on new provinces, signaling a shift towards dialogue over confrontational rhetoric.

Despite the President's more measured approach, the PPP's position on administrative restructuring and the creation of new provinces remains firm, while the PML-N has yet to formally declare its stance.
The article criticizes the trend of resolving critical national issues in private discussions rather than through open parliamentary debate, advocating for the legislature as the proper forum.

It emphasizes adherence to Article 239 of the Constitution, which mandates a two-thirds majority in both houses of parliament and the consent of the affected provincial assembly for any constitutional amendment creating new provinces.

title: A judiciary for the voiceless
author: none@none.com (Altamush Saeed, Eiraj Hassan)
content:
FROM Islamabad to Lahore, from Rawalpindi and Multan to Karachi, Pakistan’s courts have been writing the same story. It began with the Kaavan judgement in Islamabad. In Lahore, Punjab’s Animal Birth Control Policy took shape before the division bench of Justice Ayesha Malik and was enforced by Justice Shahid Karim in Eiraj Hassan vs Government of Punjab. Back in the capital, Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro recognised animal sentience in Nelofar vs Chief Commissioner ICT. Justice Malik Javed Iqbal Wains has since taken up the cause of donkeys and other draught animals, Justice Shahid Karim has protected endangered monkeys, and the honeybee is now before the courts. Judges in different cities, years apart, have reached the same conclusion. The law must protect those who cannot protect themselves.
Kaavan spent more than three decades at Islamabad’s Marghazar Zoo, much of it in chains and, after his companion Saheli died in 2012, alone. In 2020, in Islamabad Wildlife Management Board vs Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad, the Islamabad High Court under chief justice Athar Minallah ordered his release along with the other animals at the zoo, and held that animals are sentient beings whose interests the law must respect. Every case since has built on that ruling.
In Punjab, the fight was over stray dogs, which municipal bodies had long met with poison and bullets. The killing never ended rabies. The WHO, the FAO and the World Organisation for Animal Health have set 2030 as the target for ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies, and they rely on mass vaccination of dogs to get there. Litigation before the division bench of Justice Ayesha Malik helped produce a policy of sterilisation and vaccination. Culling continued anyway, until Justice Shahid Karim ordered the government in Eiraj Hassan to implement the policy in letter and spirit.
Taken together, these cases show that animal rights sit comfortably alongside human and environmental rights.
In Nelofar, decided on April 28, the IHC was shown photographs of dead dogs piled in a vehicle attributed to the Capital Development Authority. Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro banned the poisoning, shooting and indiscriminate killing of stray dogs in the capital and ordered the ICT policy enforced. The authorities were told to carry out an area-wise survey of the dog population, keep records of every animal captured, sterilised, vaccinated or euthanised, and frame procedures for capture and sheltering. He held that an animal is a sentient being entitled to be spared unnecessary pain and suffering, and that euthanasia must remain a rare exception.
Justice Soomro also reminded the state that mercy towards animals is rooted in the Quran and Sunnah. The Quran says every creature on earth and every bird that flies on its wings forms a community like our own (6:38). Surah An-Nahl, named after the bee, describes how God inspired the bee to build its home and bring forth a drink that heals (16:68-69). The Prophet (PBUH) reportedly spoke of a woman punished for starving a cat and a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. Article 227 of the Constitution requires our laws to conform to these injunctions, so a court that protects animals is applying the Constitution as written.
The same reasoning now reaches working animals. The Pakistan Economic Survey counts close to six million donkeys, alongside mules and horses. They haul bricks from kilns and pull carts through traffic in summers that cross 45°C, often without water, shade or veterinary care. In Altamush Saeed vs Government of Punjab, Justice Malik Javed Iqbal Wains has begun to set out their rights. For the families who depend on them, a healthy animal is also a secure income.
The courts have looked beyond our borders too. CITES-listed rainforest monkeys from Brazil were brought into Pakistan illegally, and half of the original 26 have died here. When the government tried to move the survivors from a rescue centre in Karachi to the Lahore Zoo, Justice Shahid Karim stayed the transfer in June 2025. Justice Khalid Ishaq later made the order final. WWF Pakistan has since recommended a species-appropriate sanctuary for the survivors and a study of whether they can be returned to Brazil.
The newest case is about the bee. The FAO estimates that three in four of the world’s food crops depend at least partly on pollinators, and heavy pesticide use is wiping out colonies here. Losing them would hit our food supply directly, and it would ruin the beekeeping families, many of them in Multan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, whose income depends on healthy colonies. Protecting the bee means protecting the farmer and the food on our tables.
Taken together, these cases show that animal rights sit comfortably alongside human and environmental rights. The One Health approach, backed by the WHO, FAO, UNEP and the World Organisation for Animal Health, treats the health of people, animals and ecosystems as one. Its reasoning is simple: most new infectious diseases in humans come from animals, so the way we keep, trade and treat them is a public health question. A vaccinated dog protects a child from rabies. A healthy donkey keeps a family fed. Articles 9, 9A and 14 guarantee life, a healthy environment and dignity, and the courts have recognised that these guarantees mean little while animals around us suffer.
Public pressure mattered too. The singer Cher campaigned for Kaavan for years and co-founded Free the Wild to press his case. In November 2020 she came to Islamabad to see him off to a sanctuary in Cambodia, where he now lives among other elephants. She brought the world’s attention to him, and a Pakistani court set him free.
The judiciary has done its share, but orders on paper still meet resistance on the ground. In September, a contempt petition had to be filed in Nelofar and in the Eiraj Hassan case because the killing of dogs in Islamabad and Lahore had not stopped. Governments now need to fund the policies the courts have upheld, train the staff who carry them out, and act against officials who ignore court orders. Parliament should replace the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act of 1890. The rest falls to us, in how we treat the animals we live alongside. The Quran calls them communities like our own, and our courts have begun to treat them that way.
The writers were counsel and petitioner in several of the cases discussed.
Altamush Saeed is a lawyer who holds an LLM in animal law, environmental law and human rights law and teaches animal law and food law at Kinnaird College, Lahore.
Eiraj Hassan is a social media manager for the PSL at the Pakistan Cricket Board.
Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

title: Helping create paths
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
ONE child, born in an affluent household, goes to one of the best private, high-fee schools, gets a lot of support from home, appears for international school leaving assessments and then makes her way to the best colleges and universities of the country or of the world. When she enters the job market, she not only has her education to bank on, and the confidence that comes with it and the upbringing she got, she has parental and university networks to support her as well.
Another child — and there are millions of children in Pakistan who face these odds — might have struggled to even be in a public or low-fee private school, is likely to drop out well before reaching college, but even if she reaches college, it is likely she will struggle to find a job afterwards. The quality of her education is compromised, she did not have much support from home for her learning, her confidence has not been built up, and she does not have a parental/family network or a university network to support her.
The state is supposed to level the playing field amongst children. Education has shown to be an amazing equaliser and the state, in theory at least, can use educational opportunities to level some of the inequalities coming from homes and families.
It is a legal and constitutional requirement in the case of basic education (Article 25A of the Constitution as well as many international commitments of our state), but it makes functional sense to do that as well: a merit-based society is likely to bring the best talent forward and that, more than anything else, becomes the engine for economic growth, social well-being and societal harmony.
    
The state of Pakistan has completely failed to deliver the promise of ‘the right to education’. But it has also failed, and quite miserably, to deliver on social outcomes.
Twenty-six million-odd children out of school, poor quality of education for most children enrolled in low-fee private and public schools, high dropout rate, small percentage of enrolled children reaching university level (roughly only 10 per cent), poor quality of university education in most private and public universities and very poor opportunities for employment even if you survive in the system and graduate from it with a degree.
State policies have, in many instances, helped develop & entrench inequalities.
Instead of equalising opportunities and levelling the playing field, state policies have, in many instances, helped develop and entrench inequalities even more. Funding cuts and restrictions for public education, both at school and university level, are a telling example as is the inability and unwillingness of the state to regulate provision of education by private, for-profit providers. Some effort has been made to provide scholarships, on merit, at high school and university level to help students who do well in public examinations, but, compared to the scale of poverty and the escalation in costs of education, all scholarship schemes, together, do not amount to more than a few drops in the ocean.
Private not-for-profit initiatives have also been working in the area, but the scale is a big issue here. They have been and can help hundreds of thousands, but they have not been able to reach millions. If experience from other countries is to be of value, the state has to step in and play its role.
The Citizen’s Foundation (TCF) is probably the largest non-profit provider of schooling in the country. It has been around for more than three decades and has served hundreds of thousands of students and employed thousands of teachers. But even today, TCF has less than 3,000 odd schools and school units that it runs. Pakistan has some 200,000 schools in operation in the country, and we still have 26m children out of school. How many TCFs do we need? It cannot be done without the state!
Equally important is the form of support that is provided. Even when the state has come in it has stepped in to either reduce tuition fees (public schools are free for students and public universities are still subsidised) or provide individual scholarships based on need and/or merit. But a lot more is needed. Again, if you look at examples from other countries young people need support for health and nutrition, academic support (where such support from home is missing), counselling support to ensure better career and occupation choices, scholarships, mentoring support, support for developing non-academic but needed skills in communication, self-presentation, confidence building, and support in making transition to the workplace.
These programmes, sadly, are almost completely missing in Pakistan. Even technical education, skills and training providers focus a lot more on specific skills than on issues of confidence, interpersonal skills, self-presentation and so on.
    
But we do need these programmes as well. Here are a couple of examples from small/local initiatives. Amal Academy does fellowships with university students to develop their skills in self-presentation, to improve confidence, to ensure better self-organisation and management. This is done over a few months through mentorship programmes that are quite structured and very interactive.
Institute of Lifelong Learning and Development, a new initiative, has a three-pronged strategy. They provide scholarships to ease access, development and mentorship programmes to focus on needed skills and confidence building and a service orientation, right from the start, to ensure benefiting students are ready to pay it forward right from the word go.
The point of these examples is to just emphasise that equalising opportunities or levelling the playing field does not get addressed through access issues (tuition fees and subsidies) only; the state needs to do a lot more. We have plenty of examples we could learn from and bodies like TEVTA and PSDF could benefit from scaling some of these programmes.
It is hard to see how Pakistan could move on the road to better human development and sustained economic growth without the state stepping in and stepping up to address some of these glaring issues of unequal opportunity sets.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

title: In hindsight
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
JUST as an important partner in the ruling coalition is starting to question the wisdom of the 26th and 27th Amendments, a report issued by the International Commission of Jurists has detailed the damage the two enactments have wrought on Pakistan’s judiciary.
Titled Judicial Capture: Independence of the Judiciary in Pakistan after the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments, the report concludes that systemic constitutional and legislative changes have placed the country’s highest courts under the control of the political and executive branches.
The ICJ comprises judges and lawyers from around the world working to “develop and strengthen national and international justice systems”. The report clarifies: “The ICJ does not take a position on the merits of political disputes between the parties. Its analysis is focused on the institutional framework in which the judiciary operates, and whether it is consistent with Pakistan’s obligations under international law.”
The most worrying flag the report raises is that the ruling parties — in what can only be read as their zeal to have these two amendments enacted — have pushed the judiciary to a state where the country’s highest courts no longer “enjoy the institutional guarantees of independence required by Article 14” of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the UN Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, among other standards.
    
It also notes that the loss of judicial independence has stripped victims of human rights abuses of their right to an effective legal remedy under domestic law and Article 2(3) of the ICCPR.
Though the ICJ agrees that prior issues in the Pakistani judiciary, especially its tendency to overreach into parliament’s domain, needed targeted reforms, its secretary-general, Santiago Canton, says the government used those frustrations as a pretext to seize full control of the judiciary rather than enact serious reforms.
    
The detailed report offers a cold examination of the path taken by the Pakistani judiciary since 2024 and brings into fresh relief what may be the roots of some of the new crises that have gripped the country since then. Its timing couldn’t have been better: there is speculation that another amendment is in the works, and those who partnered with the government on getting earlier legislation enacted are now apprehensive of what a new rewrite will entail.
As local observers have been warning, and as the ICJ’s findings now bear out, the 26th and 27th Amendments have done serious damage to judicial independence. Part of the reason why is the haste with which they were enacted. Before any further changes are made to the Constitution, it would be wise to debate all proposed amendments at length and enact them only after a careful, deliberate consensus has been built.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

title: Settling disputes
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WITH almost 2m court cases clogging the lower judiciary — most of them in Punjab — Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s nod to a proposed panchayat system to resolve local-level disputes is expected to be well received by many litigants. Several factors are responsible for a situation in which disputing parties often find themselves waiting for decades before their cases are settled. A shortage of judges, unclear rules, frequent court adjournments, and corruption at all tiers are just a few of the underlying causes. It is no wonder then that informal forums of ‘justice’, based more on centuries-old, often barbaric customs than on modern legal principles, persist in the country. Seen in this light, a panchayat system that prioritises community decision-making but with some state regulation, appears, at least theoretically, to be the right move. However, as with any initiative, it is important to closely study similar local justice schemes elsewhere before embarking on the proposed project. For instance, India’s village justice court system aimed at providing inexpensive and accessible justice to rural communities in the country, has had mixed results that should provide a useful clue for the government here. In fact, Pakistan is no stranger to alternative dispute resolution laws intended to reduce the burden on the courts. The Punjab Alternative Dispute Resolution Act, 2019 — recently repealed by the Punjab Alternative Dispute Resolution Ordinance, 2026 — is a case in point. The ‘success’ of the repealed law can justifiably be questioned. How will the proposed panchayat framework ensure better results?
It is too early to be ambitious. Small steps towards the larger goal of an integrated justice system will allow the authorities to ensure accessible legal relief for Pakistan’s rural communities — measures that are sensitive to local concerns without straying from constitutional norms. Above all, there can be no further dillydallying on reforms that strengthen the judicial system — judicial slots must be filled, procedures simplified, and corruption reined in.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

title: Islamic education
author: none@none.com (Ghulam Shabbir)
content:
WHERE the Judeo-Christian tradition — despite its long coexistence with and exposure to Hellenism — failed at the fusion of religious and pure intellectual streams of thought, Islam sutured the fabric of transcendental and empirical reality so seamlessly that it gushed forth to spread like a prairie fire from Baghdad to India, Transoxiana and further still. The Quran so vigorously fired the imagination of Muslims and implanted philosophic spirit in them that within a short time they mastered the sciences and were at the helm of world affairs.
However, orthodox elements blew this fusion of metaphysical and social reality into shreds and after a few centuries, the real ‘dark ages’ of Muslims set in. The clergy was left with little more than a threadbare formal structure of ideas. How did things come to such a pass?
It was a protracted war between orthodox elements and philosophers, fought from rigid positions which shaped the content of Islamic education and Muslim attitude towards philosophy and positive sciences, of which both Muslim thought and philosophy paid the price. The capture of Bait al-Hikma at Baghdad by the Mu’tazila, with an Abbasid inquisition board, was a shot across the bow to the ulema to make them realise how vital an education system is to state and society. So they set about to organise and control education. Thus, Nizamiyya Baghdad was the first orthodox college of higher learning where Ghazali served as professor. At almost the same time occurred the philosophical movement, which was critical of religion.
Ghazali saved religious thought from the critique of philosophers, but his wholesale rejection of philosophy and positive sciences proved a watershed event for later developments, as his community took his statements as ‘eternal truth’ rather than an overreaction to an extreme historical challenge.
Both philosophers and orthodoxy failed to mediate their rigidity.
However, he failed to appreciate that no structure of ideas can survive without constant interaction with a living and growing stream of positive and scientific thought, and banishment of positive sciences can deal a deadly blow to knowledge as an organic whole.
Ibn Khaldun warned philosophers that the balance (intellect), meant to weigh gold, cannot weigh down mountains and told orthodoxy that ulema severed from Sitz im leben and social realities cannot be the real successors of the Prophet (PBUH). In a nutshell, both philosophers and orthodoxy failed to mediate their rigidity and went off a cliff. So, where philosophers outraged theology by interpreting the Quran through the lens of Hellenistic thought, orthodoxy proscribed philosophy, positive sciences and their instrument, human reason. Free thought, by its very nature, is bound to exceed on certain points, but its remedy is not to stifle it but to keep on criticising it to reach a balanced conclusion.
However, rise of philosophy in Islam was sporadic and individual. It never took the form of a movement or a tradition of enduring roots, as was the case in ancient Greece and the modern West. Confined to theological problems, the Mu’tazila’s rationalism was not purely philosophical as the fulcrum of their thought was to know whether free will was compatible with the idea of a Just God. Muslim philosophers were too enamoured of metaphysical heights to climb down to ethics. Had they made Sharia an object of study, the subsequent history of philosophy and Islamic thought could have been different.
Thus, since orthodoxy’s triumph against philosophy, Ghazali has been leading the fleets of Islamic thought to harbour on theological rather than Archimedean principles. Ibn al-Arabi extended his premises to supplant reason with Sufi intuition. Ibn Taimiyya’s attacks against philosophy are well-known. Al-Shatibi discourages the cultivation of purely in­­tellectual disciplines since they are not related to action and denies the role of reason in formulation of law and moral imperatives, though he himself employs a generous quantum of reason in his constructs. Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi unreservedly ridicules and rejects positive sciences.
Thus, madressah education, arguably since its very inception, was destined to culminate in intellectual barrenness. The panacea lies in an organic fusion of traditional learning and modern ethos, but given the reforms at Deoband, al-Azhar and Zaituna, the ulema manoeuvred juxtaposition of the two rather than synthesis of the old and the new. The long-quarantined religious knowledge gets fossilised and an unalterable law of God is that fossils do not survive long. As it is stated in the Holy Quran, “…We did not do them injustice; but they were unjust to themselves. …” (11:101). Are Muslims ready to reform Islamic education, or are they waiting for a Luther?
The writer is an academic.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

title: Rohingya genocide
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
NEARLY a decade after the world watched Myanmar’s junta conduct a brutal campaign of extermination and displacement against the Muslim Rohingya minority, the International Court of Justice has ruled that the regime is guilty of genocide. It took a small African state — The Gambia — to lodge a case at the ICJ against Myanmar. Today, because of The Gambia’s courage and moral clarity, this verdict has made history as it is the first time a state has been held guilty of genocide. While calling out a blood-soaked campaign for what it was, the ruling also sets a legal precedent for building a strong case against another genocidal state: Israel. To recall, in 2017 the Myanmar military unleashed massive violence against the Rohingya in Rakhine state, with thousands killed, including over 2,000 children under five, rampant sexual attacks, while hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee. The Rohingya have long faced discrimination, with the regime denying most citizenship. The junta claims it had conducted ‘counterinsurgency operations’, a defence rejected by the ICJ.
Though the ruling grants the Rohingya a moral victory, it is difficult to see the community returning to their homes in Rakhine in an atmosphere of safety, as the junta is currently engaged in a civil war there with Arakan rebels. However, Myanmar should pay compensation, as ordered by the court, to the victims or their survivors, punish those involved in the atrocities, and grant the community full citizenship. The ICJ ruling, legal experts say, is also likely to strengthen South Africa’s genocide case against Israel for what it has done — and is doing — in Gaza. Many scholars of genocide, including UN experts, are convinced that Israel has conducted a genocide in the occupied Palestinian territory. Sadly, just as the international community remained silent while the Rohingya were butchered, a similar silence — punctured by ineffectual criticism — was seen at the height of Israel’s murderous campaign in Gaza, until last year’s ceasefire. The Rohingya have finally received justice after a nightmarish ordeal; the people of Palestine now await justice. Israel needs to be brought to book for its bloodletting in Gaza and the West Bank, while all those foreign states that aided and abetted its crimes must similarly be held to account.
Published in Dawn, November 21st, 2026

title: Islamabad province?
author: none@none.com (Aasim Sajjad Akhtar)
content:
OPPOSITION to it has been largely suppressed, but all is not well within the ruling regime. One way or the other, the proposal to break up existing federating units will ultimately shape the regime’s endgame.
Stage one has been completed without major resistance, the PTI disarmed through the imposition of emergency in KP, and a neo-administrative experiment comprising 12 districts in the southern and ex-Fata regions operationalised.
The ultimate prize for the establishment is the long-desired separation of Karachi from the rest of Sindh. And this is where the Bhutto-Zardari clan, facing an existential threat, will be forced to play its hand.
But before this, there are likely to be other moves expected to trigger less resistance, both within the ruling coalition and outside it. One of these is the plan to make Islamabad into a province.
The bureaucracy rules Islamabad without impediment.
The only proposal on record, finalised by a committee headed by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, has advised a 27-member assembly, headed by an elected chief minister/mayor. The elephant in the room is the viceregal institution which dictates the fates of Islamabad’s three million people — the Capital Development Authority (CDA).
Pakistani democracy is, at best, an aspiration rather than a functioning reality connected to the will of the people. Elected institutions operate under pressure, while most who claim to be representatives of the people wage class war daily. Nevertheless, the pretence of democracy remains.
The federal capital is a glaring exception. The bureaucracy rules here without impediment, the popular will be damned. There has been one citywide experiment with local government since the capital was created in 1960. The 2016 elections brought the Municipal Corporation of Islamabad (MCI) into existence, under the nominal authority of an elected mayor. The mayor and elected representatives down to the level of union councillor had virtually zero legislative and financial power. Elections never took place again, and the MCI was transformed into yet another bureaucratic feeder to the CDA.
So if Islamabad is given a legislative assembly, will the CDA be cut down to size? I choose my words carefully — because those who are poised to ‘give’ Islamabad an assembly have, over the past year or so, made their plans for the city and its environs sufficiently clear.
    
A short list of ‘achievements’ reads as follows: thousands of homes in katchi abadis and historical villages bulldozed; suburban sprawl in the form of land-grabbing real-estate schemes extended; thousands of trees razed and the city’s air poisoned by relentless construction.
With the CDA’s Master Plan flagrantly violated by its own commercial projects and big proprietors, another post-facto amendment in zoning regulations was recently approved by the government. As for what is to come, entire chunks of Rawal Lake and many villages around Bhara Kahu will be sacrificed for a 350-acre safari park, while the area adjacent to the Bari Imam shrine — where forced evictions took place earlier this year — is being given over to hotel developers.
Will Islamabad’s much-celebrated green spaces, already limited public services, and working-class settlements be left by the time the purported legislative assembly comes into place? Will the dominant imaginary of ‘development’ fronted by the state apparatus — of which the CDA is a poster-child — suddenly give way to a political-economic-environmental arrangement that serves the mass of Islamabad’s people?
    
Only the awfully naïve believe that the plans for an Isla­mabad province — which may ex­­tend into adjacent districts like Mu­­rree and Haripur currently part of Punjab and KP respectively — are driven by democ­r­atic impulses. Seen thus, the Islam-abad case provides the most obvious indication of what the new provinces hullabaloo is all about; an attempt to subjugate the political and economic interests of the mass of the population, and future generations to boot, all in the name of efficient administration.
Over the course of the past year, mainstream parties like the PPP and PML-N have made no effort to stand with katchi abadi dwellers and villagers whose homes have been bulldozed in Islamabad. They have not resisted the barrage of ‘development’ projects that have forever destroyed local ecologies.
Islamabad was always the preserve of the elite, but working people fought for their rights with some success, mainstream politicians paying heed in exchange for votes. Like in the rest of the country, Islamabad’s working masses now have to exclusively wage their own political fight. They are up against both powerful elements and political entrepreneurs who hunt with the hare and run with the hound.
The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026
