title: Leveraging the solar revolution
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
AT COP31, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told a high-level dialogue on electrification that “an extraordinary transition has already taken place” in Pakistan: nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar in two years, “a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future”. More than one in 10 motorcycles sold this year, he added, was electric.
He was right to showcase it. Few countries can match that speed. Fewer can accept that their citizens paid for it.
Nobody planned it: capacity payments rose whether plants ran or not, the rupee fell, and the 2023 IMF programme stopped the state hiding these costs in subsidies. Base tariffs doubled between FY22 and FY25, just as Chinese panels became cheap and loadshedding persisted. The IMF did not create the high cost of power. It made it visible, and achieved the revolution by accident, what policy had not.
    
The dividend is large. By the estimates of Ember, CREA and Renewables First, distributed solar avoided over $12 billion in oil and gas imports by February 2026, with $6.3bn more expected this year, and about 35 million tonnes of CO2 in FY25. Counting grid losses, it supplies about a third of the country’s electricity. On farms, solar runs 52pc of 1.83m irrigation pumps, almost entirely without state help. Banks financed less than 5pc of the $14bn invested. The official response has been to contain it, with a sales tax on panels and cuts to net metering.
A showcase needs a strategy. The leveraging should run on two tracks.
Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further.
The first is phase two. Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further. Rooftops have already displaced most of the daytime thermal power they can reach, so more panels alone bring falling returns. Three areas will win the game.
Storage, with a tariff that spreads the grid’s fixed costs fairly, so surplus daytime power serves the evening peak. Transport, where petrol imports are still growing: electric motorcycles reached 13pc of sales by August, already ahead of the New Energy Vehicles Policy’s schedule. The 30pc target should move from 2030 to 2028 for automobiles, two-wheelers, rickshaws and delivery fleets first, with battery-swap and charging corridors for bikes and freight planned along the motorways now. And solar mini-grids for the 40m people still without electricity.
The prize is worth the effort. Adding 3GW of distributed solar a year would lift avoided emissions to about 50m tonnes by 2030, as per Renew­ables First estimates, more than the power sector now emits. At this year’s rate, fuel import savings by then would approach $25bn. Electric bikes save less, but their savings will help poorer hou­seholds, which is where a transition survives or dies.
The second track is harder. If fiscal conditionality could transform mitigation by accident, what could adaptation measures achieve by design, without waiting for grants or loans?
Agriculture uses more than 93 per cent of the country’s freshwater, yet produces under $1 of output per cubic metre, against a global average near $17. Solar has made matters worse: once panels are paid for, pumping groundwater costs nothing at the margin. The rice area grew by about 30pc between 2023 and 2025, even as Punjab’s water tables fell. Flooded paddies also emit methane, so the same expansion that drains aquifers adds to emissions.
Islamabad and the provinces already hold the levers. Five would do the most.
First, conditional solarisation. Punjab already subsidises tubewell conversion; each should require drip or sprinkler irrigation and a flow meter. The Punjab Water Act 2019 allows new solar wells to be registered.
Second, volumetric abiana. The canal water charge is so low that sugarcane and rice grow where the water cannot support them. Charging by volume and crop is a provincial power, and it raises revenue.
Third, retargeted fertiliser support. IMF pressure ended most of the feedstock gas subsidy to urea plants in 2024. Blanket urea still invites overuse; the excess escapes as nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, or leaches into groundwater. Tying the remaining support, including Kissan Card credit, to soil testing and slow-release coated urea would cut the waste and the fertiliser bill together.
Fourth, alternate wetting and drying for rice. Letting paddies dry between irrigations cuts both water use and methane. Punjab and Sindh can initiate this through their extension services and Kissan/Hari cards, with a low-carbon basmati label for buyers who increasingly ask about embedded emissions.
Fifth, a satellite-enforced no-burn rule. Tying Kissan Card eligibility and wheat procurement to satellite checks on residue burning, already run for smog, is an administrative change. Lahore would breathe cleaner air.
    
None of these needs a donor. The petroleum levy brought in a record Rs1.57 trillion in FY26, and the climate support levy is budgeted at Rs50bn this year. Ring-fencing a fixed share of the first, and all of the second, would fund them without waiting on donor cycles. The provinces, which own agriculture and irrigation, ran a combined cash surplus of Rs1.45tn last year, led by Punjab; only Balochistan’s was marginal.
Those surpluses are an IMF target, which brings the Fund back in. Its $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility already lists irrigation water pricing, but its water measures are hostage to influential interest groups. The two remaining reviews in 2027 can begin the shift; the successor programme should put adaptation at the centre, with these five as structural benchmarks carrying provincial timelines. The Fund’s leverage transformed Pakistan’s energy use by accident. It can now be used on water deliberately.
Some things need capital: flood protection, climate-proofed infrastructure, livestock systems that cut methane. That is where concessional finance belongs. A country that has done the rest with its own instruments makes a far stronger case for it.
Phase one happened by accident. Phase two cannot. Islamabad should design the next transformation, in water as well as power, rather than wait for the next IMF programme to force it. The first revolution cut Pakistan’s fuel bill and emissions. The second can make the country resilient.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, November 19th, 2026

title: Structural reforms
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE country’s improving macroeconomic health offers little hope when growth remains too weak to create enough jobs or improve living standards. The State Bank’s latest annual report makes this contradiction difficult to ignore. It argues that structural reforms are essential for putting the economy on a sustainable high-growth path. The figures underline the scale of the problem. The SBP has correctly identified premature deindustrialisation, weak investment, inadequate skills and widespread informal employment as major constraints. These problems have accumulated over decades of inconsistent economic policies. The state’s reform priorities must therefore address the reasons businesses hesitate to invest and expand.
Infrastructure gaps require attention. Tax administration needs simplification, with a broader tax base. Businesses also need predictable regulations and consistent policies. Repeated policy reversals have made long-term planning difficult for domestic and foreign investors alike. The domestic labour market presents an equally serious challenge. While overall unemployment has risen to 7.2pc in 2025 from 5.7pc in 2018, low female workforce participation keeps a substantial share of potential workers outside productive economic activity. High youth unemployment reflects weaknesses in education and vocational training. Universities and technical institutions must develop skills that employers actually need. The agricultural sector needs modern irrigation, better technology and climate-resilient practices. However, the most important lesson from the SBP report concerns policy continuity. Structural reforms cannot succeed through isolated announcements or short-lived initiatives. They require political commitment across successive governments. Every change in administration should not bring another round of economic experimentation. The government must recognise that sustainable growth requires a stronger productive base. Without consistent investment, industrial expansion, better skills and higher productivity, economic stability will remain vulnerable. The real test of reform will be whether it creates productive jobs and raises household incomes.
Published in Dawn, November 19th, 2026

title: Climate change and the unforgiving laws of nature
author: Dr Intikhab Ulfat
content:
Over the years, teaching physics and working on projects in renewable energy and environmental physics have taught me a simple lesson: nature is indifferent to our speeches. It responds to forces, energy and the consequences of human activity. Governments may postpone decisions; the planet cannot suspend the laws by which it operates.

As delegates gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31), the familiar ritual of climate diplomacy resumes. There will be declarations, disagreements and, inevitably, photographs of leaders promising a greener tomorrow. Yet beyond the conference halls, the atmosphere continues its quiet accounting. Every tonne of greenhouse gases added today becomes part of a problem that future generations will inherit.

The figures are sobering. The World Meteorological Organization reports that the global average temperature from January to September 2026 stood about 1.47°C above the pre-industrial level. More revealing is Earth's growing energy imbalance: the planet is retaining more energy than it releases into space. Roughly 90 per cent of the excess heat enters the oceans, where it accumulates largely beyond public view. What is invisible, however, is not harmless.

In the classroom, I have often found that a simple physical principle can illuminate a complex social question. A small imbalance, allowed to persist, can transform an entire system. The same is true of climate. A fraction of a degree may look insignificant on a thermometer; multiplied across continents and decades, it alters rainfall, intensifies heatwaves and unsettles the delicate arrangements on which agriculture, cities and ecosystems depend.

Pakistan does not need to look far for evidence. Our summers grow more punishing, floods expose the fragility of settlements, and water insecurity reaches from farms to crowded neighbourhoods. In Karachi, concrete spreads faster than shade, while the disappearance of trees turns ordinary streets into reservoirs of heat. For many citizens, climate change is no longer a distant prediction. It is the temperature of the room in which they sleep.

There is, nevertheless, reason for cautious hope. In renewable-energy projects, I have seen how scientific ideas can become practical instruments of change. Solar power, wind energy, efficient buildings and decentralised electricity systems can reduce emissions and improve lives. But green technology deserves the same scrutiny we apply to any scientific claim. A solar panel is not an environmental absolution. Its materials, land requirements, maintenance and eventual disposal must be considered alongside the electricity it generates.

The rapid growth of clean-energy manufacturing, particularly in China, is making alternatives more accessible. Lower costs can widen opportunities for developing countries. Yet the transition will deserve the name 'sustainable' only when it also addresses responsible mining, recycling, ecological protection and fair access to technology. Progress should not mean transferring environmental damage from one community to another.

Climate justice is equally essential. Wealthier nations have a responsibility to assist vulnerable countries, like Pakistan, with adaptation, technology and finance. Such assistance must produce resilient infrastructure and measurable improvements, not merely new slogans or expensive ceremonies.

Our universities must also move beyond observing the crisis from academic distance. Physics and engineering departments can monitor urban heat, develop affordable solar solutions, improve building efficiency and work with communities on water conservation. Research earns its public value when it leaves the laboratory and enters everyday life. Students should learn not only how energy moves through a system, but how knowledge can protect those living within it.

COP31 must move beyond promises to measurable action. The atmosphere recognises no borders, and nature offers no exemptions. After a lifetime of teaching physics, I remain convinced that humanity's greatest challenge is no longer understanding climate change, but finding the wisdom and courage to confront it. The laws of nature will not bend to our convenience. Our priorities must.

title: In search of nationhood
author: Shahzad Chaudhry
content:
Two hundred and fifty million people, defensible boundaries and a veritable record of overcoming multifarious challenges prove the viability of a state. Pakistan has survived external aggression, calamities and an inconsistent political environment at home. Where geography and the people intertwine, a state is born. From 1947 till date, through baby steps and negotiating monumental events, it has found its calling. There was an attempt to force an early fermentation of nationhood through prescriptive ideology and imposed nationalism (Pakistaniat), but only when each aspect of statehood had been tested did geography and the people find relevance in the imagination. Eighty years later, we have arrived at the phase of defining our nationhood.

It helps to compare with another state founded in similar circumstances and almost similar challenges – Israel. Carved out by external intervention, despite its ideological idiosyncrasies that most of the world disagrees with, it has had to fight for its viability. It is now fighting its pariah manifestations – a consequence of its conduct and devastating policies – to find global acceptability. Pakistan has been far luckier, and the world at large accepted its institution as an independent state as a natural consequence of the passing of colonialism. The size of the population and their unique socio-religious culture that formed the new country were significant enough to gain them their right to an independent homeland. Subsequent events in this young nation's experience have only reinforced that belief. Pakistan is here to stay.

Insecurities of initial formation and unique historical experience now bridged – a perpetual adversary in India, which has done all it could to decimate the young nation, overwhelmingly blunted – the next steps to a more assured nationhood are in the offing. Looking back, only time would have brought us to the realisation that, from securing the state, the emphasis must now move to nation-building. To many, and rightly so, we could have endeavoured to do both in parallel, and there were sporadic efforts in that direction, but those stalled rather early because of weak political intent and poor conception. Inadequacies of leadership and lack of commitment to place people first came in the way. Now the people are seeking their moment of attention. They have been neglected far too much, for far too long.

For eighty years, the emphasis has been on the state. Pakistan's precarious financial state testifies to how the state has been callous in its affairs and immersed in its own viability and well-being. The entire debt stock of the nation, external and internal, for the most part has been centred around what came first to the state, not the people. Worldwide, as people begin to seek changes to traditional state structures and their policies, the sentiment finds wider resonance on the back of a more connected world of instant communication and social media. India's Cockroach Janata Party, as well as the youth movements in Nepal and Bangladesh, stand as testimony to this global trend.

The gaping hole in Pakistan, as has been evident over time, is the disconnect between the people and the state. The state is absent from people's lives, and when it does engage, it is mostly through populist rhetoric and symbolic projection. People's day-to-day lives rarely change. Big-ticket projects are announced, but if ever concluded, they serve the state and its principals. The gap has thus become increasingly difficult to bridge without wholesale restructuring of our governance and political systems. The people are increasingly being pushed into desolation and hopelessness as their cries of neglect and disappointment echo sharply.

It needs immediate course correction. The four-province state structure has turned voracious in appropriating resources for its own well-being. The belief that devolution would enable local governments at the lowest level, with fiscal and administrative authority to influence the lives of the common man per their needs, failed to materialise. All resources were appropriated to the provincial heads and their governments instead. Local governments were defied and denied in institution and in their efficacy. Where reluctantly instituted, those were neutered in their function by debilitating legislation. Such manipulation of democratic authority has not only crucified the spirit intended in the 18th Amendment, but has also distorted the nation-state construct. Because of such excesses of political masters, Pakistan is threatened with a nation-state collapse.

The dual track, thus, of ensuring full devolution to the lowest level of governance through representative local bodies, and downsizing the provinces to their more optimal levels given the vast geographical and population spread of the country, is the right course. That is real democracy – of the people, for the people, by the people; not the nominal inflection when traditional politicians seek votes in their favour around tribal and familial alliances. Pakistan's brand of democracy is patently exploitative and patronage-centred. It has produced a class of elites who arrogate power to themselves based on dynastic culture and financial exclusivity. Their proximity to centres of power, and their ability to manipulate its levers, gives them the pre-eminence in a largely poor society – forty-six per cent live below the poverty line by some calculations. Their conduct at the helm is mostly opportunistic and patently self-serving. The election process remains notoriously tainted, and the void between the people and those that claim to represent them only grows wider.

It is time to fill the void for the sake of retaining the viability of the state and securing the nation-state construct, and to avoid eruption of accumulated discontent. Any state structure must then address first and foremost the aspirations of the people. Let smaller units provide that sense of fairness and belonging to the people. Let constitutionally secured local governments under uniform country-wide laws open the door to self-governance with both authority and the resources that must devolve to that level. Let the people find their representatives from among them and win political representation away from the dynastic control and entrenched entitlement of a few.

Smaller provinces and administrative units, a uniform structure of local bodies, and a transparent, fair and free election process remain the key to Pakistan's state-society construct, giving it greater resilience and self-belief as it negotiates the next phase of its existence as a nation-state. Without it, we may be in an uncontrolled meltdown, socially, economically and institutionally. The state and its politics must be restructured. Else, the alternatives are stark.
topic: Nation-Building, Devolution, and State-Society Disconnect in Pakistan
whyMatters: This article offers a critical analysis of Pakistan's journey from state formation to nation-building, highlighting key governance failures and proposing structural reforms. It provides aspirants with profound insights into the challenges and potential solutions for strengthening Pakistan's democratic and administrative framework, crucial for essay and current affairs papers.
summary: Pakistan has survived as a state but is now at a crucial phase of defining its nationhood, shifting focus from merely securing the state to active nation-building, nearly eighty years after its formation.

A significant disconnect exists between the Pakistani state and its people, largely due to self-serving governance, populist rhetoric, and a neglect of people-centric policies, leading to widespread desolation.

The existing four-province structure has been criticized for appropriating resources, thereby thwarting true devolution and neutering local governments, which has distorted the intended nation-state construct.

The article advocates for immediate course correction through full devolution to constitutionally secured local governments, downsizing provinces for optimal administration, and reforming the exploitative, patronage-centered election process to prevent a potential nation-state collapse.

Eighty years have passed since 1947, bringing Pakistan to the phase of defining its nationhood.

title: Exchange rate & other protections
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
THERE is always something a little off when economists and other experts say that a given course of action is beneficial for industrial growth in the country, but those industries directly connected with that course of action or policy direction are silent on the matter. Normally, industry is very vocal about preserving its interests and either takes the lead in advocating its preferences, or at least responds to suggestions coming from other quarters.
These days we are seeing this happen in two areas. One is the conversation around the exchange rate. All manner of articles have been written about whether the exchange rate needs to be devalued to keep exports competitive. Those advocating this are pointing to the so-called Real Effective Exchange Rate, or REER, which, they say, is overvalued, making Pakistani products expensive in export markets by comparison to our main export competitors.
The REER is a tool used mainly by central bankers and academics to measure how a given country’s exchange rate is aligned with the inflation-adjusted exchange rates of its main trading partners.
The way it works is simple. When the REER is 100 there is, in theory anyway, alignment between Pakistan and its trading partners in terms of how well the exchange rate reflects the costs of doing business in Pakistan versus its competitor countries. But if the REER rises above 100 it is considered overvalued, meaning the exchange rate no longer adequately reflects the rising price level within the country by comparison to its competitors, and keeping it at present-day levels will render exports non-competitive.
    
The more the REER is above 100, the more overvalued the rupee is considered to be. And if it is below 100, then the exchange rate can be considered undervalued, meaning exporters are enjoying a premium in international markets by comparison to the cost of doing business that faces their competitors in other countries.
Conditions that have historically called for an exchange rate devaluation are simply not there today.
Now here is the strange thing. The REER has been above 100 for a number of months now, and is now far enough above its equilibrium level to potentially merit a devaluation. But none among the exporter community is demanding this. Not publicly anyway. All exporter associations, and other chambers around the country, are very vocal about the direction of interest rates, about the taxation burden, about electricity and gas pricing. But not a word about the exchange rate.
So what to make of a situation where economists are saying the currency needs to depreciate to make exports competitive, but exporters themselves are making no such demand?
Another example is with the auto policy that the government has been working on for many months now. A couple of years ago they brought customs duties down on imported vehicles, and are now moving to cut import tariffs further on other manufactured goods. Despite a few years of applying this trade policy, and now moving to codify the gradual elimination of protections in a new auto policy, the auto companies themselves are silent. Sharp objections are being raised by manufacturers of auto parts, organised under an umbrella grouping called Pakistan Auto and Auto Parts Manufacturers Association (PAAPAM), who rightly argue that large investments made in the manufacture of auto parts like vehicle glass, headlights, doors, bonnets, other body parts and lots more are at risk with this new policy. So far their objections have not prevailed over the cabinet, though they have found sympathetic ears within government.
What is striking is the silence of the key stakeholders — the auto companies themselves. Why are those whose business is directly in line to be impacted by this measure not saying anything about it, at least publicly?
The answer is a little obvious: the proposed measure does not adversely impact their interests. The exporters are not asking for a devaluation and auto makers are not asking for the return of the protections behind which they grew up, because their business is not going to be as adversely or favourably impacted by the proposed measures as theory might tell us.
The auto part manufacturers are a different story. They cannot sell their parts to anybody else other than the big auto makers for whom they have been vendors for many years now. Changing that would require a deep process of retooling their plant, and figuring out where auto volumes are sufficiently mature to merit retooling the plant and producing parts at industrial scale.
    
Given that the auto industry is in the middle of shifting to electric vehicles anyway, such a process of obsolescence and adaptation to a changing market reality is perhaps coming anyway, regardless of how much protection the government extends to legacy manufacturers.
Regarding the exchange rate, policymakers in Pakistan have never paid much mind to the REER in deciding the level they want for the rate. The level is usually decided more with rupee cost of external debt servicing requirements in mind, first and foremost. Adjustments to the exchange rate always come when their hand is forced by market reality, which means devaluations come when the State Bank’s liquid reserves fall below the level required to keep rampant dollarisation in check. Never have they based exchange rate decisions on export competitiveness and there is no reason to suppose they are about to change now.
Conditions that have historically called for an exchange rate devaluation are simply not there today. First, there is an abundant supply of dollars by comparison to the supply of rupees in the market, and the position is only improving. Second, there is no flight into the dollar. Third, the interbank market is virtually shut, with banks told (through silent channels) to finance their clients’ import requirements from their own inflows, while the State Bank aggressively buys these inflows at a steadily appreciating rate, to fuel its own thirst for dollars.
Under these conditions, the REER is about as relevant as the daily weather forecast. There will be no devaluation in the near future, not until their hand is forced by market reality.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Hardening lines
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE battle lines are being drawn over the creation of new provinces, as the two main partners in the ruling coalition experience a democratic reawakening. Both have recently taken to extolling the virtues of democracy — but each with their own spin.
On one side, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari is taking a hard stand against a division of the provinces “imposed by force”. He has warned it might lead to bloodshed. As an alternative, he is pushing the idea of a political reset, which would entail recognising and respecting the mandate given to opposition parties, especially the PTI.
On the other side, various government ministers, mostly from the PML-N, are lecturing anyone who will listen on the merits of a public referendum. Though the controversies that followed the general elections are yet to be resolved, they are arguing, rather earnestly, that holding a nationwide referendum on new provinces is the fairest way forward.
Mr Bhutto-Zardari made an astute observation in his Tuesday speech at the Karachi Press Club: “In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one.” More jarring was his revelation that “up until today, neither the prime minister nor a single member of the cabinet has brought up the issue [of new provinces] with the president of Pakistan or me”.
    
What is one to make of this, considering that several members of the federal cabinet, including the ministers of interior, defence and information, have been making rather forceful public statements on the topic? It suggests the issue is being litigated in the media rather than discussed among the political leadership.
Mr Bhutto-Zardari seemed frustrated with the prime minister’s silence when his ministers seem eager to discuss it. It is also strange that the president, too, has not weighed in.
Perhaps the elders in both parties, the president among them, are testing the waters by letting Mr Bhutto-Zardari and second-tier ministers lead the conversation for now.
    
But the issue will be taken up in some form sooner rather than later, and they cannot wait until the eleventh hour to make their official positions known.
The administrative reconfiguration of an entire country — one that ranks among the most populous in the world — is no ordinary task. It is not merely a question of drawing lines on a map: nearly every branch of the state will need to be restructured around the new configuration, and this cannot be achieved through fiat.
The Constitution already sets out the route: altering a province’s limits requires a constitutional amendment backed by two-thirds of that province’s assembly.
Rather than trading referendums for ultimatums, the political leadership should take the question to parliament and the provincial assemblies, and build consensus there.

title: Predatory medicine
author: none@none.com (Murad Moosa Khan)
content:
“Medicine carries a morality that is destroyed when the emphasis is placed on the bottom line. Unless humanism and professionalism remain, medicine will become just another commodity in life’s marketplace.” — Dr William W. Parmley
MEDICINE has traditionally been regarded as a profession founded on trust, compassion and an ethical commitment to heal. Patients entrust doctors with their bodies, their fears and, often, their lives. This relationship rests on an implicit promise: that medical decisions will be guided by the patient’s best interests. But what happens when the business of medicine begins to take precedence over the practice of medicine?
In his book Predatory Medicine, US cardiologist Jack Vangrow draws attention to an uncomfortable reality: healthcare can become an extractive enterprise in which patients are exploited. He describes how both practitioners and institutions who should be protecting patients, instead exploit patients’ limited medical knowledge and trust.
The commercialisation of medicine may not be inherently unethical. Private hospitals, clinics, labs and pharmaceutical firms have an important role in healthcare delivery. Medical innovation and research require investment, and healthcare professionals deserve fair remuneration. The problem arises when profit becomes the dominant consideration and the patient’s wellbeing becomes secondary.
Healthcare is a rapidly expanding commercial market in a country where millions cannot afford basic treatment.
Predatory medicine describes many practices that lead to profit-making: unnecessary investigations, excessive prescriptions, avoidable surgical procedures, inappropriate hospital admissions, inflated bills and the promotion of expensive treatments when cheaper, equally effective alternatives exist.
The fundamental problem is the profound imbalance of knowledge and power between doctors and patients. Most patients cannot independently assess whether an investigation is necessary, whether a diagnosis is accurate or whether a proposed intervention offers meaningful benefit. They depend on their physician’s integrity and competence. When that trust is exploited, the consequences can be both financial and physical.
Vangrow highlights the culture of professional complicity: doctors who recognise questionable practices but remain silent to protect their careers, professional relationships or financial interests. Predatory medicine, therefore, is not simply about a few unethical practitioners; it becomes embedded in the institutional culture.
Vangrow’s observations are highly relevant for Pakistan, where private healthcare has become a hugely lucrative business, while a chronically underfunded public health system struggles to provide even basic services. The private medical sector continues to grow exponentially, with private hospitals, specialist clinics, diagnostic labs and pharmaceutical firms dominating healthcare delivery.
According to Pakistan’s National Health Accounts 2021-22, total health expenditure stood at approximately Rs1.96 trillion, with the private sector accounting for 52.6 per cent. Much of this expenditure comes directly from household pockets. The World Bank’s latest available data show that out-of-pocket payments accounted for approximately 53pc of Pakistan’s current health expenditure in 2023. These figures illustrate the extent to which healthcare costs are transferred from the state to individual households. They also reveal a stark contradiction: healthcare is a rapidly expanding commercial market in a country where millions cannot afford basic treatment.
Public health expenditure remains around one per cent of GDP, leaving government hospitals chronically under-resourced, overcrowded and struggling with shortages of medicines, equipment and personnel. While wealthier Pakistanis can access private healthcare, the poor have to suffer the indignity of treatment at government facilities, underscoring a deeply unequal healthcare system.
A particular aspect of predatory medicine is to medicalise ordinary social problems, resulting in unnecessary lab tests, polypharmacy and doctor shopping. This is compounded by potential conflicts of interest involving pharmaceutical firms, labs, medical equipment suppliers and healthcare providers.
Pakistan’s regulatory institutions — Provincial Healthcare Commissions (PHCs), PMDC and DRAP — have important responsibilities of licensing, quality assurance, professional conduct and patient safety. However, enforcement remains poor. Regulation must be more effective and independent. PHCs need resources and authority to monitor private hospitals and diagnostic facilities. Transparent disclosure of treatment costs, standardised billing, independent clinical audits and accessible patient complaint mechanisms are required.
Addressing predatory medicine requires more than asking individual doctors to behave ethically. It requires changing the structures and incentives within which healthcare is practised. A functioning, adequately funded public health system is essential not only for providing services to those who cannot afford private treatment but also for preventing the private sector from becoming the only realistic option for millions.
Financial relationships between doctors, pharmaceutical firms, labs and hospitals should be disclosed and appropriately regulated. Clinical decisions must be based on evidence and patient need, not commercial incentives. Medical education must place greater emphasis on professional ethics, the social responsibilities of medicine and the doctor-patient relationship. Being a good doctor is not simply about diagnostic accuracy or technical competence; it is also about recognising vulnerability, avoiding unnecessary interventions and respecting patients’ autonomy.
Healthcare is not like any other commodity and a patient seeking treatment is not an ordinary consumer making a purchase in a competitive marketplace. Illness creates vulnerability, distress, dependence and desperation. The relationship between a doctor and patient cannot be driven by market principles. In Pakistan, the ethical foundations of medical practice receive insufficient attention. We may have internationally accredited hospitals and specialists, yet still fail in our obligation to provide equitable and compassionate care.
The purpose of medicine is to heal, relieve suffering and protect human dignity. When profit displaces these obligations, medicine becomes predatory. We not only need more hospitals and better technology, but also a commitment to the ethics and social responsibility that should define the medical profession.
The writer is professor emeritus of psychiatry, Aga Khan University.

title: Resetting the system
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE issue of administrative restructuring is back on the political agenda. The interior minister has called for a referendum to seek public approval for the creation of new provinces, arguing that the existing system of governance has “collapsed” and needs a fundamental reset.
In recent months, this contentious issue has been discussed at seminars and other public forums, while political leaders have voiced their individual opinions.
The idea of holding a referendum on such a complex issue is apparently being floated to bypass the constitutional process. Coming from the interior minister, the proposal leaves little ambiguity about whose plan it is. Securing parliamentary approval for a referendum may not be difficult in a pliant house. But can a simple “yes” or “no” referendum resolve the intricate and politically sensitive question of creating new administrative units?
There are certainly compelling reasons to restructure the existing provinces to improve governance. But the approach now being pursued is likely to open a Pandora’s box, creating chaos and further aggravating political instability. Several proposals for creating new administrative units may be circulating, but no political party has come forward with a concrete blueprint.
    
While the PPP has rejected any move to divide Sindh or create new administrative units in the province, the ruling PML-N has yet to adopt an official position, although individual ministers have expressed their views.
There has been an intriguing silence on the issue from Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Nawaz Sharif. Not surprisingly, the smaller coalition partners, widely seen as close to the powers that be, have emerged as strong supporters of the restructuring plan, despite its contours remaining unclear.
The question of administrative restructuring cannot be divorced from the broader democratic process. Mr Naqvi, himself a product of a system whose legitimacy remains contested, argues that a referendum is part of democracy. “We all talk about democracy. Parliamentarians represent the people of Pakistan. I request all political parties to consider that most survey reports suggest that new provinces should be created for better governance,” he maintains.
Good governance requires rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable institutions.
Indeed, an elected parliament represents the will of the people and, in a democratic system, is the supreme legislative body mandated to initiate such changes. Yet, in this case, the debate on a major constitutional issue has not begun in parliament but has instead been initiated from outside it. Has there been any meaningful debate on this critical matter in the legislature, however contested its legitimacy?
The interior minister’s appeal to political parties to take note of “survey reports” favouring the creation of new provinces is equally questionable. Opinion polls may offer some indication of public sentiment, but they cannot serve as the basis for constitutional change.
Moreover, we know how limited in scope and reach many such surveys are in Pakistan. Has the minister also taken note of the numerous other surveys reflecting public dissatisfaction with the existing political order?
More importantly, the Constitution clearly lays down the procedure for creating new provinces. The proposal for a referendum appears designed to circumvent these constitutional provisions. The Constitution also prescribes a well-defined procedure for its own amendment. There can be no shortcut to such a fundamental change.
The 18th Amendment provides a useful example. It altered almost one-third of the Constitution, but only after nearly 18 months of intensive deliberations by a multiparty parliamentary committee, which eventually forged a consensus. Why cannot the same democratic and parliamentary process be followed for an issue of such national importance, rather than seeking to resolve it through a referendum?
There is much talk about resetting a system of governance that has supposedly collapsed. There can be little disagreement that the country’s political and governance structures are deeply dysfunctional and require fundamental reform if Pakistan is to move forward. It is odd, however, that the rhetoric of resetting the system comes from those who are themselves equally responsible for its present state.
Governance cannot be improved merely by creating new provinces. It requires, above all, a system founded on the rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable democratic institutions.
Those now championing administrative restructuring and a reset are also responsible for undermining the democratic process and curtailing judicial independence through the 26th and 27th Amendments, further eroding the Constitution’s fundamental principles.
With democratic freedoms increasingly constrained, the country is moving towards authoritarianism. Creating new provinces or redrawing administrative boundaries will do little to improve governance or rescue a collapsing system in such circumstances.
    
Phrases such as “resetting the system” and “referendum” are familiar instruments. Military rulers in the past have used similar language to consolidate their power and legitimise authoritarian rule. This time, too, the signs are hardly reassuring. The exercise looks less like a genuine attempt at reform and more like an effort to salvage a failing system through cosmetic adjustments.
There has also been talk of a 28th Constitutional amendment. While the contours of the proposed amendment remain unclear, indications are that it could further tighten political control while incorporating administrative restructuring into a broader package of changes. This raises serious questions about the real objectives behind the proposed reforms.
There is certainly an urgent need to break with the status quo and restore the democratic process. But that is not the kind of reset Mohsin Naqvi and others appear to be advocating. Neither a proposed referendum nor an impending 28th amendment, pursued outside a genuinely democratic process, is likely to bring political stability.
What Pakistan needs is political stability built on constitutional supremacy, democratic freedoms and strong, independent institutions. Administrative restructuring may well be part of the solution, but it must emerge from an open, inclusive and constitutionally mandated democratic process — not be imposed from outside it.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Not another Yalta
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
WHEN the leaders of the USSR, US and UK gathered at a Crimean resort in Feb 1945 for a weeklong trilateral summit, an extensive agenda awaited them. With the Nazis caught in a pincer movement between the rapidly advancing Red Army and its western allies, the European segment of the world war had entered its endgame. The architecture of peace needed to be sketched out.
Historians still argue about whether Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill conceded too much to Joseph Stalin in delineating ‘spheres of influence’, but it was indisputably a momentous occasion. For better or worse, many of the decisions made at Yalta endured for decades, and some still resonate. No comparable outcome can be imagined from this week’s summit in Shenzhen.
It may well turn out to be little more than a grandiose photo-op. A domineering presence on the global stage has additional appeal for Donald Trump following his domestic humiliation in the midterm elections. Vladimir Putin is inevitably keen to be counted among the ‘Big 3’. By many accounts, Xi Jinping is a reluctant host — perhaps partly because there’s only a vague agenda — “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”, according to Beijing. And he’s naturally wary of Trump’s tendency to grandstand.
The Iran war could figure in discussions at Shenzhen.
The Iran war is expected to figure in the discussions. Some good could possibly come out of that if both Xi and Putin urge the US president to recognise the error of his ways. The conflict is particularly painful for China, given its reliance on Iranian crude.
On the brighter side, China’s oil imports have decreased by design, while exports of its cutting-edge green tech — including solar panels — have substantially increased. Russia, on the other hand, has been delighted by a sanctions reprieve and a surge in petroleum exports, largely due to the transport hiatus in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits. Besides, the US/Israeli conflict helps Russia portray its war against Ukraine as a comparable venture aimed at safeguarding its security. Moscow’s stance makes slightly more sense than the justifications from Washington and Tel Aviv for their aggression against Iran. China sees both wars as huge strategic errors.
Trump seems to believe the Israeli propaganda that Tehran must be prevented from acquiring a nuclear weapon, an outcome that now logically seems likelier than it did before the attacks. That may help to explain why nuclear proliferation was among the topics he hoped to broach at his talks with Xi and Putin. Back in February, his administration turned down Moscow’s proposal to extend a strategic arms reduction treaty, with Trump aspiring for a new deal that includes China, whose expanding nuclear arsenal appears to have alarmed Sinophobes in the US. Given that even its projected stockpiles are a fraction of what’s stored in Russian and American silos, Beijing does not wish to play ball.
Shortly before flying to Asia, Trump noted that denuclearisation, Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite topic, Ukraine” would be up for discussion. Volodymyr Zelensky is alarmed by the possibilities, but a carve-up without Kyiv at the table is hardly likely. China sees Ukraine as a European issue that should be discussed at a more appropriate forum. Trump is disinclined, meanwhile, to bring up the Nvidia fiasco after the US chip-maker’s CEO Jensen Huang was ousted over revelations about an affair with a purported Chinese ‘asset’.
America rem­ains determined to deny China superiority in artificial intelligence throu­­gh curbs on chip exports. But that’s probably another lost battle. Exactly what the three lea­ders will talk about remains to be seen. Climate change won’t be on the agenda. That’s being thrashed out at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, where there’s no official US representation, given the Trump administration’s focus on exacerbating global heating despite rapidly mounting evidence about its catastrophic consequences, from the devastation in Nepal caused by glacier collapse to an estimated 50,000 heatwave deaths in Europe during a scorching summer, not to mention the ecocidal aspect of the Pales­tinian genocide as well as the Iranian, Ukrainian and Sudanese conflicts. Not to mention the ginormous carbon footprint of proliferating US data centres.
As Swedish activist Greta Thunberg accurately spelt it out in Antalya, “The planet is not dying, it is being killed.” And the outgoing UN Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, was equally correct in pointing out: “It’s make or bake time.” He might have erred, though, in comparing fossil fuels to dinosaurs and claiming the latter “did not have a lobby”. They do, and some of its components might be congregating in Shenzhen right now.

title: Rabies elimination
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Aftab Gohar)
content:
IT begins with a fever, a headache and a restlessness that will not settle. Then the patient panics at the sight of water. After days of going from hospital to hospital, the family learns that a dog bite weeks or months earlier, long healed and forgotten, carried rabies. The virus has reached the brain, and there is no cure.
This scene plays out in hospitals across Pakistan every week, yet every such death is preventable. Sindh, where reporting has improved, recorded 285,000 dog bites in 2025 and over 200,000 by September 2026, with at least 41 rabies deaths this year. The Indus Hospital also saw rabies cases from Balochistan, and eight more came through teleconsultation from across the country. Punjab reported more than 1.3 million dog-bite cases between 2021 and March 2026. Estimates put Pakistan’s rabies deaths at 2,000 to 5,000 a year, most of them poor and many of them children.
A study published this year in eBioMedicine, a Lancet journal, which I co-authored with Indus Hospital and Erasmus MC colleagues, shows how widely the virus circulates. We found rabies virus in 64 of 100 severe dog-bite wounds in Karachi, and two-thirds of the patients were children. It covered only severe bites, so it does not mean two in three biting dogs are rabid, but the warning is stark. If this is the picture in a city with the province’s best-equipped bite clinics, it is unlikely to be better elsewhere in Sindh or Pakistan.
Elimination needs action on five fronts. The first is surveillance. Behind every reported case is a grieving family. Much of the recent rise reflects improved surveillance, and the true burden is still hidden. Many families believe the patient is possessed and turn to a shrine, not a hospital; others die in hospital undiagnosed. Surveillance must keep improving, with human rabies and dog bites notifiable at every level, so that reliable data reveals the true burden and where to focus resources. Swabbing bite wounds can also track the virus without catching dogs.
Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility.
The second is awareness. Children, especially boys, often tease street dogs and cannot defend themselves when attacked; peaceful coexistence starts with how we treat community dogs. Every household should know to wash a bite wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then seek immediate treatment at an anti-rabies centre, since washing reduces the virus but does not remove it. These messages belong in school curricula, mosques and the media.
The third is correct treatment. Rabies is almost 100 per cent preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, and in our study nearly 96pc of patients developed protective antibodies. Yet roughly half of the rabies deaths reported at our centres occur in people whose treatment was incomplete or wrongly given. Immunoglobulin remains scarce, and too many patients drop out before finishing the course. Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility, and every doctor and nurse treating bites must be trained to WHO guidelines. The Sindh government’s ongoing rabies campaign deserves credit and, if sustained, can save many lives.
The fourth is mass dog vaccination, because treating people alone will never end rabies. When at least 70pc of dogs are vaccinated year after year, the virus stops circulating. In September 2026, WHO validated Bhutan as the first country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted human rabies.
The fifth is effective dog population management. Uncollected garbage feeds street dogs, which is why katchi abadis have the most dogs and the most bites. Views differ on the best methods, but any approach must be hu­­mane, gu­­i­ded by evidence and international standards, sustained over time, and backed by proper waste management and responsible ownership. Local governments, veterinary services and communities must agree on what works locally and monitor results.
None of this can succeed in isolation. Health, livestock, local government and education departments each hold a piece and must work together under the One Health approach. The federal health minister’s in-principle approval of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework in July 2026 offers real hope. With timely notification, sustained funding and clear, measurable targets, it could become the turning point Pakistan has long awaited, with the media and civil society holding every institution to account.
The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030. Bhutan has shown it can be done. A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.
The writer is technical lead, Rabies Prevention, Management & Training Services at the Indus Hospital & Health Network, Pakistan, and part of the National & Provincial Technical Working Advisory Group on Rabies.

title: Peace prognosis
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
AFGHAN foreign and domestic policies are a curious mix of tribalism, revanchism and ideological confusion that shun human rights and statecraft in favour of support for terrorist groups based on Afghan soil that pose a clear danger to regional peace. Unfortunately, all attempts at positive engagement with the Afghan Taliban by Pakistan as well as regional countries have been scuttled due to Kabul’s lack of willingness to rein in terrorist outfits operating under its benign gaze.
A belief has gained traction amongst the Afghan Taliban that their successful armed struggle against Nato/USA could also be emulated by their ideological comrades like Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM, the TTP etc in pursuit of their political objectives. Rooted in medieval notions of tribal honour and revenge, the regime offers a propitious environment for growth of terror networks. The flow of external funds into the Afghan regime’s coffers has encouraged the obduracy of the Taliban, which continues channelling these funds to its ideological allies, sustaining the vicious cycle of terrorism and crime.
    
Afghanistan is acting as a generous host for terrorist outfits that use its soil to generate economic rents through narco-trafficking, ransom, and smuggling. These groups are confident that their base of operation and sources of income would remain protected under the Taliban. A mere look at the figures showing the funding of this terror haven by the unsuspecting international community indicates why Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remains a threat.
Since August 2021, donors have confirmed paying $8 billion in humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan through various international organisations, with a further $3.78bn committed and $94 million pled­ged. Billions more were reportedly received by the Taliban regime in direct foreign grants. Western capitals remain the biggest financial contributors to Afghanistan.
The Afghan economy is kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.
Afghanistan imports goods worth around $12bn annually against exports of only $1.7bn, leaving an annual trade deficit of $10.3bn. It is intriguing how the Taliban regime is bridging $10.3bn every year. The answer lies in $17.5bn in foreign grants received since 2021, besides billions of dollars earned through narco-trafficking. It is clear evidence of an economy kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.
But the biggest question is: should such a regime that hosts terrorist groups be kept afloat through the largesse of international donors who might soon feel the heat from violent groups based in Afghanistan? If the international community thinks it can wean the Afghan Taliban away from terrorists, it needs to have a look at Pakistan’s 17 sincere attempts through ministers, the national security advisor, special representative, and joint coordination committee interactions, besides internationally mediated parleys in Doha, Istanbul, Riyadh and Urumqi.
The reason for Afghan obstinacy is hubris and ideological narcissism that are pampered through foreign indulgence, despite zero concessions by the Kandahar-based ruling clique on political inclusivity, women’s education and minority rights. Pakistan has tried bilateral channels and has exhausted relevant regional fora like the trilateral group (Pakistan, China and Afghanistan) where in 2023 the Afghan foreign minister agreed to stop the flow of terrorism from Afghan soil.
The Moscow Format, which evolved out of a quadrilateral forum which was abandoned by the US after the Ukraine War, kept pressing the Afghan regime to abide by international counterterrorism obligations till its seventh meeting. However, it failed to elicit a positive response from the Taliban delegation during its eighth iteration at Mos­cow on Oct 5.
    
The Taliban’s reluctance to even acknowledge the need to stop the ac­­tivities of terrorist groups from Afghan soil betrays a mindset that is sympathetic to these violent groups. This should be a clear message to countries like Russia that are giving space to the Taliban regime in pursuit of narrow security goals.
The fact is that all development and connectivity goals like TAPI, Casa-1000, and Trans-Afghan Railway, as well as mines and mineral exploration in Afghanistan, would remain a pipe dream till the time the Afghan Taliban stop sponsoring terrorism.
The proceeds from illegal mining go to support the Taliban’s military infrastructure. Moreover, since 2021, it has established thousands of madressahs against 269 modern schools, replaced 90,000 teachers with around 100,000 Taliban-aligned clerics, abolished 18 university disciplines, rewritten 200-plus subjects and banned 679 textbooks.
Until the Taliban regime gives up its support for terrorism and provides verifiable guarantees to Pakistan, meaningful normalisation, regional connectivity and lasting stability will not materialise.
The writer is a PhD from NUST.

title: Water crisis
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PUNJAB’S looming water crisis should serve as a wake-up call for both federal and provincial policymakers. A new assessment by the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation warns that water demand in the province already exceeds supply across all sectors. Even more alarming is the annual depletion of 5.5bn cubic metres of groundwater. The province needs an additional 10bn cubic metres of usable water every year to bridge the supply-demand gap and sustain its aquifer. This shows the consequences of years of neglect and an approach to water management that has placed little emphasis on conservation. The FAO findings are based on water accounts covering 2012-17 but the trends hold. Punjab’s agricultural economy, expanding cities and growing population are placing increasing pressure on a resource that is already under severe stress.
Agriculture, which accounts for the bulk of freshwater use, must be central to any serious conservation strategy. Much of Punjab still relies on traditional flood irrigation, an inefficient method that results in substantial losses. There is an urgent need to encourage a transition towards water-efficient technologies. This can help farmers produce more with less water. Crop choices also need to reflect local water availability. Furthermore, there is a case for developing smaller, distributed water storage facilities along riverbeds and suitable locations in the riverine belt. Such reservoirs, including off-channel storage and recharge ponds where feasible, could capture surplus flows during periods of high availability for use when supplies fall. This would offer a complementary and potentially cheaper option to large dams, whose construction involves substantial financial, environmental and social costs. Much of the rain that cities receive is channelled into drainage and sewerage systems due to rapid construction and the spread of concrete. Better urban planning must make rainwater harvesting, permeable surfaces, recharge wells and retention ponds integral to new housing schemes and public infrastructure. Cities need investment in systems that capture and store rainwater. Wastewater treatment and reuse, too, should become part of the province’s water strategy. The FAO’s proposal for a provincial water commission similarly deserves serious consideration.

title: Being civil to begin with
author: none@none.com (Jawed Naqvi)
content:
THAT Pakistan is sending a minister to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi on Nov 20 should be applauded even if it’s not clear that this could be the proverbial ice breaker between the perpetually aloof neighbours. It is, however, worth hoping for.
The agenda for a civilisational dialogue should be fun for the participants, although India’s decade-old Hindu revivalist government may drag its feet on the issue. Bilateral ties can still improve despite this handicap. Reports are circulating of cross-border trade also picking up — albeit discreetly — between India and Pakistan in recent days.
Renowned political analyst Trita Parsi used a phrase to describe the options for a low-key US retreat from the war-torn Gulf region, which may be relevant for India-Pakistan ties. Parsi likened Donald Trump’s options for a face-saving pullout from his self-created mess to Swiss cheese. Sanctions on paper and holes inside, like the bubbles within a good Swiss cheese. The US could keep its formal sanctions on the books so the administration can publicly claim it is still maintaining pressure on Tehran. In reality, the enforcement is invisibly relaxed. Which is what might work, if nothing else does, for the South Asian neighbours — an unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities.
Behind the scenes, in Parsi’s version of a workable Gulf resolution, the US gradually loosens its naval blockade and stops aggressively enforcing sanctions. This creates large “holes” in the economic pressure — much like the Swiss cheese — allowing Asian, Middle Eastern, and Gulf countries to resume trading with and investing in Iran without fear of US retaliation. At some opportune moment, even if the currently tense atmosphere results in another catastrophic flare-up, peace would be the only game in town, possibly giving credence to Trita Parsi’s face-saving device.
    
The immediate trigger for the latest round of signalling, if it indeed adds up to some kind of undeclared rapprochement, springs from very practical and commonsensical exigencies that require all neighbours to collectively deal with the huge economic challenges dogging the world. The platform offered by the SCO has been used and abused by both sides in the past to launch verbal attacks on each other. Could the tide have turned?
The agenda at hand for Dr Musadik Malik, Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, representing Pak­is­tan at the meeting could present challenges as well as chances to resolve them. However, the lar­ger theme of a civilisational dialogue that brings all SCO members together may have to confront some predictable handwringing from India.
An unannounced, even surreptitious discarding of different stages of hostilities could work for South Asia.
The idea of civilisation imagines a palpable and unbroken link between the past and the present. In its understanding of India’s past, however, the Hindutva establishment in New Delhi has manufactured demons to comply with a narrow political agenda. Its search for a golden past requires changing names of streets, and identifying, abusing and occasionally lynching the conjured enemy.
Pakistan has been through this motion in the past. That’s when schoolchildren were given controversial ideas about non-Muslims. An instructive moment came when a Muslim journalist from India who accompanied Atal Bihari Vajpayee on his visit to Pakistan in 1978 went with his colleagues to meet his cousins. At the emotional meeting, they also wanted to know discreetly if K.K. Katyal, Raghu Rai and Sumit Chakravarty were Hindu. “But they are just like us,” one cousin reportedly observed after being told of their Hindu identities.
Today many centres in Pakistan are exploring and retrieving old names of their neighbourhoods with a view to restoring their Hindu or other non-Muslim identity. India, with the advent of Narendra Modi, is heading in the opposite direction. Mughal rule is being airbrushed from school curriculum.
If more Indians could travel to Pakistan they would be able to see things similar to what I saw. A few days before the Lahore summit, I travelled with Sushma Swaraj and K.R. Malkani to the fabled Katas Raj Temple abutting the Lahore-Islamabad motorway. Malkani, an atheist, stood there looking amused as Swaraj dipped her hands into the sacred pond thought to have been used by the Pandavas during their exile. The caring way this temple and countless others have been preserved for Indian tourists will make more sense when people travel across the borders.
This is not to say that minorities don’t face prejudice in Pakistan. Pakistani human rights activists have spoken strongly against forcible marriage of Hindu girls. The government has made some laws to deter the phenomenon but its impact is not uniformly felt.
    
The prevalent bigotry on the Indian side finds state support often enough as it assumes the form of homes, mosques and churches being vandalised or bulldozed accompanied by the occasional lynching of individuals from minorities. There seems to be a competition between bigots from both sides.
At the SCO dialogue, a two-day session will centre on civilisational and cultural expression, art and architecture, language and literature, and religious and philosophical traditions. Delegates will also deliberate on filing joint multinational nominations for Unesco World Heritage recognition based on centuries of shared cultural exchange. Much of this will be problematic for the current ruling dispensation in India.
In 2015, it had dubiously rejected a Unesco plan to declare Delhi a World Heritage City encompassing Old Delhi with its Mughal-era icons and British-era Lutyens’ New Delhi.
To conclude, a telling story from the Maldives where Muslim zealots set fire to a Pakistani pavilion during a 2011 Saarc event and India watched the mayhem without a word of camaraderie with Pakistan. The event involved a display of national cultural treasures by Saarc states. Pakistan showcased its Buddhist heritage with tableaux of relics from Moenjodaro’s Indus civilisation. Extremists set fire to the Pakistan pavilion. The SCO dialogue offers as good an occasion as any to make amends to this witless aloofness between the two.
The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.

title: Taxpayers’ burden
author: none@none.com (Mohammad Younus Dagha)
content:
IN challenging times, ordinary citizens and businesses may be called upon to shoulder higher tax burdens to meet the unavoidable costs of maintaining a sovereign state. But citizens should not be expected to bear the burden of costs that are largely avoidable.
When debt servicing consumes 125 per cent of the FBR taxes retained by the federal government, 68.5pc of its total revenues, and nearly three times the defence budget, such an extraordinary burden demands closer scrutiny. Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently?
In Pakistan, where a large proportion of the population comprises practising Muslims, many people prefer to keep their savings in bank accounts that pay no interest. As a result, nearly 40pc of all bank deposits are held in current accounts, on which banks pay no interest. This gives Pakistani banks access to an exceptionally cheap source of funds, which they invest in government securities at exorbitantly high returns.
According to the State Bank of Pakistan, banks paid an average interest rate of just 5.53pc on their total deposits in September 2026, including current accounts that pay no interest. Yet, in October 2026, the government was borrowing through 12-month treasury bills at 12.79pc — a gross difference of 7.26 percentage points.
Is our public debt being managed prudently and efficiently?
A prudent borrower would certainly have sought to negotiate a much narrower margin, perhaps 1-2 percentage points. Yet our government continues to borrow at substantially higher rates, raising serious questions about the management of public debt. Ultimately, taxpayers are asked to bear the cost of such generosity. The burden falls on petrol and diesel consumers paying the Petroleum Development Levy, as well as investors paying effective income tax rates of 50-60pc.
High returns on relatively low-risk government securities have encouraged banks to attract more low-cost deposits, particularly current accounts. By June 2026, these accounts held Rs15.3 trillion, nearly 40pc of total deposits, up from 37pc a year earlier. SBP confirms that the Rs3.67tn increase in deposits during the first half of 2026 came mainly from current accounts.
While much of Pakistan’s productive economy has struggled, bank deposits have tripled from Rs13.35tn in December 2018 to nearly Rs41tn in September 2026. But where has this enormous pool of savings gone? Into new industries, businesses and jobs, or increasingly into high-yield government securities, earning banks substantial returns at taxpayers’ expense?
According to SBP, commercial banks held Rs40.36tn in government securities in September 2026. Applying the prevailing gross interest-rate differential of 7.26 percentage points to these holdings gives an estimated annualised differential of approximately Rs2.93tn.
If government borrowing rates were limited to 1-2 percentage points above banks’ average deposit cost, the estimated annualised gross savings could reach Rs2,100-2,500 billion, subject to debt maturities and repricing. Even part of these savings could ease the lives of millions of households and thousands of struggling entrepreneurs by reducing the Petroleum Development Levy, multiple taxes on energy bills, and high income tax rates on salaries and businesses.
Such a policy would also reduce SBP’s annual interest earnings by approximately Rs118bn, which would be just a fraction of the overall savings.
What needs to be done?
The government should introduce a law that limits the interest paid to commercial banks on government securities to a reasonable 1-2 percentage points above what banks pay their depositors on average. The implementation process should ensure that monetary policy, government borrowing operations and financial stability are not disrupted.
In order to bring transparency into debt management operations, the law should require the Ministry of Finance and SBP to publish quarterly reports showing how much the government borrows from banks and other investors, the interest it pays, and the cost of funds to banks. These reports should also disclose how much the government actually saves through lower borrowing costs.
The potential annual savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, once realised, should be passed on to taxpayers and businesses that have long borne the burden of excessive taxation, rather than being absorbed by increased government expenditure. The priority should be to reduce the Petroleum Development Levy and General Sales Tax on electricity bills, thereby lowering fuel and transport costs, easing the cost of living and production, and reducing inflationary pressures. The government should also double the annual income-tax exemption threshold from Rs600,000 to Rs1.2 million, providing much-needed relief to salaried individuals and low-income taxpayers.
The government should also restore the Final Tax Regime for exporters, making tax deducted from export proceeds their final income tax liability, even if the rate remains 2pc. This would simplify taxation, eliminate uncertainty and improve the competitiveness of Pakistani exporters by bringing their tax treatment closer to that of competitors in peer economies.
Equally important is the complete abolition of the super tax, which reportedly generates around Rs400-500bn annually, but has become a major deterrent to new investment. The highest effective income tax rate on corporate, business and other incomes should be capped at 35pc, making Pakistan more attractive to investors while leaving greater disposable income available for savings, consumption and investment.
Many such measures could be financed through the proposed annual debt-servicing savings of Rs2,100-2,500bn, provided the government pursues the necessary reforms with determination and ensures that the resulting fiscal space is used to reduce the tax burden rather than expand public expenditure. These measures would provide a much-needed stimulus to economic growth, encourage investment and job creation, and help alleviate poverty, which has become one of the country’s most pressing challenges.
Reviving economic growth requires reducing the excessive tax burden on ordinary citizens and businesses — a burden that stifles investment, discourages enterprise and holds back economic activity.
The writer is former federal finance secretary and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council.
